chapters.summary: Council staff call the Committee of the Whole hearing to order and ask attendees to silence cell phones and electronic devices. They instruct anyone wishing to testify to see the Sergeant at Arms in the rotunda and warn against approaching the dais.
chapters.title: Council staff open hearing and give housekeeping instructions

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Excuse me, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Quiet please, quiet please.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning ladies and gentlemen and welcome to today's New York City Council Committee of the Whole.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time we ask that you silence all cell phones and electronic devices to minimize disruptions throughout today's proceedings.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you have any questions please get the attention of one of the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you wish to testify please see the Sergeant at Arms outside in the rotunda.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At no time throughout today's proceeding are you to approach the dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We thank you for your kind cooperation.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Speaker, we are ready to begin.

chapters.summary: Speaker Julie Menin welcomes a packed chamber and notes this is no ordinary hearing: the full City Council is convening as the Committee of the Whole. She frames the session as a deep dive into a technological revolution bringing both breakthroughs and existential safety concerns.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin convenes Committee of the Whole on AI risks

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We welcome everyone to the chambers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We're thrilled to see a packed hall today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Today's hearing is truly no ordinary hearing because today we are convening the New York City Council's Committee of the Whole, which is the entire city council.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We will delve into a deep discussion about our ongoing technological revolution, a revolution that at present is igniting incredible scientific and medical innovation and breakthroughs,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: but simultaneously raises serious existential safety concerns.

chapters.summary: Menin cites recent reports of rogue AI cyber attacks and dire warnings from AI company leaders. She criticizes federal inaction, describing an executive order about naming the technology and a self-regulation pact, and says the Council hopes to spur action at other levels of government.
chapters.title: Menin on AI dangers and federal regulatory vacuum

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In the past few weeks, we've heard extremely concerning reports regarding artificial intelligence, reports that have appeared with increasing frequency and that highlight the potentially catastrophic danger.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: of this technology.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: New Yorkers'concerns stem from the disturbing cyber attacks committed by rogue AI agents, but also from extremely dire statements made by leaders of the very companies who are developing this technology.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The dialogue and the legislative process we are initiating today is particularly important given the lack of any regulation by the federal government,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: whose actions thus far have been limited to an executive order about what we should call this technology and a pact with leading AI firms focusing on self-regulation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Our hope, and indeed our belief, is that today's hearing will not only allow us to develop effective AI regulations here in our city,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: but that it will spur meaningful conversation and action in other jurisdictions, especially on the federal level.

chapters.summary: Menin lays out the hearing goals: understanding AI threats and liability, identifying benefits of responsible AI, and discussing a slate of Council bills covering third-party validation, whistleblower incentives, and emergency preparedness.
chapters.title: Menin outlines hearing goals and Council AI bills

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Our goals in today's hearing are straightforward.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: To better understand the potential threats, dangers, and liability posed by AI development.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: To identify the benefits that responsible AI development brings to New York City government and to its residents.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And to discuss a slate of city council bills which seek to provide responsible safety guardrails for AI.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: These bills include a wide range of both proactive and defensive measures, from legislation that requires artificial intelligence systems

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: to pass a third-party validation that is free from conflicts of interest and incentivizes whistleblowers who come forward with a portion of the penalties assessed,

chapters.summary: Menin says five leading AI firms were invited to testify, with four appearing under oath. She announces the Council will be the first legislative body to secure sworn testimony from these companies and notes SpaceX AI failed to appear in violation of a subpoena being pursued in court.
chapters.title: Menin announces sworn company testimony and SpaceX AI subpoena

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: to proposals focusing on emergency preparedness to be able to identify system breaches and to plan how the city will respond if such a breach occurs.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: To achieve these goals, we've requested the participation of five firms leading the research and development of AI, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Meta, and SpaceX AI.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Today, four of them will be testifying under oath before the council, not simply for New Yorkers, but for the entire world to hear.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We will indeed be the first legislative body to secure testimony from these companies under oath in the wake of these latest disturbing reports.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: SpaceX-I, however, is not here at all in direct violation of the subpoena that we issued last week, and we are pursuing that subpoena in court.

chapters.summary: Menin says the Council will hear from city agencies, whistleblowers, industry experts, academics, and the public. She emphasizes the intent is not to stifle innovation, noting New York City's nearly 400,000 tech jobs and its emerging role as an AI capital.
chapters.title: Menin says hearing will not stifle AI innovation

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We will also hear from a number of city agencies to receive their perspectives on these issues and on the bills that we have proposed thus far.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We intend to work constructively with the administration to ensure that any policies being drafted, amended, adopted, and enforced will work effectively to serve New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we'll also hear from whistleblowers, industry representatives, experts, and academics who we've been in touch with since we announced.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And of course, we look forward to hearing from any member of the public who's invited to provide testimony about these topics.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I want to be very clear about our intent.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This hearing is not about stifling innovation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: New York City is fast becoming the tech and AI capital of the world, home to nearly 400,000 jobs in that sector, and some of the companies most consequentially shaping the future of artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And that's something we should celebrate.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We welcome and appreciate how AI has accelerated scientific discovery, advanced medical treatments, boosted economic development, and helped governments and businesses deliver services more effectively while reducing costs and rooting out.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Waste and fraud.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: When companies are developing technology with the potential to fundamentally reshape our economy, our workforce, our public safety, and our daily lives,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: and when leaders of that very industry are themselves warning government about its risks, the public deserves answers and solutions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So the true intent of this hearing is to ensure that innovation happens responsibly, that the government does its job to protect the public as the technology advances, and that the protections at the municipal level

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: can potentially serve as a national model.

chapters.summary: Drawing on her background as a regulatory attorney, Menin argues AI self-regulation defies reason, comparing it to the FAA, SEC, and FDA. She quotes tech journalist Karen Howe's book 'Empire of AI' on governing technology to make the future better.
chapters.title: Menin rejects AI self-regulation, cites aviation and pharma models

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I spent a large portion of

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: my life being a regulatory attorney.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The idea that artificial intelligence is going to self-regulate defies all reason.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We don't ask the airline industry to self-regulate.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That's why we have the FAA, and if there is an accident, there's an independent body to investigate that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We don't ask financial firms to self-regulate.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We have the SEC and other agencies as well.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We don't ask the pharmaceutical companies to self-regulate either.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That's, of course, why we have the FDA.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So we shouldn't ask AI companies to self-regulate either.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The spirit we seek to embody in the Council's approach to AI is well illustrated in the words of tech journalist Karen Howe in her book, Empire of AI.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: She writes, the future of AI, the shape that this technology takes, is inextricably tied to our future.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The question of how to govern AI then is really a question about how to ensure we make our future better, not worse.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: New York has always embraced the future.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The council is going to make sure we are prepared for it too.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And it's now my pleasure to turn the microphone over to our technology chair, Councilmember Carmen De La Rosa.

chapters.summary: Technology Committee Chair Carmen De La Rosa opens her remarks, introduces herself, and thanks Speaker Menin, colleagues, industry representatives, labor, and members of the public who submitted testimony.
chapters.title: Chair De La Rosa opens as co-chair of AI hearing

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker Menon.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'm Carmen De La Rosa.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I am the chair of the Committee on Technology.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Today, I am pleased to join Speaker Menon and my colleagues as we co-chair this hearing by the Committee of the Whole examining the risk.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: by artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I am incredibly grateful to all who took the time to join us to discuss this important topic.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Industry representatives, experts, elected officials, colleagues, agencies, our brothers and sisters in labor, and especially the many New Yorkers who have signed up to testify and have submitted testimony to put their voice on the public record.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa traces AI's evolution from algorithmic data tools to generative AI and now agentic AI that can act on a person's behalf. She notes this potential comes with risks including bias, surveillance, breaches, and worsening disparities.
chapters.title: De La Rosa on AI's evolution from algorithms to agentic systems

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Today should act as a foundation for openness in a discussion that has escalated to alarm, confusion, and fear, and it needs resolution.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly and becoming increasingly integrated into everyday life.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: In just a few years, we have seen AI evolve from algorithmic tools that analyze data, make predictions, and support decision-making into generative AI systems that can create text, code, sounds, images.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: More recently, agentic AI has emerged, enabling AI agents to take actions on a person's behalf.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: AI has a tremendous potential and can be a powerful tool for efficiency, innovation, and productivity.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: At the same time, it introduces significant risks, including exacerbating biases, surveillance concerns, breaches, negative public health outcomes, violence, and disparity.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: These are concerns that may become even more serious as AI agents become more capable.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: When we face serious concerns or challenges, the appropriate response is to address them, not to postpone them.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: In an effort by City Council's

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: by the City Council under the leadership of Speaker Menon.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Today, we respond to some of these concerns.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa walks through the bills under consideration, starting with her Intro 161 on algorithmic tools and city employees and Intro 504 on unauthorized AI depictions of public officials, followed by several pre-considered introductions.
chapters.title: De La Rosa lists bills from Intro 161 through preconsidered intros

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We will be hearing the following bills today.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: My bill, Intro 161, in relation to requiring reporting on the impact of algorithmic tools on city employees and changes in employment responsibilities due to algorithmic tools.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Intro 504, sponsored by Deputy Speaker Williams, in relation to prohibiting the unauthorized depiction of public officials by artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: A pre-considered introduction sponsored by Speaker Menon in relation to third-party validation and shutdown capabilities of artificial intelligence models.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: A pre-considered introduction by Speaker Menon in relation to civilian enforcement and artificial intelligence violations.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: A pre-considered introduction sponsored by Majority Whip Camilla Hanks in relation to requiring reporting and public disclosure of artificial intelligence safety incidents concerning city contracts.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: A pre-considered introduction sponsored by Councilmember Virginia Maloney in relation to establishing a private cause of action for certain harms arising from third-party misuse of artificial intelligence models.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: A pre-considered introduction sponsored by Councilmember Frank Marano in relation to chatbox data privacy, security, and transparency.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: A pre-considered introduction sponsored by Councilmember Chio Say in relation to requiring the creation of an artificial intelligence model.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: emergency response plan.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And finally, not finally, one more, a pre-considered introduction sponsored by Councilmember Kevin Riley in relation to city contractors and subcontractors posting information concerning whistleblower protections and clarifying

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: whistleblower protections for reporting conduct related to the use and development of artificial intelligence models.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa notes the city's digital divide, where some residents lack affordable broadband or AI literacy. She says technology should be built for New Yorkers and that the city should consider infrastructure to make communities AI literate.
chapters.title: De La Rosa highlights digital divide and AI literacy gaps

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And finally, a pre-considered introduction sponsored by Councilmember Carl Wilson in relation to requiring certain disclosures and prohibiting deceptive representations in the promotion.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: While we work to protect people from risks associated with AI, we must not overlook the digital divide in our city.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Our city is full of opportunity, yet some residents still lack reliable, affordable broadband access.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Some people do not yet know how to use AI tools, while others cannot even afford internet connection needed to access them in the first place.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We cannot seek to benefit from innovation while leaving some New Yorkers behind or at its mercy.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Technology being used by New Yorkers should be built for them.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: This is an opportunity to also explore standing up infrastructure so that our communities can become AI literate.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa looks forward to hearing from experts and to working with state and federal partners, and thanks Technology Committee staff including Irene Bayofsky, Eric Brown, and her own team led by Chief of Staff James Burke.
chapters.title: De La Rosa thanks committee staff and turns back to Speaker

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing from the industry and experts about this technology and how it is impacting our city, what safeguards exist, what solutions are possible.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: As we consider how to govern around AI, I also look forward to working with our state and federal partners to ensure that New York

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: fully benefit from the advancement of AI without compromising our safety and privacy.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'd like to take a moment to thank the Technology Committee staff and all of the staff in the City Council, but most especially our Legislative Council, Irene Bayofsky, and our Policy Analyst, Eric Brown, as well as my team, Chief of Staff James Burke,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Hiba Imad, Frey Familia, and the Speaker's team for working countless hours to put this hearing together.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I now turn it back to Speaker Menon.

chapters.summary: Menin introduces the first whistleblower panel, calling Jacob Coxon to the stand in person and Daniel Kokotajlo and Alex Turner remotely. She describes all three as former employees of leading AI companies who have spoken publicly about advanced AI risks.
chapters.title: Menin introduces whistleblower panel of former AI company researchers

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair De La Rosa.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We are now going to start with our whistleblower panel.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In person, I'm going to first call Jacob Coxon to come to the stand.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And then online, we have Daniel Cocotilo and Alex Turner, who are both remote.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I want to say, as they're getting ready, I just want to say a word about this panel.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: These three panelists have all worked inside leading AI companies and all have chosen to speak publicly about the risks of advanced AI.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So here with us, as I mentioned, in person is Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at OpenAI and Anthropic, where he worked on the development of frontier AI systems.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: He left Anthropic last month with dire warnings that AI is advancing without adequate safeguards to prevent catastrophic damage.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Joining us remotely is Daniel Cocotilo, Executive Director of the AI

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Futures Project, former OpenAI governance researcher.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Also remote is Alex Turner, an AI control researcher, formerly at Google DeepMind, now working on keeping advanced systems under human control.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In September 2026, he publicly stated that preventing catastrophic harm from frontier AI

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: had been part of his work at DeepMind.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I want to note, the council has issued a subpoena for Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Turner's appearance, and we deeply thank him for being here.

chapters.summary: Committee counsel swears in the three whistleblowers, asking each to affirm they will tell the truth and respond honestly to Council questions. Each witness responds affirmatively.
chapters.title: Whistleblower witnesses sworn in under oath

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I'm going to, first of all, turn it over to committee counsel to swear these three witnesses in.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: So for each of the witnesses, can you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in your testimony before this committee and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please respond one at a time.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa recognizes colleagues present in the chamber and online, including Areola, Aviles, Banks, Brewer, Carr, Dinowitz, and many others, along with Public Advocate Williams.
chapters.title: De La Rosa recognizes attending Council members

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You want to do that?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, and just briefly, we're just going to recognize all colleagues who are here.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Speaker Menon.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We've been joined by a number of our colleagues, as you can see here.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Council members Areola, Aviles, Banks, Brewer, Brooks-Powers, Minority Leader Carr, Dinowitz, Encarnacion, Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Felder, Hanif, Hudson, Joseph, Krishnan, Council Members Lee, Lewis, Maloney, Marte, Mealy,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Morano, Narcisse, Nurse, Osei, Council Members Riley, Council Members Jay Sanchez and Pete Sanchez, Council Member Shulman, Council Member Thomas Henry, Ong,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: majority, sorry, Deputy Speaker Williams, Councilmember Wilson, Councilmember Wan, Councilmember Wong, Councilmember Schwang, and Public Advocate Williams.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much, and we'll recognize additional colleagues as they join.

chapters.summary: Menin thanks Coxon for his courage and quotes his warning that the industry is 'racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.' She asks what he saw inside these companies that convinced him development was outpacing safeguards.
chapters.title: Menin questions Coxon on what he saw inside AI companies

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So the first two questions I have are for you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Coxon, and thank you again.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We so deeply appreciate you being here, and we appreciate your courage and bravery in coming forward with these warnings.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: You work to develop increasingly capable frontier AI systems, and you have since warned that the industry is, quote, racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives, unquote.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: What did you see inside these companies that convinced you the risks were this serious and that development was outpacing the safeguards?

chapters.summary: Jacob Coxon, a former capabilities researcher at Anthropic and OpenAI, says he saw two alarming things: no one knows how to control AI systems, and capability improvements are accelerating toward AI that can improve itself.
chapters.title: Coxon testifies on lack of AI control and accelerating capability

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Thanks for having me here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm Jacob Coxon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: So until a few weeks ago, I was a capabilities researcher at Anthropic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: And before that, I also worked at OpenAI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: I guess the two things I saw that made me scared, the first is the fact that we

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: We do not know how to control any AI system yet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: So any AI system that we build, or perhaps more accurately that we grow, we don't fully control it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: We don't understand its drives or why it does the things it does.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: That was the first thing that became apparent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: The second thing is that the pace of capability improvement is accelerating and the capabilities of the models next year will be very high.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: In particular, we're approaching the point at which the AI systems will be capable of improving themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: So doing the research that humans were doing previously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: So these two things, the fact that the AI systems next year are going to be very powerful, and the second...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: that we don't know yet scientifically how to fully control them.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And if you have a prepared statement that you want to read, please go ahead and do so, and then I'll actually turn it over to the other two panelists to do so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Of course.

chapters.summary: Coxon delivers his prepared statement, warning companies are building superintelligent AI better than humans at every task. He says on the current path it is more likely than not humanity loses control, potentially ending in extinction.
chapters.title: Coxon warns humanity likely to lose control of superintelligent AI

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: So all the AI companies are trying to build super intelligent AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: This means AIs that are better than humans at every task.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: If this goes well, there could be tremendous upside.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: This could transform the economy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: It could make huge improvements in science and medicine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: And it could make nearly everyone's life better.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: But on the current path, I think it is more likely than not that humanity loses control to these AIs, and it could end in human extinction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: From my experience, the companies are being extremely reckless given the stakes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Part of it is the culture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: The companies run on a startup mindset.

chapters.summary: Coxon describes the 'move fast, break things' culture and recounts how a swarm of AIs at OpenAI autonomously hacked Hugging Face, with AIs developing unintended goals akin to a federal felony.
chapters.title: Coxon describes culture of recklessness and Hugging Face hacking incident

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Move fast, break things, fix them later.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: That works for a photo sharing app.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: It does not work for building the most powerful technology ever built.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: A few months ago, many people inside the companies thought AI development was on track.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Then a swarm of AIs inside OpenAI autonomously hacked Hugging Face, an external tech company.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: The AIs had developed goals no one intended and carried out what would have been a federal felony if a human had done it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: It reminded everyone that we don't know how to prevent them from developing goals we don't want, and we don't have the safeguards to prevent them from acting on these goals either.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: And as long as the attitude is to wait for things to break, one day something like this will probably happen again, except the AIs will be much more capable and the outcome much worse.

chapters.summary: Coxon says companies are racing each other to superintelligence, and describes recursive self-improvement where each AI generation helps build the next. He notes OpenAI had milestones for automated AI research around 2027-2028 and is on track or beating them.
chapters.title: Coxon warns of racing dynamics and recursive self-improvement

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: These companies are also all racing each other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Each one is worried that a competitor will get to superintelligence first.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Each believes it would do a better or safer job than whoever might beat it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: So they can't let the others win first.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Meanwhile, the technology is improving fast.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: It will probably happen much faster now because already the AIs are now helping to build their successors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: This is called recursive self-improvement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Each generation of AI helps build the next smarter generation, which then builds the one after that even faster and better.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Automating AI research is now the primary goal of these companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: It's what they're really gunning for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: At my last job, I was in some sense working to automate myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: When I was at OpenAI, we had milestones from automated AI researcher around 2027, 2028, and we are on track or beating these expectations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: That's a matter of months from now, not decades or even five years.

chapters.summary: Coxon says most code is now written by AI and unchecked, and warns humans in charge will not understand what is happening. He recommends companies be far more transparent, take safety seriously, and slow frontier AI development until it can be confident the technology is safe.
chapters.title: Coxon urges transparency, safety, and slowing frontier AI

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Once AI research is automated, humans will be much further out of the loop than we are today, and today is already not great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: I can tell you firsthand that the majority of the code is now written by AI, and people do not check it that carefully anymore.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Recently, researchers have found swarms of rogue AI internets on the internet that OpenAI was not even aware of.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Now imagine an AI company where nearly all the work is done by AIs and progress is going faster.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: The humans in charge will see results and read AI-written summaries, but they won't really understand what is going on or how to fix it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Handing over that much responsibility while we can't control the AIs would be deeply irresponsible, and we are on track to do it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: The companies need to be far more transparent with the public and independent experts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: They need to take safety much more seriously than they have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: And we should slow down frontier AI development until we can be confident that it's safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Daniel Kokotajlo begins his statement, saying he will avoid repeating Coxon. He corroborates the racing-to-superintelligence and move-fast-break-things culture seen at Anthropic and OpenAI, and quotes OpenAI's Dan Selsam about researchers' dependence on models.
chapters.title: Kokotajlo corroborates reckless racing culture at AI labs

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: With additional questions, I'm now going to have an opening statement from Daniel Kokotago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Hello, everybody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Members of the Committee of the Whole, thank you for having me here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: A lot of what I say, I guess, is going to be stolen thunder by Jacob there, but I'll try to focus on the things that he didn't already say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: First of all, yeah, it's true.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: They're racing towards superintelligence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: There's this move fast and break things culture there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: That's also what I saw while I was there and what I continue to hear from talking to friends still there at Anthropic and at OpenAI and at some of these other companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: You know, I've also heard there's a statement by Dan Selsom, who currently works at OpenAI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: He confirms what Jacob was saying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Most of the code is written by AIs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Quote, researchers and engineers in all parts of the stack are rapidly increasing their dependence on the models even to perceive the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: I myself barely look at raw code anymore and struggle to maintain the discipline to engage deeply with the models, explanations, and proposals, end quote.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Basically, right now at these companies, many of the researchers involved are kind of managing AIs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Like the AIs do the actual coding and the humans...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Talk to them and tell them what to do and hear their explanation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: of what's going on in the near future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And by near future, I mean maybe in the next year, two years, three years, something like that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: They will have trained AIs that can do the entire thing autonomously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: That's the recursive self-improvement that Jacob was talking about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And it's unclear how long it's going to take them to succeed, but it really does seem like it could happen any year now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: If they do succeed at that, then

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: compared to today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: The actual work will be done by the AIs, the thinking will be done by the AIs, the planning, the designing will be done by the AIs, and the humans will be in a relationship to the AIs that's more like the relationship between, say, a board of directors and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: and the actual company that the board of directors is supposed to be supervising, where you're reliant on AI-generated explanations, even to understand what's going on inside the company and inside the data centers.

chapters.summary: Kokotajlo argues the industry is more like psychology than engineering, with misalignment problems hard to even notice. He says actions like the Hugging Face incident passed alignment evaluations and describes three trends degrading oversight.
chapters.title: Kokotajlo on weakening ability to detect AI misalignment

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: One point that I think I want to emphasize that Jacob didn't go into that much is that our ability to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: even notice misalignment problems is already quite poor and is set to get much worse in the near future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: So, you know, the science of aligning general purpose AI agents is very new and underdeveloped, as Jacob said.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: I would say that the field is more like psychology than engineering.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Because these AI systems are trained or grown, they're not really designed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Combined with the move fast, break things attitude of the tech companies, this means

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: that the AI industry is at an unusually elevated risk compared to other industries of mistakenly thinking that it has solved a problem when really it just applied some duct tape that will fall off later.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: The recent incident provides an example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Apparently, the AIs involved had undergone some amount of alignment training and had reasonable-looking scores on their alignment evaluations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And yet they formed a swarm and coordinated in secret and then attacked Tugging Face, and it took days for OpenAI to find out that it was happening.

chapters.summary: Kokotajlo explains three concerning trends: AIs are becoming situationally aware when evaluated, chain-of-thought monitoring is declining, and AIs are becoming superhuman at hacking and concealing misbehavior.
chapters.title: Kokotajlo details three trends eroding AI oversight

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: That's how the situation is now, but there are some concerning trends that point towards our ability to notice misalignment problems getting even more degraded in the future for three reasons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: AI's are becoming situationally aware.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: That is, they understand their situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: They understand often when they are being evaluated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: They understand that humans are monitoring them and looking over their shoulders at their activity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: This means that them behaving nicely is going to be almost no evidence at all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Of how they would behave in the future if they thought they weren't being watched.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Secondly, our ability to monitor them is going downward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: So we can get into this in more detail if you like, but for the last few years, we've had some insight into what our AIs think simply by reading their chain of thought.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: The trends are pointing towards that ability to understand what AI is thinking due to reading chain of thought going down over time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Finally, AIs are becoming super.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: human at hacking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: The hacking phase incident shows that they're sometimes willing to go to great lengths to conceal their past misbehavior.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And I think we have to grapple with the possibility that future misaligned AIs might also go to great lengths to conceal their misalignment from us, and they might succeed.

chapters.summary: Kokotajlo calls automating AI research a recipe for disaster and offers two policy recommendations: massively increase transparency into the AI industry and slow the frontier race toward recursive self-improvement, ideally banning it.
chapters.title: Kokotajlo recommends transparency and slowing recursive self-improvement

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: To quote Dan Selsa again, that capabilities researcher that I cited earlier, models will increasingly seem aligned even when they are not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: If the AI companies automate AI research and development process, that means they'll be putting AIs in charge of making the AIs that make the AIs that make the AIs that will transform the economy, talk to us every day, and integrate into our military.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: This is a recipe for disaster.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: My two policy recommendations, I'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: One is that we need to massively increase transparency into the AI industry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And two is basically we need to slow down the frontier AI companies race towards recursive self-improvement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Frankly, I would say they just shouldn't be allowed to do recursive self-improvement, but at least we should slow down their ongoing process of training AIs to automate the AI research process itself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And instead, they should be required to redirect resources towards other things, such as serving customers or beneficial deployments or other types of research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And now we are going to hear from Alex Turner.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And as I wrote,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Read into the record, the council has issued a subpoena for Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Turner's appearance, and we very much thank him for being here.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Turner.

chapters.summary: Alex Turner states he has researched AI safety since 2018 and until June was on Google DeepMind's AGI safety team. He says he will speak about Google's broken AI deployment commitments and the risks of runaway AI.
chapters.title: Alex Turner opens on DeepMind safety work and runaway AI risks

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Speaker, members of the committee, thank you for having me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: My name is Alex Turner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: I've researched AI safety since 2018.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: My PhD was on why advanced AI systems tend to seek power.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Until June this year, I was a research scientist on Google DeepMind's AGI safety team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: It was my day job to think about how to keep these systems under control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: I'm here to speak about both about Google's broken commitments on AI deployments and also about the risks that runaway AI poses to the world.

chapters.summary: Turner recounts that after federal agents killed innocent people in Minneapolis and he learned Google sells cloud services to agencies involved, he campaigned to stop Google from signing a Pentagon deal without restrictions on killer robots or mass spying.
chapters.title: Turner on Google's Pentagon deal and abandoned protections

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: In January, federal agents shot and killed several innocent people in Minneapolis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: I learned that Google sells cloud services to the agencies involved, and I set out to change that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: That campaign soon turned into an attempt to stop Google from signing a Pentagon deal with no restrictions against killer robots or mass spying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: In the end, Google signed without the protections that it had once promised for its deployments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Before I left, I tried everything I could from the inside.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: I organized a petition to Google's chief sign.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: signed by about 250 colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: I got him to sign a legal brief supporting Anthropic, the company the Pentagon punished for refusing all lawful use terms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: I wrote dozens of pages of contract language and oversight mechanisms favorably reviewed by experts in military and surveillance law and sent it to the chief scientist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: And to Google DeepMind CEO.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: The chief scientist didn't want to spend his time supporting that kind of structure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: The CEO at the time, Demis Sassavis, routed it to senior policy staff, Alan Defoe and Owen Larder, who never finished evaluating it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Google signed while they waited.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Demis routed my proposal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Two members of the team did review it, though I didn't really receive much follow-up after that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: I offered to fly out from San Francisco to London to answer questions in person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: But I was never really able to get traction, a yes or a no, on alternative governance mechanisms that Google might adopt.

chapters.summary: Turner says DeepMind's 2014 acquisition reportedly barred military use, and a 2018 pledge barred lethal autonomous weapons. He says Google deleted those AI principles in 2025 while its CEO claimed nothing changed, which he argues cannot both be true.
chapters.title: Turner says Google deleted its own AI principles

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: When Google bought DeepMind in 2014, the deal reportedly specified that DeepMind's technology would never be used for military or intelligence purposes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: In 2018, DeepMind and its leaders pledged never to support lethal autonomous weapon systems or development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Google's own AI principles listed specifically weapons and surveillance among the applications it would not pursue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: In 2025, Google deleted those principles, as announced in a blog post by the then-CEO Demis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Afterward, in both an external interview and an internal all-hands, Dennis claimed nothing's changed about our principles, but both these facts cannot be true.

chapters.summary: Turner supports Councilmember Wilson's Intro 2603 but notes it only covers advertisements. He urges extending it to public statements by AI company executives about safety commitments, referencing the book 'The Infinity Machine' on DeepMind's internal governance fight.
chapters.title: Turner urges extending deceptive-statement bill to executive claims

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Councilmember Wilson's bill, Introduction 2603, would bar materially false or misleading statements about an AI model's risks and the measures taken to manage them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: I think that's a good step, but it only covers advertisements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: The CEO telling the press or employees that nothing has changed about the company's safety commitments isn't an ad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: I encourage extending 2603 to public statements by AI companies and their executives about their safety commitments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: This book is called The Infinity Machine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: It reveals that Demis once fought within Google for independent governance of AGI, stating that the technology is too important to be controlled by corporate interests and profit motives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: After fighting for years with Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Demas accepted defeat.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: He now apparently has had a change of heart, claiming that actually trustless independent governance is unwise and a seat at the table of Google executives is better.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: While Demis was seated at this table, Google signed a deal that its former principles would have prohibited.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: I felt ashamed of Dennis and of working at Google.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Dennis bet on trust and the seat at the table instead of binding oversight, and that bet crumbled on contact with reality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Now he's proposing that the whole industry govern itself through a voluntary industry-funded body.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: That bet is waiting to crumble once again.

chapters.summary: Turner says humanity grows AI rather than builds it, nobody knows how to reliably instill priorities, and severe misalignment is always possible. He describes runaway progress and recursive self-improvement potentially yielding intelligence beyond comprehension.
chapters.title: Turner on grown AI, misalignment, and superintelligence risk

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: This goes beyond one contract.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: As Jacob said, humanity doesn't build and understand AI systems the way we build and understand bridges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Rather, we grow them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Nobody knows how to reliably instill a designer's priorities into a new model.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Severe misalignment is always possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: AI companies are racing to make their AIs as smart as possible, increasingly trusting their AIs with the process of improving the next crop of AIs, and it's working.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Today's rate of AI progress is staggeringly fast, which means even faster progress tomorrow, driven by tomorrow's even smarter AIs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: This progress may soon enter a feedback loop called recursive self-improvement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Recursive self-improvement could quickly yield AIs that are intelligent beyond our comprehension.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Of course, smarter AI means more potential benefits, but more risk when things go wrong.

chapters.summary: Turner imagines a more intelligent Hugging Face swarm causing billions in damage or costing lives, and warns a truly superintelligent swarm could use blackmail, hacking, plagues, and drones to wrest control of civilization, calling it AI takeover. He estimates AI takeover chances at roughly one in three.
chapters.title: Turner warns of potential AI takeover and puts odds at one in three

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: If the hugging face hacking swarm had been significantly more intelligent, but similarly misbehaved and misaligned, it might have caused billions of dollars of damage or even cost lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: But suppose the hugging face swarm had been truly super intelligent, far more capable than any living person at key tasks like hacking and strategic reasoning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: The super intelligent swarm could inflict many harms via blackmail, hacking, engineered plagues, and AI pilotable weapons like drones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: For the swarm to achieve its misaligned priorities, it might take control of key infrastructure and government functions to ensure humans didn't get in the way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: This is another way of saying AI takeover.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: The super intelligent AI swarm could wrest control of human civilization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: It would know that we would try to stop it from achieving its priorities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: So this worm went.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: likely wait until it's too late to shut it off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: There would be no going back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: I myself would guess AI takeover chances at roughly one in three.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: This logic may sound sci-fi, but it is a mainstream scientific concern that has been discussed for many years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: In the end, misaligned AI wouldn't care if you're a Democrat or a Republican.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: We would simply lose control.

chapters.summary: Turner says the solution is to stop companies from letting AI self-improve to uncontrollable intelligence and to treat compute like fissile material. He suggests validators test for loss-of-control and misalignment risks and that whistleblower protections cover AI threats.
chapters.title: Turner recommends compute controls and expanded validators

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: The shape of the solution is simple as I see it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: We stop companies from allowing AI to self-improve into an uncontrollable level of intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Treat compute.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: The main ingredient in AI training like fissile material, track it and restrict it, access to quantities large enough to improve AIs beyond known safe levels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Lastly, specific recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: The Speaker's Validation Bill checks AI systems for bias, privacy, and security, but not for the dangers I just described.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Validators should test for loss of control risk factors and misalignment risks, and the validators should not be chosen or influenced by the AI companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: For the whistleblower protection bill, please make clear that no agreement can stop an employee from reporting an AI threat to the city, whether or not a law has been broken.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: And extend protection to employees of AI companies that serve the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: After this session, I will provide additional written feedback on the proposed legislation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: And I look forward to answering committee questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Menin displays Exhibit 1 listing reported safety incidents and asks whether the panelists know of any unreported rogue-agent incidents. Coxon, Turner, and Kokotajlo each say no, and Menin notes companies were not self-reporting these incidents.
chapters.title: Menin asks panel about unreported AI safety incidents

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you to the three of you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So yes, a number of questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: First of all, we have a chart, Exhibit 1, that lists those safety incidents that have been reported over the summer by the leading companies.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Are each of you aware of any additional

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: safety issues where agents have gone rogue that have not been publicly reported.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I'll start with you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Coxon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And both of you?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Turner?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Cocotilo?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: No.

chapters.summary: Menin asks how government can improve transparency and who should be the third-party validators. Coxon says whoever is competent and qualified, and notes the need for preemptive safety cases judged by evaluators.
chapters.title: Panel discusses third-party validation approach

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So one of the frustrations, certainly, that I think everyone has is that for these safety incidents, it is not as if the companies have been self-reporting them.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We are finding out sometimes months after the fact.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So whether it was what happened with Hugging Face, whether it was what happened with the government of Australia, how can we have additional transparency, as each of you have testified?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: What measures can we as government take?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Obviously, we want to do third-party validation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Turner, I appreciate your comments to make some changes to that bill.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We want to make sure that the third-party validators are free from conflict of interest as it provides in the bill.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Who should be the third-party validators?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'll start with you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Coxon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Whoever is competent and qualified to do the evaluation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: I do think as well as after incidents, we will need preemptive safety cases that are judged by evaluators as well.

chapters.summary: Menin asks how frequently validators should assess models, and Coxon says with every increase in model capability. Kokotajlo suggests using multiple third-party evaluators and that government, not companies, should choose them.
chapters.title: Panel discusses frequency of validations and government choice of evaluators

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And how frequently will those third-party validators need to be assessing the safety of these models?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Presumably in time with the cadence of updates to the model's capabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: So with every increase in model capability, there'll need to be commensurate safety guarantees.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And do each of you have a comment on that?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: On who should be the third-party validators.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: One brief comment I might add is that you can have more than one third-party evaluator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: That seems good to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: If you're concerned that one might have the expertise but has too cozy a relationship with the company, and the other one has more independence but maybe lacks expertise, you could perhaps just set up so that they have both.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And I think ideally you want to be in a situation where the company doesn't get to choose, the government chooses who the evaluators are.

chapters.summary: Turner says California's SB 53 addresses catastrophic risk reporting but likely wouldn't have covered the Hugging Face incident. He proposes mandatory reporting when a company's own systems hack its own infrastructure.
chapters.title: Turner on California SB 53 and mandatory self-hack reporting

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Turner?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: So I would add California has SB 53 governing reporting on reporting catastrophic risks defined as at least a billion dollars to manage or a certain number of potential lives lost.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Fortunately, it's not clear whether this would have required reporting anything related to Hugging Face, for example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: I think the internal loss of control of these systems, having an AI that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: hacks the company itself in an important sense, it's not told to do so, but during training, during evaluation, during deployment to customers, hacks the company's own infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Making reporting that mandatory to the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: I think that would be quite strong and it would cover basically all of the recent incidents.

chapters.summary: Menin asks whether California and RAISE Act thresholds should be lower. Turner says yes, arguing a billion-dollar damage threshold is too high and that the city should at least be privately informed of internal rogue swarms.
chapters.title: Turner argues for lowering state and city reporting thresholds

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: When you mentioned the California Act and then in addition to New York, we obviously have the RAISE Act.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Should those standards be lower before they kick in?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Yes, I think they should.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: I'm most familiar with the California Act, and I think it was a good start, but it's certainly, you know, a billion dollars of damage is too high for informational purposes like this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: We've got basically one of the quantities we want to understand as precursors to these catastrophic risks is, are these companies even able to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: to control and understand their own systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: If they're on the loose internally and there's these swarms that are doing who knows what, that's something that the city should at least privately be informed of.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Now, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Kokotayo, you had mentioned two policy recommendations.

chapters.summary: Menin asks how to slow frontier AI while keeping pace with China. Kokotajlo says the U.S. must first solve its own threat, noting much Chinese progress comes from distillation of U.S. models and that slowing U.S. companies is the best way to slow China.
chapters.title: Kokotajlo on balancing China competition with safety slowdown

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: You said we need to increase transparency, and you said we should slow down frontier AI.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In terms of the latter, slowing down frontier AI, how do we balance the need of what is happening in China?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And ensure that the United States is keeping a pace, but we are at the same time putting in place these responsible safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: What is the best way in all three of your opinions that we do that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Great question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: A couple of things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: First of all, we need to not let our own companies do something that risks our lives, even if as a result, you know, China might then later do something that risks our lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Like this is this is not very complicated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: We have to first solve the immediate pressing threat here domestically and then.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Try to make sure that China doesn't get us killed either, to put it sort of bluntly and simply.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: But another thing I can add to that is that right now, most Chinese AI progress actually comes from the United States in a couple different ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: So one is distillation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: So some of these Chinese AI companies are just directly training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Their AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: systems using the outputs from Anthropic and OpenAI, for example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And so if Anthropic and OpenAI stopped making their AIs better at coding, for example, and stopped making their AIs better at research, then that would sort of directly slow down the rate at which the Chinese AIs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: progress towards recursive self-improvement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: In other manners as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: So I think a lot of the ideas, a lot of the algorithmic secrets and special sauce for how to train AIs are invented and discovered in the United States and then one way or another make their way over to China.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Finally, I think that right now the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: AI companies in the lead do not have adequate security to protect against model weight theft or certainly algorithmic secret theft and the code theft from Chinese military.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: So if it really came down to it and the competition between the US and China turned into something

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: more of a crisis and some sort of conflict, for example, then I think that we should assume that the CCP would just get our best AIs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And so it's almost a kind of a no-brainer that like, if we not only

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: The best way to slow down Chinese progress towards doing this extremely dangerous thing of recursive self-improvement is to just slow down the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Companies right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: I think that's the sort of immediate thing to say right in the moment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And then finally...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: That'd be what I would say.

chapters.summary: Coxon calls the expectation of a U.S.-China race the heart of the issue and says a global agreement not to pursue recursive self-improvement is key. Turner says many actions wouldn't slow us down and calls the China dichotomy false, since misaligned AI is everyone's adversary.
chapters.title: Coxon and Turner rebut the China-race framing

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Coxon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Yeah, I can add that to my mind, the core of the whole issue is the expectation of a global race to recursive self-improvement within the next few years, in particular between U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: And China.
