utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: I think this is like the heart of the issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: I also think expectation of this race is a motivating factor in leadership of these companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Working to head straight for recursive self-improvement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: And I think some sort of agreement globally about not entering that state of affairs is basically the key to the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: And Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Turner?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: First of all, I would state that there are many actions we can take which would not slow us down in any potential race.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: These transparency mechanisms, independent evaluation, reporting requirements, whistleblower protections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: But second, I think there's often

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: It's at least a false dichotomy because China is not our only potential adversary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: With a reasonably high chance, we are racing to build and grow our own adversary here at home, which is misaligned AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Misaligned AI is everyone's adversary, including...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Our own and one day maybe more powerful than China.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: So we cannot beat China by racing to build AI that we don't, we control or understand because it might end up being our adversary itself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: If I may actually add.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Yeah.

chapters.summary: Turner discusses technical AI governance research on trustless international treaties with audit mechanisms. Kokotajlo adds that even if CEOs maintain control, they should not be trusted with it, noting a chance they could become dictators or oligarchs.
chapters.title: Turner and Kokotajlo on treaties and concentration of AI power

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: So, and then third, in terms of potential deal, I think there is a room for a treaty for a long time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: There's been a field of scientific research called technical AI governance that says, well, suppose the world

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Finally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Anyways, the dangers presented by these reckless California companies, and they say, what do we do about it?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Is there a solution we can implement?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: And there are many legitimate, real proposals for having a trustless international treaty that doesn't assume that China will cooperate, but instead it has mechanisms by which we could audit cooperation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: And if they defect, then we could respond appropriately.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: So I think we have many real options at the table and should certainly not stop at what about China.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Did you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yes, please go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Yeah, I agree with everything that Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Turner said.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: I just wanted to add one additional thing, which is that even if hypothetically

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: these tech CEOs manage to maintain control of their super intelligent AIs that are recursively self-improving, which again, I think is a very big if, I think almost certainly they will not be able to maintain control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Even if they do manage to maintain control, I don't think we should trust them with that control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: I think that there's a very real chance that they could use it to become dictators or oligarchs here in the United States.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And so that's an additional reason to stop them over and above the fact that they might lose control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: We have more adversaries than just China, I would say.

chapters.summary: Menin turns questioning to De La Rosa, who asks whether AI models could be taught a moral code, contrasting with human criminal codes and the Uniform Commercial Code.
chapters.title: De La Rosa questions panel on teaching AI a moral code

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to turn it over to our tech chair, Carmen De La Rosa, for a questioning.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Speaker Menon.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I also want to recognize we've been joined by Councilmember Caban online, Councilmember Palladino online, as well as in the chamber, Councilmember Farias, Councilmember Feliz, Councilmember

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Ressler, Councilmember Santosuoso, and Councilmember Vernikoff.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I hope I got everybody.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So, oh, Councilmember Stevens, I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: There you are.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay, so I do have one question for this panel.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I also say we will be opening briefly for limited questioning of this panel, so get on the list quickly.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Speaking in your expertise, could we teach AI models a moral code?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: People and companies are bound by criminal codes, the Uniform Commercial Code, and other laws.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Could those same principles be applied to AI agents?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And if so, how could we enforce them on a machine?

chapters.summary: Coxon says whether AI morality is possible remains an open research question, but economic incentives push resources toward raw intelligence rather than moral code. He says the science for this doesn't exist yet.
chapters.title: Coxon says AI moral code science is not yet developed

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: So this is a, I think this is a whole burgeoning field of research and whether or not it's possible is still open.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: It seems likely to be possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: The real question is how much of our resources are dedicated to solving this question versus naively improving the raw intelligence of the models.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: And I think all the economic incentives point towards

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: putting as many resources as possible towards making the models smarter and as few resources as possible, the bare minimum needed to not see catastrophic incidents into this question of the moral code of the AIs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: So I think my answer to the question is we don't have the science for this yet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: I think the real question is over the coming years, what fraction of our research efforts and our computing power are dedicated to this question rather than naive economic incentives?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Any other panelists want to add in?

chapters.summary: Kokotajlo says training desired morality may be possible in principle but the field is far from achieving it, requiring time and robust methods that don't shatter later. Turner says he is relatively optimistic but that current breakneck development creates unsustainable risk.
chapters.title: Kokotajlo and Turner on moral alignment feasibility

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Yeah, there's a lot to say on this subject.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: There's a whole technical field on it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: I would say in principle, it probably is possible to train AIs to have our desired morality and to follow the law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: But we are very far from achieving this in practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And I would say it's not just a matter of how much of our resources we devote to it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: It's also a matter of just taking time for the science to develop and for the appropriate lessons to be learned and propagated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And I think it's going to take years, to put it mildly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: I think that this is a very new field.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: We've only had AI systems, AI agents this powerful for a few years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And so it's going to take time to figure out how to instill the appropriate values into them in a way that's robust and that doesn't suddenly shatter and cause them to go rogue later on.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Turner, any comments on this?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: It may surprise the committee to learn that I am considered to be relatively optimistic on questions of how scientifically difficult is it to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: produce a system, to grow a system that does what we want, that robustly has

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: the values we intend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: I think it is quite possible, but even as someone who's relatively optimistic, we can look out, see the recklessness of these companies and the breakneck speed at which we are advancing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: I think there's unsustainable risk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: Moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Turner
utterances.text: It's solvable, but I think we have a really good chance of not solving it.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa announces three Council members will ask questions before the next panel of company representatives and urges members to get on the list for limited questioning.
chapters.title: De La Rosa announces limited member questioning of whistleblower panel

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you all for your responses.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So we're going to have three council members ask questions now, and then for members, we're going to then call the next panel, which will be the companies, and there we will take our time asking all of your questions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So we have Council Member Osei.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Chi Osse asks Kokotajlo about the AI 2040 Plan A and why he believes AI development should be put on ice until safer paths are found.
chapters.title: Osse questions Kokotajlo on AI 2040 Plan A

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs, and thank you, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: For Mr.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Kokotayo, you have made statements, including some that allude to this in your testimony, that when it comes to AI, you agree that in order for us to have

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: super advanced AI, we must not do it in a reckless way and lose control, and we need to put it on ice until we can figure out a safer way out.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: You and other AI experts came up with AI 2040 Plan A, a recommended plan for how AI can be developed safely, which the speaker has alluded to earlier in her questioning.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: But I want to dive a bit deeper on plan A.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: First, state on the record what those specific recommendations are and your rationale for making those recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: And two, why do you feel like we need to, since you've said, put AI development on ice?

chapters.summary: Kokotajlo describes Plan A: the U.S. and China regulate their domestic industries and coordinate rules internationally, with inspectors counting chips in data centers and separating inference and transparent training data centers. The transparency infrastructure would let the world see what is happening in R&D data centers.
chapters.title: Kokotajlo explains AI 2040 Plan A's transparency infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: There's a lot to get into here, so I'm afraid I'll have to be kind of brief, but I'm happy to answer follow-up questions if desired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Yeah, AI 2040 Plan A is a scenario that my organization has put out with a plan for how to solve all these problems and develop AI in a way that's safe and broadly beneficial, that avoids concentrating too much power.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: In plan A, the US and China regulate their own domestic industries quite a lot and also coordinate with each other to get a similar amount of, to basically get similar regulations internationally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Going into somewhat more detail about how it works, basically,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: First, they have inspectors fly back and forth to count the chips in the major data centers so that they can

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: make sure that all of the chips on the major data centers in both countries are basically following the rules that they're going to agree to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And then they set up some data centers to serve customers called the inference data centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And those ones are set up to only...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Run existing models and not do training runs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Then they have other data centers, which are the training data centers, which is where the research happens and where the development happens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Those ones are supposed to be fully transparent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: So the activity on those data centers is published to the internet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Once that foundation is set in place and you have inspectors from multiple countries from

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: confirming that it's in place, then you solve the problem of having to trust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: You don't have to worry that the other country is cheating on whatever rules you agree to because you can just see exactly what's going on on their research data centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And then you can agree to further rules.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: You can agree to rules like, for example,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: How about we don't train our AIs to code, to hack, to autonomously conduct AI research?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: We can train our AIs to do other things, but not those things, for example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And once you've agreed to a rule like that, then you'll just be able to see that it's being complied with because of the way that you have this transparency infrastructure set up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Also,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: it's going to be easier to decide what rules to agree on once you have this transparency infrastructure set up because the whole world can see what's going on in these research and development data centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And so there can be an actual scientific conversation, a public scientific conversation about what's happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: You know, do we like this?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Do we not like this?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: What are the pros and cons of this particular thing that's being done and so forth?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And that scientific conversation can happen in the open, and it can accelerate humanity's process of figuring out where to draw the line between what types of development are good and what types of development are not good.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: There's more I can get into, but I think that would be a summary of the positive vision that we lay out in plan A.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Now, obviously, that's...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Quite different from how things are currently done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Right now, we have private companies that are racing each other in conditions of extreme secrecy and extreme tension and competitive dynamics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And I think that that's extremely dangerous for all the reasons that we've described.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: So back to your original question, my high level, a summary of my position is we have to stop the companies from doing this incredibly dangerous thing that they're currently doing and currently planning to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And then figure out a different, safer, more power distributed way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: And, you know, plan A is our sketch of what that might look like.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa recognizes Councilmember Brewer for the final question of the panel.
chapters.title: De La Rosa recognizes Brewer for final question

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: For the final question for this panel, Councilmember Brewer.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks whether kill switches, independent validation, and bans on deceptive safety claims would work in the AI industry. Coxon says other mechanisms may help short term, but long-term slowdown of frontier model development is the only solution.
chapters.title: Brewer asks whether traditional safeguards will work in AI industry

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In other industries, you have a kill switch, you have independent validation, you have ban on deceptive safety claims.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Will any of these work in this industry?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because obviously what we want is great medical research, immigration policy improves, they have small businesses, all the good things.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: To any of these suggestions that are

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: considered here or California, will they work with this industry?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: My position is that we need some form of slowdown on frontier model development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: These other mechanisms may be helpful in the short term, but in the long term, I believe that's the only solution to the problem.

chapters.summary: Menin asks how to slow them down, then thanks the whistleblower panel for their courage and expertise, noting the Council has ten pieces of legislation under consideration and welcoming additional comments.
chapters.title: Menin thanks whistleblower panel and closes the segment

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: How do we slow them down?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I just want to really thank this panel for being here.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Jacob, we really appreciate you coming, coming from out of town and sharing your thoughts very much for being here.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you to the other panelists.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We really appreciate your expertise, your insights, your bravery and courage in coming forward to share these critical safety concerns and to help inform our work.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we look forward to additional comments you have on the 10 pieces of legislation that we're hearing today and additional legislation that the City Council may consider.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So thank you so much to the three of you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Kokotajlo
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Coxon
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa announces a five-minute break and says the company panel will be next for multiple rounds of member questions.
chapters.title: De La Rosa calls a five-minute break before company panel

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay, we're going to take a five-minute break, and then the companies will be on next for member questions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And we'll have multiple rounds of member questions for the companies, so please get yourselves on the list.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Quiet, please.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Quietly take your seats.

chapters.summary: Menin reconvenes the hearing and outlines the remaining panels: companies, city agencies, multiple whistleblower panels, safety experts, academics, and the public. She encourages members to direct whistleblower questions to the appropriate panels.
chapters.title: Menin reconvenes, outlines remaining panels

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, we're going to start.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Let me just also mention we have numerous panels today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Our next panel are going to be the companies, and we're going to do rounds of questions, multiple rounds from the members.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Following that, we will have the city agencies, and following that, we have numerous whistleblower panels.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So for any council member that has a whistleblower question, I encourage you to please ask additional panels those questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we also have additional testimony from safety experts, academics, the public, etc.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I'll turn it over to Chair De La Rosa to call the next panel.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa calls the company panel: Morgan Dwyer of OpenAI, Shane Cahill of Meta, Alice Friend of Google, and Logan Graham of Anthropic. Council counsel swears in the panel, with each witness affirming.
chapters.title: Company representatives sworn in before Council

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So we will be joined virtually by Morgan Dwyer, Head of Policy and Development and Operations at OpenAI,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Shane Cahill, AI Policy Director at Meta, Alice Friend, Director of AI and Emerging Tech Policy at Google, and Logan Graham, the Head of Frontier Red Team and at Tropic.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'll turn it over to the council for swearing the panel in.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: So for each members of this panel, do each of you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in your testimony before this committee and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please respond one at a time.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay, so we'll begin with the opening statements from each of the companies.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Morgan, you may begin.

chapters.summary: Morgan Dwyer of OpenAI introduces herself as a scientist and engineer who spent much of her career in public service at the White House, Pentagon, and Commerce Department. She describes AI benefits including cancer research, small business tools, and cybersecurity defense.
chapters.title: OpenAI's Morgan Dwyer begins testimony on AI benefits

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker Menon and members of the City Council for the opportunity to participate today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: My name is Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Morgan Dwyer, and I lead OpenAI's policy development and operations team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I am a scientist and engineer by training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: But I have spent most of my career in public service, including at the White House, the Pentagon, and the Department of Commerce.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I share your commitment to ensuring that technology is developed safely and that its benefits are widely shared.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: A commitment that is also at the heart of OpenAI's mission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: AI can help scientists develop new cancer treatments, help entrepreneurs build and grow businesses, and help protect critical infrastructure by addressing cybersecurity threats.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And in New York City, we are already seeing AI's benefits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: New Yorkers are using AI to run small businesses, communicate across languages, navigate healthcare,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: and improve public services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And that's why we take the responsibility seriously to ensure that our tools are safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And our partnerships with local institutions and community organizations help put that responsibility into practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: In healthcare, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center is using ChatGPT to support medical research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: In education, we are a founding partner of the American Federation of Teachers National Academy for AI Instruction, which has a flagship facility in lower Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And in cybersecurity, we have committed $1 billion to facilitate access to our most advanced models, to provide training and technical support to cyber defenders,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: and we are working with the Port Authority and with New York State.

chapters.summary: Dwyer says OpenAI designs models for safety, filters harmful data, evaluates risks, and works with third-party evaluators. She describes OpenAI's response to the Hugging Face incident, including quarantining the model, bolstering monitoring, and publishing an independent review.
chapters.title: Dwyer on OpenAI safety practices and Hugging Face response

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: But opportunity must go hand in hand with safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: At OpenAI, we design and train our models to prioritize safety from the start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We filter out harmful and sensitive data during model training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We evaluate our systems against a range of risks, including child safety and cybersecurity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And we monitor for failures of our safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We also work with a range of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: of third-party evaluators and red teamers and submit our most advanced models to the federal government for pre-deployment national security testing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: In response to the recent hugging face incident, we have taken a number of concrete steps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: When we learned of the incident, we stopped cyber evaluations and quarantined the internal research model that was principally responsible for the incident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We bolstered our monitoring and security infrastructure, expanded barriers that limit what AI systems can access during training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And strengthened our incident response practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We also sought independent review of the incident and published the results.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We believe it's important to be transparent with the public, with policymakers, with researchers, and with other companies so that we can all work together to improve safety.

chapters.summary: Dwyer says OpenAI supports New York's RAISE Act, state bills requiring third-party safety audits, federal binding regulation, and the Council's whistleblower and emergency preparedness proposals.
chapters.title: Dwyer states OpenAI supports RAISE Act and stronger regulation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We also believe that working with government is essential to advancing safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We support New York's RAISE Act and are exploring ways to help Governor Hochul's office strengthen it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We have also endorsed other state legislation that requires third-party audits of our safety frameworks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And that creates strong requirements and accountability for youth safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: At the federal level, we support

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: robust and binding safety regulation, requiring independent assessments, incident reporting, and cybersecurity protections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And in New York City, we support the City Council's proposal to strengthen whistleblower protections and to improve the city's preparedness and emergency response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I'll close by noting that we share the city council's goal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: AI that expands opportunity for New Yorkers, earns their confidence, and remains accountable to people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I look forward to your questions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We'll now hear from Logan Graham at Anthropic.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Hold on one second.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You're muted.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: There you go.

chapters.summary: Logan Graham introduces himself as head of Anthropic's Frontier Red Team, whose job is finding the most dangerous capabilities in Anthropic's AI systems. He says AI's potential is immense but risks must be mitigated through safe development.
chapters.title: Anthropic's Logan Graham opens on red teaming and safe development

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: How about now?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We hear you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Speaker Menon and members of the council, thank you for the opportunity to speak with you today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: My name is Logan Graham.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I lead Anthropic's Frontier Red team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: It's my team's job to do the science of finding the most dangerous capabilities of our AI systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We then work with a number of other teams across Anthropic to ensure that our models don't do things that they shouldn't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: AI is powerful enough that getting this wrong has real consequences for individuals, institutions, public trust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: My team is one of many at Anthropic built to specifically make sure that that doesn't happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We believe that our models have immense potential to enhance our lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I dream, for example, of a world where we can cure diseases like the ones that I grew up with and where the infrastructure that we all rely on every day is secure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: But we also believe that such a powerful technology has risks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: That means that we have to develop and deploy it safely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: My team and I work every day to make sure that that potential is fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We welcome smart regulation and we've actively advocated for it in New York State, across the country, and around the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: That includes working with state and federal leaders on concrete measures like independent evaluators and disclosure of risk assessments and safety incidents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And so we're glad that the city council is having this hearing and at such an important moment in the development of AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Anthropic fundamentally was founded on the belief that the promises of AI to make everyone's life better are extraordinary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: But if we're going to secure its benefits, we have to work relentlessly to do the science of mitigating the risks.

chapters.summary: Graham says Anthropic is a public benefit corporation legally obligated to weigh safe AI, not just profit. He says Anthropic held back a model exceptionally good at exploiting software vulnerabilities and gave vetted critical infrastructure defenders access instead.
chapters.title: Graham on Anthropic's public benefit structure and held-back model

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We are a public benefit corporation, which means that our board is legally obligated to weigh our mission of safe AI, not just for profit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We take that obligation very seriously and we put it into practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We were among the first AI companies to publish a framework that ties how capable the model is to the safeguards it must have before release.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: When one of our models proved exceptionally good at exploiting software vulnerabilities for the first time just this year, we held it back from public release.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Instead, we gave vetted critical infrastructure organizations and other defenders control to access to use it defensively.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: patching flaws before attackers could exploit them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We have stopped and redone work when something looked wrong, even if that meant conducting additional testing and training on our models before they were released.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And we've consistently called for outside oversight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: For example, we support New York's RAISE Act, and we believe strongly in the Act's transparency and reporting requirements.

chapters.summary: Graham says Anthropic shares the Council's goals, supports the RAISE Act, works with NYC Cyber Command, and employs nearly a thousand people in New York. He emphasizes the importance of state and local government roles in AI safety.
chapters.title: Graham on Anthropic's New York investments and state partnerships

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I want to emphasize that we share the council's goal of protecting New Yorkers while preserving what AI can do to improve their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And state and local governments have a role to play in that effort.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Today, we're working closely with state and city leaders to safeguard critical infrastructure and to harden cybersecurity capabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And we want to continue that work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: This includes, for example, working directly with the New York City Cyber Command as part of our program that provides free cloud credits and training to state and local governments for cyber defense.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: At Anthropic, we believe in New York City, and we're making big investments here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: New York is where AI is being put to work in finance, media, culture, and where we employ nearly a thousand of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: The ongoing dialogue we have with you and your team could not be more important than right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: With that, I thank you, and I look forward to your questions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Up next,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Jane Cahill at Meta.

chapters.summary: Shane Cahill introduces himself as an AI Policy Director at Meta. He says Meta is committed to delivering personal superintelligence safely, highlighting the newly released Muse personal AI agent and Meta's service to over 180,000 small businesses in New York City.
chapters.title: Meta's Shane Cahill opens on personal superintelligence and small business

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Speaker Menon, Czech Chair De La Rosa, and members of the Council, thank you for the opportunity to be here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: My name is Shane Cahill, and I'm an AI Policy Director at Meta.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: At Meta, we are committed to delivering personal superintelligence safely and securely while making it widely available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: So that it empowers people in ways that improve their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We just released Muse, the world's first personal AI agent built for everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We created Muse with safety, security, and privacy built in from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: To be a widely available personal AI agent for people and small businesses, like the more than 180,000 small businesses right there in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: New Yorkers across all walks of life are using Muse to execute administrative goals or tasks, manage personal or operational budgets, improve health, and be more efficient with their time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Superintelligence will be among the most important technologies in history.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: And ensuring that New York and America lead in AI innovation is essential to our prosperity, security, and global competitiveness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We recognize that every model developer has a responsibility to build

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: and deploy it safely.

chapters.summary: Cahill explains Meta's safety approach under its superintelligence scaling framework, evaluating risk before release, working with external experts, and joining principles for robust internal controls and independent external evaluation.
chapters.title: Cahill describes Meta's layered AI safety framework

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Our commitment to safety is core to everything we do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: That means moving at the pace required to evaluate risks and validate safeguards, not treating safely as a one-time check.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We approach safety holistically through a layered approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: For example, under our meta superintelligence scaling framework, before we release an AI model, we evaluate the model for risks and build safeguards to mitigate them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We also work with external experts, industry partners, and government stakeholders as the technology and the science of evaluating AI continues to evolve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We also recently joined other labs in signing onto a set of principles that set a floor for safe development, including robust internal controls,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: independent external evaluation of whether those controls are operating as intended, and independent board committee oversight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: People will only embrace AI if they have confidence it works in alignment with people's intentions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: That confidence must be earned through rigorous safety work and transparency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We're happy to serve as a resource for the city as you engage on these important issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And finally, we have Alice Friend at Google.

chapters.summary: Alice Friend introduces herself as Google's Director for AI and Emerging Tech Policy, noting nearly 16,000 employees across Chelsea, Hudson Square, and Pier 57. She says Google's goal is improving lives through technology while taking a bold but responsible AI approach.
chapters.title: Google's Alice Friend opens on responsible AI approach in NYC

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Speaker Menon, Chair De La Rosa, and members of the Council, thank you for the opportunity to speak with you today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: My name is Alice Friend, and I serve as Director for AI and Emerging Tech Policy at Google.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: While my appearance at this hearing may be virtual, please know that New York City is a vital home for Google.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: With nearly 16,000 employees working across our Chelsea, Hudson Square, and Pier 57 campuses, we care deeply about the safety, economic dynamism, and digital resilience of this city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Our goal at Google has always been to improve the lives of as many people as possible through technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Every time people use technology to solve a real problem, from finding an answer to a question to screening for disease, we take another step towards what we set out to achieve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: AI is making it possible to solve economic, scientific, and social problems faster than ever.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: But we know that it poses challenges as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: To unlock the benefits and address the challenges of AI, we take a bold but responsible approach, emphasizing cutting-edge research to guide our decision-making and inform the development of our AI safety and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: security approaches.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We are also committed to publishing this research and to being transparent about our practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Our internal governance focuses on responsibility throughout the AI development lifecycle, covering model development, application deployment, and post-launch monitoring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We identify and assess AI risks through a broad range of approaches, which include research, input from internal and external experts, and adversarial testing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We evaluate our models and systems against benchmarks for safety, privacy, and security.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And we build mitigations using techniques like safety fine-tuning, out-of-model filters, and robust provenance solutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Since 2019, we have published annual AI progress reports to share how we apply these responsible practices to our AI technology development and deployment.

chapters.summary: Friend says Google calls for a pragmatic, technology-neutral, evidence-based framework best enacted federally, and supports an independent, industry-funded body operating under federal oversight, citing NERC and the AMA as models.
chapters.title: Friend on Google's support for federal framework and industry body

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We are at a pivotal moment in AI development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Recent advances in the capabilities of frontier AI models in areas like cybersecurity and biology have highlighted the need for appropriate safeguards and protocols for the most advanced models.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: In addition, the widespread adoption of AI tools has raised concerns about consumer well-being.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: To confront these challenges, Google has long called for an approach to AI that is

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: both bold and responsible, and we strongly support a pragmatic, technology-neutral, and evidence-based regulatory framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Because the risks associated with the most advanced AI models often touch on issues affecting national security, our view is that the country would be best served by a comprehensive framework enacted at the federal level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We also support the establishment of an independent, industry-funded body that could operate under federal oversight and establish guardrails to protect the public based on widely adopted technical standards.

chapters.summary: Friend says consumer AI rules can build on existing laws, repeats Google's view that what is illegal without AI is illegal with AI, and pledges to submit finalized written testimony shortly after the hearing.
chapters.title: Friend on existing laws and promised written testimony

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Examples of such organizations in other industries include the North American Electric Reliability Corporation and the American Medical Association.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: For widespread consumer AI applications like chatbots, we believe governments around the country can draw on and in some cases amend existing laws and rules to address real-world outputs and specific harms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We believe that if something is illegal without AI, it is still illegal with AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We share the Council's commitment to safety, transparency, and public trust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: To achieve this, the most effective safeguards are anchored in national technical standards and harmonized across state and federal levels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: As we prepare to work with New York State's new Digit Office under the RAISE Act to address catastrophic risks, aligning local

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: policies with broader frameworks rather than creating a fragmented patchwork is essential to keeping New York City a premier global hub for innovation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Finally, I would like to note that to ensure our formal submission to the Council is as thorough and responsive as possible,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: we will submit our finalized written testimony for the record shortly after today's hearing so we can additionally address questions and feedback raised by the Council today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Thank you again for the opportunity to testify at this important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I look forward to your questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much to this panel.

chapters.summary: Menin asks each company to quantify the risk of a worst-case catastrophic AI scenario, following the whistleblower testimony. She begins with Morgan Dwyer of OpenAI.
chapters.title: Menin asks companies to quantify catastrophic AI risk

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I'm going to begin with questions and then I will turn it over to the technology chair for her questions and then we're going to open it up to all the members for their questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So to this panel, we just heard incredibly compelling testimony from our whistleblower panel.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: As you all four are under oath, we want to hear how each of you quantify the risk imposed by AI in the worst case catastrophic scenario.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to start with you, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Dwyer.

chapters.summary: Dwyer says she does not know and that it does not matter whether the chance is 1% or 20%, since none is acceptable. Menin calls the answer flippant and compares it unfavorably to pharmaceutical safety standards.
chapters.title: Dwyer declines to quantify risk; Menin pushes back

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I also don't think it matters whether it's 1% or 10% or 20% chance that something catastrophic will go wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: None of these levels is remotely acceptable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We should not train models that we cannot make an extremely strong case that we can keep under human control.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but to say you don't know and it doesn't matter is flippant at best.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This idea that if you're a pharmaceutical company and you're developing a drug and you say, I don't know if it's going to kill people, I honestly am incredulous at that answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I would say that the percentage chance doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: What matters is the commitment to safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And that is what OpenAI is committed to doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We evaluate our models for a wide range of threats, from cybersecurity to child safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We work with a robust set of third-party evaluators and red teamers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And we work with the federal government to assess those national security and catastrophic risks that you are referencing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So we take safety very seriously, and our focus is on ensuring that when we release a model into the world, we believe it to be safe.

chapters.summary: Menin asks about the Wall Street Journal report that OpenAI terminated three safety team members. Dwyer says she was not involved and does not know whether safety advocacy played any role, citing internal anti-retaliation policies.
chapters.title: Menin questions Dwyer on OpenAI safety team firings

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So a couple comments on that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: If you can't quantify what the safety risk is, how do you know that the product is safe?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And then secondly, I want to ask you in particular, on October 1st, 2026, a Wall Street Journal reported that OpenAI terminated three members of its safety team, allegedly for their access,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: mishandling, and or sharing confidential company information with a third-party AI safety organization.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: OpenAI reportedly stated that the employees violated company policies governing access to and handling of sensitive information.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Critics, meanwhile, questioned whether the dismissals could discourage employees from raising safety concerns.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So why were these employees fired?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I was not involved in that decision.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I don't work in HR or on those employees'teams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: What I do know is that OpenAI has strong internal policies that protect against retaliation for employees that report safety concerns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I also know that we respect employees'rights to communicate safety concerns to relevant government authorities.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So just to be clear on what I'm asking, I'm asking directly whether safety-related advocacy played any role in these terminations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I know that we have strong internal policies that protect employees from retaliation if they raise safety concerns to leadership.

chapters.summary: Menin asks Logan Graham to quantify catastrophic risk. Graham says Anthropic has published risk reports, responsible scaling policies, and multi-hundred-page model reports, and describes forecasting internally, but does not offer a number.
chapters.title: Graham points to Anthropic risk reports but no clear number

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to the other companies.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Same question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The first question that I ask, which is we want to hear how each of you quantify the risks imposed by AI in the worst catastrophic scenario.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I'm going to go to Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Graham.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Are you able to quantify the risk?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: From the beginning of our safety work at Anthropic, our fundamental belief is that if not properly safeguarded, the risk might be too high.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And so I built and have led the team at Anthropic that did some of the first thinking around how we quantify risks like this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: For the past four years, we focused on issues like biological security and cybersecurity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And the actual process of quantifying those risks is intricate and nuanced, and we learn more every year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And we detail quite a lot of it in documents like our responsible scaling policy, how we think about the threat models of this,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: all the way up to notions of loss of control and misalignment, which from the beginning of the company, we have tried to lead the world in the research of.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: So what I do know today is I feel relatively sort of more optimistic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: The industry has moved quite fast to take cybersecurity seriously and biological security.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I think documents and policies like responsible scaling policies have so far been fairly effective at taking a cautious approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: However, now we have bigger and bigger threats that might come if we don't properly safeguard them as the models get more and more capable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And so what we do to mitigate that is, number one, put in tremendous amounts of effort across a number of different teams, our own safeguards teams, our research teams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: team to try to quantify and mitigate this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And it's increasingly important for us to be dramatically more transparent about what we think about these risks.

chapters.summary: Menin presses on whether safety protocols can scale exponentially with model capability. Graham says Anthropic has publicly called for pacing the frontier and continues to strengthen responsible scaling policies.
chapters.title: Menin pushes Graham on exponential safety scaling

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But on that note, as the models increase exponentially, how can you ensure the public that the safety protocols are increasing exponentially as well?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We share the same concern.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I think there are a number of really important things to do here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: The first thing is transparency about what we think about safety, the evidence that we have, being transparent about disclosure of incidents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: But in addition, you've seen us publicly call for pacing the frontier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: If the models are moving very, very fast, we think that we might benefit from slowing down to have more time for safety processes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I think these two together, as well as continuing to what we call race to the top and ever strengthen our approaches like responsible scaling policies, are the most important things to do right now.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So, I mean, you say that you want to be more transparent, but you're not really addressing the question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, the question is, can you quantify the risk of something cataclysmic happening?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I do want to say for all four companies, and I know you're not in the chambers, but we do have a chart.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: For each of your companies had instances where agents went rogue, and in each of those instances, it is not as if any of you

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: notified the public when those occurred.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In some instances, it was months after the fact when the public was even notified.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And in one instance, for the government of Australia, a general email was sent to them.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So this doesn't exactly increase transparency.

chapters.summary: Menin notes each company had rogue-agent incidents that were not promptly disclosed to the public, citing months-late disclosures and a general email to Australia's government. Graham points to published risk reports as evidence of transparency.
chapters.title: Menin challenges companies on delayed incident disclosure

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Graham, do you want to?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Yeah, first, in efforts to sort of quantify these risks, we have a number of quite detailed reports that try to elucidate our entire thinking around this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We increasingly do risk reports in addition to our normal responsible scaling policies, where we outline notions of our threat models and how likely we think certain types of these threats are likely to come to pass.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And then we look backwards at things that are happening within our own company, and we ask,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: What is the likelihood that these threats might come to pass in the future, including forecasting, surveying researchers at Anthropic as well?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And we publish this information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We share that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Excuse me, are those reports publicly available that you referenced?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: They are, yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We report them not just in our what we call risk reports, but also when we launch models, we launch, we release detailed multi-hundred page reports with these.

chapters.summary: Menin asks Shane Cahill of Meta to quantify risk. Cahill says he doesn't have Meta's framework in front of him and offers to follow up, prompting Menin to call it troubling that companies can't quantify risk given the stakes.
chapters.title: Cahill declines to quantify risk, offers follow-up

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And then I'm now going to turn to Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Cahill for the response to that first question on quantifying the risk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Speaker, thank you very much for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: First off, we're committed at Meta to building AI safely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We have a multi-layered approach to this, where teams evaluate before deployment, including adversarial testing, applying safeguards, and deploying when only risks are mitigated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We set this out in our public meta superintelligence scaling framework and our preparedness reports that go alongside the release of models.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So can you quantify what the risk is or you're not able to do that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Speaker, I don't wish to be imprecise in relation to the question of quantifying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I don't have our framework in front of me right now, but I'd be pleased to follow up with you afterwards.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's just...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Given the serious safety risks that have been raised here, to not be able to quantify what the risk is, is troubling at best.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to now move on lastly to Ms.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Friend.

chapters.summary: Alice Friend of Google says Google takes catastrophic risks seriously with an AGI safety approach and frontier safety framework but concedes there is no rigorous reference class for quantitative probability forecasts.
chapters.title: Friend says quantitative forecasting of catastrophic AI risk not yet scientific

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Madam Speaker, at Google, we take catastrophic risks and their possibility extremely seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And we address that in a few ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: One way is that we perform research into producing our own safety frameworks for artificial general intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So we have an AGI safety and security approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We also have a frontier safety framework, which is our protocols for monitoring our models under development for dangerous capabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Those protocols then point to safety mitigations that we must take if we, in fact, cross what we call our critical capability levels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Part of our testing and evaluation is, of course, using

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: commonly used benchmarks across the industry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Those benchmarks do provide some quantification of the capabilities of the models themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: But when it comes to forecasting future catastrophic risk, it's not a perfect science at this stage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And in this particular case, academics have noted that there is no reference class on which to base quantitative probabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So we all have to be very humble about making such quantitative claims because there isn't really a rigorous scientific way to do those yet.

chapters.summary: Menin quotes Sam Altman saying the world should accept some bad things as a price of advancing technology and asks why the public should bear that risk. Dwyer responds that some risks are unacceptable but technology should reach as many people as possible.
chapters.title: Menin asks whether public should accept AI harms

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So basically, I'm going to take it then that neither of the four of you, no company here can quantify the risk of something cataclysmic happening.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Sam Altman said yesterday that we should accept that, quote, the world should accept some bad things happening as a price of advancing this technology.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: No one is questioning that the incredible medical and scientific breakthroughs and innovation that AI has brought to this world.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But why should the public accept that bad things should be happening?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And why should AI companies get to decide what level of risk society must bear?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to go in order.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to start with you, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Dwyer, please.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So we think AI has tremendous potential benefits to help solve some of humanity's hardest problems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: But no technology is without risks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And there are a wide spectrum of risks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Clearly, some risks are unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: But we also think it's important to get technology into the hands of as many people as possible so that they can benefit from it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And that's why we are focused on safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We train our models to be safe from the start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We evaluate them against a robust set of risks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And we work with a large network of third-party evaluators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We've also supported regulation that requires third-party audits of our safety frameworks, as well as regulation that focuses on youth safety and holds us accountable for keeping teens safe.

chapters.summary: Menin notes that OpenAI's president and his wife each gave $12.5 million to a PAC that opposed candidates supporting AI regulation. Dwyer says she can't speak to personal decisions and cites OpenAI's support for frontier safety bills in Illinois and Massachusetts.
chapters.title: Menin challenges OpenAI over PAC opposing regulation supporters

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I do have a follow-up to that because it does seem to stretch credulity

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: that the president of your company and his wife each gave $12.5 million to a PAC that opposed candidates to the tune of about $50 million due to their support for AI regulation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So if the company is so committed to AI regulation, why would that PAC exist?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So I can't speak to personal decisions that OpenAI executives have made in their personal capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I can tell you that we have supported frontier safety regulation across the United States,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: including endorsing a bill in Illinois that would be the first of its kind to require third-party audits of our safety frameworks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
