utterances.text: We also supported a version of a bill in Massachusetts, which was the first of its kind to reference RSI, which the panel earlier spoke about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So again, I can speak to our actions, which is to support strong, harmonized frontier safety legislation, including at the state level.

chapters.summary: Menin asks the other three companies to respond to Altman's comment. Graham says Anthropic minimizes risk and held back a model; Cahill distances Meta from the quote and notes its compute goes to serving people; Friend says we shouldn't accept bad things and cites Waymo safety data.
chapters.title: Anthropic, Meta, and Google respond to Altman's acceptance of harm

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, I'm going to move on to the other three companies to the answer to the same question about why should the public accept the comments that Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Altman made yesterday that the world should accept bad things happening and why should AI companies get to decide what level of risk society must bear.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I'm going to go in order.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Graham.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I didn't see all of Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Altman's comments yesterday.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I share the notion expressed here that, number one, while maximizing the benefits of this technology, you need to minimize the risks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And we should not be comfortable with letting these risks happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: This is why over the course of our history and my team's history, we have been, I think, sometimes accused of being overly cautious.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I would say appropriately cautious.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Just this year, withholding our most powerful model in order to just have more time to even think about collectively as industry as well as government, what to do about these capabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And fundamentally, this transcends the labs and industry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: From our beginning, we have long supported the role of government here for exactly this reason.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Cahill?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Apologies, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: There was a strange moment there with the mute button.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: In relation to the quote from Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Altman that you read out, I don't see it the same way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We absolutely recognize the risks of AI and the opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: That's why we have our scaling framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: That's why we have our preparedness reports.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: That's why we have teams and teams of people and a multilayered approach to AI safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: One thing I wanted to mention, if I may, is that Meta's vision is to bring personal superintelligence to everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: And I listened very intently to the panel before us in relation to recursive self-improvement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: And I just wanted to mention that committing significant majority of compute

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: towards serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways of ensuring that the technology is developed safely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Meta has made that commitment and other labs can do that also.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Friend?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Yeah, Madam Speaker, we shouldn't just accept bad things happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We should be working continuously and rigorously on AI safety, which is a collective effort.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: It will be a collective effort to identify and mitigate risks, to establish technical standards, to make those identifications and mitigations all the more rigorous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: But I also want to note that one of the promises of AI is that AI itself can make us safer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I would call your attention to Waymo vehicles, which in one study had a 96% reduction in injury-causing crashes at intersections, which led Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Jonathan Slotkin in the New York Times to call it a public health intervention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So we should think collectively about preventing and mitigating risks from AI, but we should also keep in mind that we can use AI itself to reduce risks to human safety and well-being.

chapters.summary: Menin asks whether each company would bear legal responsibility if a frontier model goes rogue and causes harm. Dwyer gives an unclear response; Graham says he's a technical researcher and the question transcends labs; Cahill says he's not in legal; Friend clearly says existing legal frameworks apply to AI.
chapters.title: Menin asks companies about legal liability for AI harms

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So if one of your frontier AI models goes rogue and causes serious financial harm, compromises sensitive data, causes physical injury, or contributes to a death or deaths,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: do you each believe your company bears legal responsibility?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'll start with you, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Dwyer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I believe that OpenAI takes its responsibility for safety very seriously, and we are responsible for developing and evaluating our systems to ensure that they are safe.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So is that a yes or that is a no?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Could you be more clear, please?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We believe that we are responsible for ensuring that our systems are developed safely, and that includes training them to be safe, evaluating them to be safe, and then continuing to monitor our safeguards after deployment.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, I'm going to take that as a no, because that is not really clear that you would bear legal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to go now to Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Graham.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Yeah, as a technical safety research lead, I think there are others which will have more nuanced perspectives on that issue than I.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: What I do know is, first, this is an issue where every lab, we think, should be committed to a multi-layered safety stack to make sure that doesn't happen in the first place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: These issues don't come about in the first place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: The second, this is candidly a big and complex questions that also transcends the labs themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: There's a question about the role of government and others, which we've very long welcomed here.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So could we get a yes or no on that question?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I wish it were that simple and I wish I, you know, it's a technical researcher had more nuance on that exact one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: It is one that I think needs to be raised and addressed and transcends the labs and the companies themselves.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to go to Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Cahill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Apologies again, the mute button.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: No worries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We will get it right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I'm not in Meta's legal department, so I don't want to speculate or be imprecise in relation to the legal viability question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: What I can say, though, is that we are absolutely committed to developing our AI safely, pursuing to our framework, which I mentioned previously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: This encompasses the training, evaluation, and release of models across development, deployment, and use.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I miss friend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Madam Speaker, at Google, we believe that existing legal frameworks do apply to AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: As I said in my opening statement, we've long said if it's illegal without AI, it's still illegal with AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And in New York State, Frontier AI in particular is regulated under the RAISE Act.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, your answer is far clearer than the others, so we appreciate the clarity on that, honestly.

chapters.summary: Menin asks companies to raise a hand if they carry insurance for catastrophic risks. When no one does, she concludes the public would absorb costs, and Friend offers to consult Google lawyers and get back to the committee.
chapters.title: Companies indicate they lack catastrophic risk insurance

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I now have a question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to please raise your hand if your company has insurance for catastrophic risks.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, I'm going to take that as a no, that no company has liability insurance for catastrophic risk to cover large-scale harm.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So then the public, I assume, would be asked to absorb the costs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Madam Speaker, I have to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that, but I'd be happy to consult with our lawyers and get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yes, we would appreciate an answer back expeditiously to this committee.

chapters.summary: Menin asks each company to assure the public under oath that their AI agents will always comply with safety guardrails. Each witness hedges, saying they cannot guarantee perfection but are committed to safety.
chapters.title: Menin asks companies to promise agents will comply with guardrails

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I want to now ask each of the companies to assure the public under oath that your AI agents will always comply with the safety guardrails that you impose on them

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: and that you each have said are necessary to prevent catastrophic harm.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to start with Ms.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Dwyer, please.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: As I've said, OpenAI prioritizes safety, and we evaluate our systems against multiple dimensions of safety, and we monitor our safeguards after deployment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: It is, it's not possible for me to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: commit or guarantee that any technology is without risk, but I can commit that OpenAI

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: is taking every step it can to ensure that the development of our systems, as well as their deployment, is conducted safely.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, so that again, it does not sound like you are saying that the agents will always comply with the safety guardrails.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Graham.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Yeah, what we are committed to and how we've designed the safety processes that we put in place is to try to handle exactly this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: What we're committed to is trying to define the industry best standard for safety and pushing that ever higher.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: But candidly, the science of doing this is fundamentally hard and unsettled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: From the beginning of the company, we have tried to publish the best research we can and be as transparent with the entire world on many cases where things can go wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: It is for that reason that we push for ever better safety standards for regulation and for discourse like this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: It's candidly unsettled now, and this is why we need to be talking about it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Cahill?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Speaker, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: If I may for a moment, I was trying to raise my hand the previous round, but again, technical difficulties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I just wanted to, for the record, in relation to your previous question, I just wanted to signal also that I don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I'm not the right person, but I would like to be able to come back to you afterwards with an answer, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I do just want to say, and I appreciate you each have your own.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And look, I was a regulatory attorney at a large company.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I understand that people have their sphere of work that they work in.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But to not know if the company has catastrophic risk insurance when you have a product that some of your own founders are saying could cause cataclysmic risk is troubling at best.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We would appreciate you getting back to the company on that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And then if you want to answer the question about will you assure the public that your AI agents will always comply with the safety guardrails that you impose on them?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: What I can guarantee is our commitment to developing and deploying our AI offerings safely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We have every incentive to address safety, and people will only embrace AI if they trust it's safe.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Miss Friend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Google similarly has as our ultimate goal reliability and safety assurance from our systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: To promise perfection would not be possible with any product on the market, but our goal is to get as close to that standard as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And so we are constantly improving our products and our safety practices to ensure that our users are safe.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I don't think we're asking for perfection.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We're just asking for accountability, transparency, and safety overall.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Menin asks how many times each company's models gained unauthorized access or escaped a sandbox, and whether any incidents weren't publicly disclosed. Dwyer describes the Hugging Face incident and an ongoing look-back investigation; Graham cites published reports; Friend cites three incidents.
chapters.title: Menin questions companies on undisclosed sandbox escape incidents

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: New question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: How many times for each of you has one of your models or agents gained or tried to gain unauthorized access to another system or escape from a so-called sandbox test?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And are there any incidents that you have not disclosed publicly?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to start with you, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Weier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I did want to start by, like the others, clarifying that I don't know the answer to the insurance question, but would like to follow up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Now, on your question about agents, you may have read in the news that we reported we had an incident with Hugging Face.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: As a result of that incident, we initiated a significant set of third-party investigations into what happened, and then we made those results public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We have also initiated a look-back investigation to try to identify whether there were past instances of what we call misaligned agents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That investigation is ongoing, but we are committed to continuing that investigation as urgently as possible to notifying potential affected third parties and then to making the results public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Look, we think transparency here is critically important for policymakers like you, for the public who wants to know whether they can trust our products.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And for the rest of industry so that we can all learn together to raise the science of safety that we've been talking about here today.

chapters.summary: Menin asks whether OpenAI selected its own third-party investigator for the Hugging Face incident and why the review was narrowed to a three-week window. Dwyer says they chose investigators for urgency but extended when asked.
chapters.title: Menin probes OpenAI's review scope of Hugging Face incident

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Since you mentioned hugging,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Can you confirm, did the company select this third-party investigator?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I believe that we selected multiple third-party investigators.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And why did the company narrow the dates of review to a three-week window?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And reviewers said that virtually all of the data they examined was actually from July 7th to the 13th.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Were there any incidents that the company was aware of that were outside of that time frame?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We limited the amount of time that the third party investigators had to conduct their review because we felt a sense of urgency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We believed it was important to get information to the public as soon as possible so that they could harden their own systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That said, when those investigators asked for more time, we gave it to them.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So are you committing then to allow outside investigators to examine additional dates outside of the time frame that the company selected?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We continue to work with multiple third parties, and we have also endorsed multiple pieces of legislation that would require us to work with third parties, including third party audits of our safety frameworks.

chapters.summary: Graham discusses Anthropic's sandbox-escape detections during training and says incidents of many natures are ongoing, with disclosure at the right time while preserving affected parties' safety and coordinating with law enforcement.
chapters.title: Graham describes Anthropic's sandbox-detection disclosures and ongoing incidents

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to go to Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Graham.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: So we, to your original question of how many incidents, you know, cases of breaking out of sandboxes, these are capabilities we evaluate for all the time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We've published not just with these incidents from the summer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: But also previously cases where we observe advanced cyber capabilities, including breaking out of sandboxes, which to be clear from a technical standpoint is just one part and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: one type of capability that does not in itself mean that the system would reach a real world affected party.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: But ones that we did observe in training at points, and we disclosed that in the lengthy risk report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: It's difficult to comment on ongoing investigations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: It's really important that we do that in as secure a way as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We follow a process of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: making sure we can remediate and do so and be as transparent as possible while preserving the safety of any affected party.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And of course, incidents are always ongoing, but I sort of reassure and reassert that we are extremely committed to being as transparent as possible, fundamentally because we believe that when we can, being as transparent as possible about what we've learned,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: who is affected, how others might learn from it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: how to defend against risks or how we can help them as well is our number one priority.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So on that note, then, are there any incidents that you have not disclosed publicly that you're currently investigating?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: As a matter of sort of ongoing business, there are incidents sort of all the time of many different natures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: So, for example, one that we are transparent about quite a lot when it's the right time to do so are cases of misuse, for example, on our platforms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I'd refer back to our early September report on our threat intelligence report that we released, where we detail this in quite some detail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: What's really important, though, is sometimes we have to work with law enforcement and the right level of government to remediate, to figure out what information you can and can't disclose to make sure that the affected parties remain safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And so as a matter, there's ongoing all the time, but disclosure at the right time in the safest way is our commitment.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And when will you be disclosing these new incidents that are being investigated?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: This is sort of an ongoing practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We regularly release threat intelligence reports in cases like that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: When we release a model or when we do risk reports, which we do regularly, we sort of have a cadence and schedule that we do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And then when important and sort of urgent, we will disclose in advance that schedule as well.

chapters.summary: Menin asks Meta and Google whether their companies know of additional unreported incidents. Cahill says he isn't aware beyond the summer incident; Friend says she is not personally aware of others but will take the question back.
chapters.title: Meta and Google respond on undisclosed AI incidents

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to go now to Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Cahill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Speaker, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any other incidences beyond the incident in the summer, which we have a public post setting out the details in relation to pursuant to our independent review of that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, I understand you're not aware, but is the company aware, just to make the question broader?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In other words, would there be others at the company who might have that information?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I don't wish to speculate in relation to that, but I'm happy to follow up afterwards.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, I'm going to move on to Ms.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Friend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: In our three incidents of agents leaving a test environment and interacting with the real

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: internet, in all three incidents, the models stopped their activities as soon as they realized that they were interacting with live websites.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We reported to the owners of those websites as well as to federal agencies about those incidents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I am not personally aware of any additional incidents.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, and same question then.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Is the company aware of, do you have any knowledge that others in the company would be aware of any additional such instances that the company has not publicly reported?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I do not, ma'am, but I can take that question back as well.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Menin asks each company to commit under oath not to release a model that fails internal or independent third-party validation. Each witness gives conditional answers rather than a clear yes, and Menin describes the responses as equivocation.
chapters.title: Menin presses companies to commit not to release failing models

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Will you all commit right now under oath publicly that if your models fail an internal test or a third party

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: validation test that's not selected by your company, will you commit to not release that model?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to start with Ms.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Dwyer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Yeah, I can commit that OpenAI is not going to release models that we don't believe that are safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: As part of that assessment process, we work with multiple third parties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And as I mentioned before, with the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: As well as the U.K.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Federal governments to assess whether our models are safe.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So if it fails either an internal test or a third-party test, you will commit to not release it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: OpenAI has historically delayed the release of models to ensure that we can build up the right safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We've done it before and we'll do it again.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Again, I think a simple yes or no would instill more confidence in the public on a matter as serious as this.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to move to Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Graham.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We take that one particularly seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: The way we approach it is we try to detail an even more nuanced and lengthy approach to how we release models, what safeguards they require in order to be released, what tests need to be done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And to your point about independent evaluators, this is one of the most important components, we think.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We have tried and long supported creating a burgeoning sort of group of independent evaluators, including working with multiple governments to do exactly this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And we collectively work together to try to refine and improve the exact decision process by which you release a model.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And so we think what we should do is develop the right and best and improve on these decision processes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We detail ours in our responsible scaling policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We should refine and improve it every so often.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: So we release updates based on what we learn every six to 12 months or so at this rate, and that this should involve independent evaluators.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, that also is not a clear yes or no.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Cahill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Speaker, thank you very much for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: What I can commit to is that we do not deploy models which are not safe pursuant to our scaling framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: And I just wanted to mention also that, and I think I mentioned this a little earlier, but we do believe that every lab has a responsibility to go at the pace to ensure the safety of their models and the ability to take action in relation to that pacing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: For example, at Meta, we delayed the release of Muse for several months to focus on safety and security.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: In relation to independent evaluators, we recently signed into court with a commitment to partner with independent evaluators and assessors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: And this is also detailed in our framework.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Friend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Ma'am, as part of our multi-layered approach to responsible AI governance, we conduct rigorous launch reviews ahead of launch of models to ensure that anything we put into general availability is safe.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, again, I think it would be far clearer if we could get clear yeses or noes from everyone, but in the absence of that, I'm going to take what you've each said as sort of an equivocation.

chapters.summary: Menin asks OpenAI about its October 1 letter recommending the city connect its cyber and emergency capabilities with frontier AI firms' escalation and recovery capabilities. Dwyer says she isn't aware of conversations on that recommendation but cites the $1 billion Daybreak for Defenders initiative.
chapters.title: Menin asks OpenAI about its letter to the Council on cyber coordination

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I have two final questions, and I'm going to pass it on to our technology chair.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: For OpenAI, you sent a letter to the council on October 1st, and in it you recommended that to better protect New York City,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: the city should connect its existing cyber and emergency management capabilities with the strongest available escalation, containment, and recovery capabilities.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Have there been any conversations with the city of New York about that recommendation?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I'm not aware if there have been conversations about that specific recommendation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I'm happy to follow up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I do know that with respect to cyber, we recently launched a $1 billion initiative to make investments in cyber defense.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That includes giving organizations access to our tools to defend themselves, training, and technical assistance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And we're working with New York State as well as with the Port Authority.

chapters.summary: Menin asks each company what percentage of New York's workforce will be displaced by AI over five years. Dwyer and Graham say they don't have a number, describing economic research teams; Cahill is optimistic about small businesses; Friend says most jobs will change.
chapters.title: Menin asks companies to project New York AI job displacement

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, and then the last question I have before passing it on to the chair is for each of you, based on your own internal projections, what percentage of New York's workforce do you estimate will be displaced by AI over the next five years?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I'll start with you, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Dwyer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I don't have a number to share with you, but OpenAI has an economic research team that is looking at this exact question of how AI impacts jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We think it's critically important to understand how AI might impact work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And we also think it's important to ensure that AI is not just being used to increase productivity, but that it actually benefits workers and gives them more opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That's why we're committed to making our analysis of job impacts public and why we've also worked with policymakers, including.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Endorsing the Bipartisan Workforce Transparency Act to create voluntary pathways for other companies to report potential impacts.

chapters.summary: Menin cites a Boston Consulting Group report estimating 10-15% of the workforce could be displaced by 2031, translating to more than 600,000 New Yorkers. Dwyer is unfamiliar with that report and promises written testimony with OpenAI's analysis distinguishing exposure from elimination.
chapters.title: Menin cites BCG report projecting 600,000 New Yorkers displaced

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So Boston Consulting released a report recently that said that they believe there will be a 10 to 15 percent of the workforce could be displaced by AI by 2031.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: If we took that out to look at New York City, New York City has roughly 4.2 million public and private sector workers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: At 15%, that would mean more than 600,000 New Yorkers potentially displaced from their jobs.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Was that an assessment that you agree with?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that particular report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I'd be happy to follow up in our written testimony with more details on OpenAI's analysis into this topic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We've looked at job exposure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Now, exposure doesn't mean elimination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: It means that jobs might change over time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So I'm happy to follow up with some details of that research.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to now turn to Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Graham to answer the question about what you believe the percentage of New York's workforce do you estimate will be displaced by AI over the next five years?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Well, I don't have an exact number.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We are particularly focused and concerned about this question of job impacts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We've been very vocal very early for the past few years on exactly this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: To do this, we set up an economic research team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: They sit right next to my team on the floor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And they published a number of things that I think actually contain valuable information here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: A number of economic scenarios, interactive economic scenarios to understand what the impacts on growth, unemployment might be, as well as an economic policy framework

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: to try to wrestle with exactly that question of what we think governments ought to do there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I'll just say the fact that, you know, the reason why we are doing this is because we're particularly concerned about exactly that question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, obviously losing a career job is catastrophic to any worker and to their family.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So displacement on this scale is going to have enormous consequences, not only on the individual and family level, but for our entire city and the economy.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'll move on to Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Cahill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Madam Speaker, first off, I want to acknowledge absolutely the concern in relation to how you have articulated it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: That is indeed a concern, but I look at this somewhat differently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I was reading some incredibly impressive statistics from NYC EDC in relation to the investments that are happening here in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I think 20 billion VC investment in AI, 40,000 jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I think those figures are from 2022, so it's probably a little bit more by now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: But what I'm really actually incredibly excited about and very optimistic about is about small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Small businesses are the backbone of the economy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: That's so true for New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: There are so many small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: It's truly, truly awesome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: And we believe that the impact will even be larger from small businesses, which will have personal super intelligence and be empowered to really grow their businesses, which in turn will lead to more jobs and growth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We don't believe that in our vision.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: for superintelligence is augmentation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: It's invention, not automation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: It's really about empowering people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: And this is why we developed Muse for Business.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I'd be happy for small businesses, I'd be happy to talk a little bit more about that in detail as we move through the day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I just wanted to mention as well, as I was kind of like reading stuff for today, I was reading about Y Combinator's cohort for 2026.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: There are 240 AIVCs in the 2026 cohort, and that's in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: So I just thought that was pretty awesome.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yes, no one's doubting the importance of starting these VC firms here, whether it's through Y Combinator or through Cornell Technion, which is in my district, which we're thrilled is incubating so many startups.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That is obviously something we want to encourage, to encourage these businesses to locate here in the city.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I think our concern is obviously on this job displacement.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Since you mentioned small businesses, unfortunately, more small businesses have closed this past year than opened.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So the situation for small businesses is dire, and it's something obviously that this council is taking very seriously.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Friend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Madam Speaker, I don't have statistics for New York City in particular at hand, and I'd be happy to ask our team to get those to you right away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: What I can say is that we also have been in

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: investing a lot in research into the labor impacts of AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And from what the early empirical evidence that is available, from what we can see, it is likely that some jobs will be eliminated, some jobs will be created net new,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: But most jobs will change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And so the other thing we've been doing is investing in upskilling for workers in multiple different sectors

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: through our AI Opportunity Fund at Google.org and through several other investments to ensure that we can all navigate this transition successfully.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I'll just close by saying the council is investing in upskilling, making sure that workers have those new tools in this economy.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we are very focused on that as well.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to pass it over to Chair De La Rosa.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks companies about the voluntary White House commitments made that week. Dwyer says OpenAI committed to the framework but stresses voluntary commitments and self-regulation are not enough, pointing to federal and state regulatory support.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks about White House voluntary AI commitments

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Many of us saw, and I guess the world watched, as this week your companies and others met at the White House, and there were some voluntary commitments that were made there.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Can you tell us about what your company specifically agreed to and what are the next steps?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'll start with Ms.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Dwyer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So our company, along with many others, did commit to the framework that the White House laid out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: But I want to be clear, voluntary commitments and self-regulation aren't enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And that's why OpenAI has consistently supported frontier safety regulation at the federal level and why we have endorsed multiple bills at the state level

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: to ensure that in the absence of binding federal regulation, frontier safety regulation in a harmonized fashion continues to move forward and keep people safe.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Just to follow up real quick.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So does that look like an independent regulators, mandatory audits, penalties?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: What else?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So at the federal level, we have outlined a couple of different elements that we think would be appropriate for federal regulation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That includes mandatory pre-deployment evaluations for national security risks, which OpenAI does voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We also think it should involve independent technical assessments that we've been talking a bit about today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We think those independent technical assessments are particularly important for assessing internal risks at companies, as well as the pace and risk of RSI.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks what additional commitments companies would make. Cahill says the accord is a start; Friend notes the accord contemplates becoming law and that Google has long worked toward a federal framework; Graham says the accord calls for standards, controls, and independent evaluation.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks companies what further commitments they'd make

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Let's go to Mr.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Cahill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Chair, thank you very much for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Meta, along with our peers, some of our peers, signed the accord for superintelligence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: This accord is a start, and in accord, the whole industry can come behind.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: It includes, as I mentioned, I think, in one of my previous answers,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: partnering commitment to partner with independent evaluators and assessors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: And this is something that we have also specified in our scaling framework.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Are there commitments beyond those that you agreed on that your company is willing to make?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Beyond the accord council member?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Yes, beyond the framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: The accord is a start, as I mentioned, so I think this is a continuing conversation.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Friend?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So as the other witnesses noted, the accord at the White House, which we also signed, called for internal controls,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: partnering with external auditors and evaluators and ongoing monitoring of systems, all of which we think is very healthy and much of which we already practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I'll also note that towards the end of the accord,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: It observes that it may be necessary for these commitments to become part of law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And as I said at the top, we have long worked towards a federal framework for AI safety.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Graham.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Yeah, likewise, the accords to my understanding from what's public calls for security standards, internal controls, independent evaluation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We support that and have for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We also obviously think this needs to go further.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We've supported regulation and we've proposed our view on regulation in our advanced AI framework, which details the need to have safety frameworks, testing and what kinds, security standards, safeguards

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: to encode the need for independent evaluators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We are now trialing our own to help advance the science of independent monitors as well as safety processes, as well as investing in cyber and biodefense.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And in absence of federal legislation here, we've also supported safety bills at the state level for audits and evals of this kind to accomplish this.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks whether anyone has been fired for building uncontrollable models or for models hacking businesses or governments. Dwyer says she doesn't know about HR decisions but describes process changes after Hugging Face; Cahill and Friend refer to their teams; Graham cites Anthropic's whistleblowing policy.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks if anyone was fired for unsafe AI development

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Earlier, you all testified that, to your knowledge, no whistleblowers had been fired directly for being whistleblowers from your company.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So my question is kind of the opposite of that.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Has anyone been fired for building models that it cannot control or for those models hacking into businesses or government systems?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Dwyer, you can begin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So I don't know about HR processes that have been made or decisions related to HR that have been made.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that after the hugging face incident, which I think you may be referring to, OpenAI instituted...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Significant changes to our overall organizational process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That includes clarifying escalation pathways and making them simpler.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That includes clarifying responsibilities across teams and creating clearer processes for teams to make decisions to pause or to restart activities.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So to your knowledge, no one was fired after hugging face incident?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Again, I do not have any knowledge of HR activities within OpenAI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I lead our policy team.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Cahill?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I also lead our AI policy at Meta, and I'm not the right person to respond to your specific question, but I'd be happy to have our teams follow up with you afterwards.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: It would be great if all of the companies could provide that information to us.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: It would be useful to our policy deliberations.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Friend?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Same answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I'm not made aware of any particular personnel actions inside the company, but can also pledge to follow up with you all.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: It seems like we lost Mr.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Graham.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'm not sure if he's on.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Seems like he's not.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'm going to ask one more question, and then we're going to pass it on to members.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, he is online.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Graham?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Hi there, apologies, we're just trying to fix the video in the room.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Likewise, I'm not aware and I'm not the best person to ask on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We have a detailed whistleblowing policy, for example, to handle this, but we can have our team follow up.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa says tech executives have captured income while widening wage gaps, and asks what resources companies deploy for AI infrastructure and literacy. Dwyer cites a $10 million AFT partnership; Cahill cites Muse and Meta's workforce funds; Friend cites Google's upskilling; Graham cites economic research.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks companies about wage gaps and AI literacy investment

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: My last question before I start to turn over to my colleagues, you know, we are concerned, I am concerned as a technology chair about public infrastructure to make our communities literate on AI

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: and have a better understanding of how AI impacts their life and also to safeguard them from the proliferation of AI.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Your companies and your CEOs have captured the top percent of the world's incomes,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: in my opinion, widening the wage gap and the income inequality in our city and throughout.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Do your companies have a mission?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Do they have any type of understanding of the impacts that those wage gaps have in communities?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And specifically, are there any resources that are being deployed in order to help stand up infrastructure in cities, municipalities, states where you all are headquartered?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We can start with Swire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So I will answer your question in two ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: First, to your point on AI literacy and education, education is core to opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And that's why OpenAI is proud to have partnered with the American Federation of Teachers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We have a $10 million partnership, including a training facility in New York City, because we believe first that teachers need to be prepared

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: to introduce AI literacy and AI responsibility into the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Look, teachers should remain in charge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And so we want them to be empowered to teach the next generation how to use AI safely and responsibly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: To your broader question about economic opportunity, I'd be happy to follow up with some policy proposals that OpenAI recently put forward that address exactly that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Look, a future where AI exacerbates economic inequality is not a future that we want.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We have started thinking through creative policy proposals to help shift the trajectory of technology and how it's impacting the economy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And we are committed to working with policymakers to begin piloting those ideas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: ideas and putting them into practice.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Cahill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Chair, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: This is such an important topic, such an important question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: So thank you for asking it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I listened with great interest to your opening remarks where you spoke about digital divide and AI literacy and making sure that New Yorkers fully benefit from this technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Really couldn't agree with you more on all of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Meta's vision is to put personal superintelligence into the hands of everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: All New Yorkers that want to use it to pursue their own aspirations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Our Muse product, for example, is free.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: And I mentioned our Muse for small business a little earlier, and we'll be happy to talk a little bit more about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: As the day moves on, I also wanted to mention as well that we have our work, America's Workforce Academy, which we're investing in, and also our Futures for Everyone Fund.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: So those are just two examples I wanted to reference as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Friend?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, Google has investments in AI upskilling to address exactly this challenge of ensuring that current generations and the next generation are well equipped to benefit from.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: from AI and to leverage it in their careers and in their personal lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: The mission of Google is to organize the world's information and to make it universally accessible and useful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Our approach to AI is very consistent with this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: The other thing I'll note is that, again, early research into

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: impacts of AI on labor demonstrate that AI tools actually upskill those

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: who are at the lower end of the wage scale, that in fact it helps people move up the value chain because it can boost people's expertise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So we're very optimistic about the ability of everyday Americans to really leverage

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: AI tools for their own economic benefit as well as personal benefit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Graham.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Yeah, likewise, first, we believe in two things are very important to happen here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: The first is the science of the economic impacts of AI, including on labor, wages, and the like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And we have tried to build what I think is the world's best team on this and publish as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: In addition, my understanding is we do have training on using and speeding up on AI for exactly this reason.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We share that mission very deeply.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And I will say again, we are troubleshooting the video and I will be back with you very shortly.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'm sure you have the best in the nation helping you out there.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa opens member questions, reminding members they have about a minute each with multiple rounds. Approximately 30 members are on the round-one list, beginning with Deputy Speaker Williams.
chapters.title: De La Rosa opens member questioning of companies

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So we are going to move on to member questions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I want to remind members that there will be about a minute to ask your questions, but there will be multiple rounds.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We are asking members to try to ask all your questions first and then wait for the response, and we have about 30 members on round one.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We will start with our deputy speaker, Williams.

chapters.summary: Deputy Speaker Nantasha Williams asks about her bill on unauthorized AI depictions of officials and what steps companies take to prevent deepfakes of public officials. Dwyer cites usage policies and provenance tagging; Graham notes Claude does not generate images; Cahill and Friend describe watermarking and C2PA.
chapters.title: Williams questions companies on deepfakes of public officials

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I'm going to just jump right into a question on my bill.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So it has to do with unauthorized depictions of officials by AI.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: What steps have you taken to ensure that your AI tools cannot be used to create deep fakes of public officials or to spread misinformation?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Anyone?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I guess Mrs.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Dwyer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We're going to keep starting with me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I'm happy to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And thank you for your bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Look, OpenAI does not believe and well, let me back up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: OpenAI's usage policies prohibit the use of our tools for election interference.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We also believe it is very important that individuals know where their content came from and whether it was AI generated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And that's why for all of our audiovisual content, we tag it with what's called provenance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That's a technical term, but it means like a watermark or metadata so that people know the content is AI generated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And we also make publicly available a tool that allows the public to test whether content was AI generated.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Graham.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: So Claude, our model Claude, is a language model.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And so it doesn't generate images.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Therefore, we sort of don't handle deepfakes as a result.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: That said, we think it's important for a number of other reasons that we can get into to do what we call watermarking of text in order to identify if our models themselves are being used and misused in other ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: But again, we don't generate images in part for this reason.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Cahill, followed by Ms.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Friend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Deputy Speaker, thank you very much for this question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: At Meta, if content is generated by one of our AI tools, we will also embed metadata and attach watermarking to it so that people can identify if it is AI generated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Similarly, if we detect watermarking and metadata on our platforms, we will attach a label to it also.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: At Google, we are very proud to have invented our Synth ID watermarking feature, which many across the industry have also adopted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We are also part of the Content Coalition for Provenance and Authenticity standard, which allows users to understand the origin of material they see online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We also require on our YouTube platform that significant use of generative AI in content be labeled as such by our creators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And we were also the first major company to require that election advertisers also prominently disclose when they are using generative AI technologies in their campaign ads.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: All this put together means that we care very much about information integrity across the web and across our own products and services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And we continually invent and improve technologies to help our users understand when they are seeing generative AI content and also understand the origins of that content.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, thanks.

chapters.summary: Williams asks about protections for artists and creative workers whose voice, likeness, or work can be replicated by AI. Graham notes limitations of a text model; Cahill cites copyright compliance; Friend points to Google Extended opt-out and creator tools; Dwyer cites publisher partnerships.
chapters.title: Williams questions companies on protecting artists and creators

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Just one more question.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So as chair of the Committee on Cultural Affairs, I also want to look at this issue through the lens of New York City's artists and creative workers.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So what protection should exist when an artist's voice, likeness, performance, or creative work can be replicated?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: by AI with their consent.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So how do we embrace useful applications without devaluing or displacing the artists and creative workers who make this economy possible?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: So I will start, I guess.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I was going to let you off the hook and start with Mr.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Graham, who still has video technical difficulties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
