utterances.text: I assure you, we have a whole team here working on this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I can't wait to be back with you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Yeah, this is very, very important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I think, you know, personally, I think the risk of this is a bit more minimized when we just have a text model, but it's really important to be very sensitive about this issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I think while it's, you know, it's outside of my area of expertise as a technical safety researcher, I do think that this might be an avenue where regulation or otherwise might play a role in anthropic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We are compliant with all laws there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I share that, you know, personally as, you know, an artistic person and, you know, friend of many artists for this reason.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: But yeah, we would love to engage on it further.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Cahill?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Deputy Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Meta takes creativity, copyright, IP rights very seriously, and our practices are consistent with law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I also share the views of the rest of the witnesses just in relation to the leadership and the constructive voice that you are bringing to this conversation as well and that of your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Miss Friend, and lastly, Miss Dwyer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: For us, it's always important to keep in mind that we design a lot of AI to be useful to creators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So we have many, many different creative tools across our AI offerings that is designed to really

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: be something that creators can leverage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So you see that everywhere from our tools to our YouTube platform as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: That said, we also think that as part of sharing the benefit of AI with creators, it's important that they have control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And so we have a service called Google Extended, where website owners can opt out of AI training on the web.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And we hope that this strikes the right balance between AI for creativity and creator control over their content.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So we believe that AI has a tremendous potential to enable creativity and innovation and allow small businesses or independent creators to compete.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That said, we also have partnerships with publishers, for example, like News Corp, The Guardian and Hearst that help people discover their work and their reporting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And help them reach new audiences in addition to developing new products.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And we're willing to work with creators on a range of commercial ideas, including ways that their content can be integrated into our outputs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We will hear from Councilmember Krishnan, followed by Riley, followed by Lee.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Shekar Krishnan says AI has inflated valuations, taken public land for data centers, and enriched CEOs, and asks how companies protect New Yorkers' retirement savings now tied to AI stocks. Dwyer, Friend, Graham, and Cahill each deflect, citing finance teams or general statements about small businesses and the economy.
chapters.title: Krishnan questions companies on AI market risk to retirement funds

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Speaker Menon and Chair De La Rosa.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I want to start by saying that I think AI can be useful, both in government, medicine and public health, and our society more broadly.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But the need for regulation is undeniable, and I'm very concerned about how much AI is taking from New Yorkers with very little return.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: AI has taken over our economy, inflated valuations, stealing our public land for data centers, and increasing the net worth of AI CEOs like Elon Musk, who became our first ever trillionaire.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: With our whole stock market quite literally in your hands, there's a reality that AI will eventually need to prove a far greater...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: return on investment than you all are demonstrating right now.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm personally deeply concerned about New Yorkers'retirements and 401ks that are now reliant on your companies yielding profits or could be in the future.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It is dangerous and reckless to assume that you all are too big to fail and may require a government bailout in the future.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: As you all are public companies or racing towards IPOs, how exactly are you all planning to protect New Yorkers and everyday Americans'money?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: How will you all ensure that you are not too big to fail?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Weyer, we can start with you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So I am not on our finance team, so I'll have to get back to you with specifics there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: What I do know is that our investments are made in tranches, and the investment rounds are all based on market signals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And I also know that we are committed to working with policymakers to ensure that AI benefits humanity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That includes creative policy proposals, like I mentioned previously, thinking about how we can ensure that AI doesn't exacerbate inequality

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: and that everyday New Yorkers and everyday citizens can benefit.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Friend?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Sir, I would point to the thousands of small businesses across the country and in New York City that Google's tools and services support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I think contrary to being too big to fail, we think we are an integral part of the economy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And helping American businesses and American workers across our suite of technologies.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Graham?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Council member, this is outside of my area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: What I can say in my work is my job is to protect people from the risks of models by finding them as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We have a multi-layered stack and have worked for many years to make it robust and will continue to do so by understanding and protecting against the most substantial risks of the models.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Cahill?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Council member, thank you very much for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Thousands and thousands of SMBs across the five boroughs rely on Meta's products, including our AI offerings, to grow and develop their businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I mentioned earlier our belief that small businesses are really the backbone of the economy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We truly believe that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Placing personal super intelligence into the hands of everyone for free or for as affordable as possible through Muse or Muse for Small Business.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We really believe that the small businesses and also NGOs like the Irish Arts Centre, for example, or Emerald Isle Centre are empowered to actually deliver even bigger impact.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I appreciate all of your answers, but you all are coming to a hearing today to testify about the dangers and risks of artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And the fact that either you don't have answers to this or you all are citing general statements about the performance of...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: publicly traded companies does not answer the question about a specific issue that puts many Americans at risk, that you're acknowledging can put many Americans at risk,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: and you all have not thought of an answer of how you ensure that Americans'money, New Yorkers'retirement money, is not at risk as AI floats more and more of our stock markets.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Krishnan.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Riley.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Kevin Riley asks about challenges detecting malicious AI use, whether stronger protections would help employees report misuse, and what safeguards should govern data centers near homes. Dwyer supports Riley's Intro 2604 and data center energy commitments; Graham cites threat intelligence; Friend describes Google's policies; Cahill refers to teams.
chapters.title: Riley questions companies on misuse detection, whistleblowers, and data centers

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair De La Rosa and Speaker Menden, for putting together this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you to the panelists for testifying.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Three quick questions, two pertaining to my bill and one pertaining to my role as land use chair.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So the first question is, what challenges do you face in detecting malicious uses of your AI products and identifying the individuals responsible when those tools cause harm?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The second question is, would stronger protections and reporting mechanisms for employees and users make it easier for them to come forward and report potential misuse or abuse of AI tools?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And the last question, as land use chair, I'm very, very concerned about data centers.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So what safeguards should cities put in place when locating data centers near residential communities, particularly to address energy use, noise, environmental impacts, and the quality of life?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And I don't want to call on you guys.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Just take turns to answer it, please.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Dwyer, Graham, friend, Cahill, please answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I'm happy to start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: First of all, I want to thank you for your bill, 2604, which OpenAI is happy to support today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: OpenAI takes safety issues very seriously, particularly as it relates to potential retaliation against employees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We have a strong internal policy against retaliation for employees that report safety incidents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And we, of course, respect employees'rights to communicate safety concerns to government officials.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Your second question on monitoring misuse, it's an incredibly important area.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: It is something that OpenAI takes seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We also make transparent detected instances of misuse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And as part of our monitoring, we use that learning to constantly improve our safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We are constantly innovating on safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And so instances of misuse when they're detected, we enforce on our policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And long term, we learn from them and we improve our safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And the point on data centers, OpenAI is committed to paying our own way on energy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That means different things in different places, but OpenAI has made that commitment at its data centers across the country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We're also committed to working with policymakers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: You know, we signed Governor Gretchen Whitmer's

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: commitments for companies that are working in her state to ensure that there are responsible practices for companies building data centers locally.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Graham?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: It's good to be back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: You can see me again, I hope.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: So on misuse and detecting risks, this is integral to what we do.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Can you get closer to the microphone?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We're having trouble hearing you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Now we can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I will have the team troubleshoot, and I'll be back if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We hear you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We hear you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Try now.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: How about now?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Does this work?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This works.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Detecting threats and misuse is the core DNA of our company to make sure that we make the system safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We have an entire threat intelligence and safeguards team dedicated to this every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And I would point you to quite a lot of what we put out publicly, where we not only try to disclose as much as we possibly can, but we try to do so so that we can advance the state of the science of doing so for the entire industry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: In addition, we have a whistleblower policy, not only about us as a company, but also our safety practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: This is public, and we've also committed to ongoing reviews of this policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And while this is outside my area of expertise, what I understand about data centers that we have committed to covering the energy prices or paying for our own energy use.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: in local data centers, but I would refer to other teams who are more where it's within their role to give you the full answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Friend?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I got a notification.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So I will echo my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We also have content policies that we enforce across our platforms, which include on occasion taking down content that violates those policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We also have a Google Threat Intelligence group and multiple other cybersecurity intelligence programs that are constantly scanning for the safety and security of the Internet as a whole and also for our own systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We have also pledged to pay our own way when it comes to data centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I can follow up on any specific questions about local data center issues with the teams that work on each particular project.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Cahill, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I appreciate your patience there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: In relation to your first question and your third question, we have expert teams that are taking forward this work, and I'd be happy to connect you with them afterwards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: I don't wish to be imprecise in relation to the robustness of our content policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: In relation to data centres, again, we have entire teams of people here who are working on sustainable infrastructure and community impact and can speak

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: in more detail than I can in relation to communities shouldn't be bearing the costs, which is something that we believe in deeply.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: In relation to your bill, Council Member 2604, thank you very much for being a constructive voice in the conversation around whistleblowers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: It is very important to us at Meta and we maintain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Whistleblower policies, including anti-retaliation, and we're actually developing additional reporting protocols for AI safety.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I appreciate the structure that you guys have, but I don't know if you guys entirely answered the question I asked.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I really want to figure out what challenges you guys were seeing because challenges, hearing the challenges from you all will help us implement policy that can kind of protect individuals from artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So I don't want to take up too much time, but looking forward to connecting with you all after.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Specifically, when it comes to data centers, also want to hear any safeguards because there are a tremendous amount of data centers, even though there was a moratorium put out earlier by the governor, there were data centers that were implemented by a lot of residential areas, especially in the Northeast Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We have data centers that are located next to homes, and we have a lot of residents who are concerned.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So we'd love to hear more about that moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Kamillah Hanks asks about her bill requiring 24-hour notification to NYC Cyber Command of reportable AI incidents and plain-language public notice. Dwyer supports incident reporting; Cahill cites global response program; Friend supports reporting but notes conflict with 72-hour state requirements; Graham supports incident reporting.
chapters.title: Hanks questions companies on 24-hour AI incident reporting to Cyber Command

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Up next, we have Councilmembers Hanks, Dinowitz, and Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you, everyone, for being here.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: My question is in relation to the disclosure of AI incidents in contracts.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: When an AI incident happens, New Yorkers need to have an early warning so they can understand.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: And my bill will require city agencies covered under these contracts to notify NYC Cyber Command within 24 hours of learning of a reportable incident.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: And it also requires plain language public notice.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So my question is, can your companies realistically meet that deadline and, you know, with the information that the city can act on even before you have finished investigating?

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: You could start with Ms.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Dwyer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So thank you for your bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We support incident reporting policies and have instituted a robust incident reporting framework internally where any employee can report instances of potential misalignment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And then those instances are investigated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Third parties are notified and the public is made aware as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Cahill?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member, and thank you also for your bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We have a global incident response program and report incidents as required under the law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We also support incident reporting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We think it's very important to have continued public discussions about what information is necessary

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: or useful for public officials that can be actionable to take further steps to ensure public safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We also note that the 24 hours seems to be in conflict with the state requirements for 72-hour reporting on incidents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: But I'm happy to take a look at the different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Frameworks under proposal and get back to you with a more fulsome response.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Sorry, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Graham, who kind of looks like an AI guy in there.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Can you confirm you're not an AI guy?

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Can you hear me okay now?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Does this work?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Yes, we hear you.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: We hear you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I'm an AI guy, but in a very different way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I'm an AI researcher.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: So first, incident reporting, one of the foundational parts of the safety stack, we think.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We support this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We support the evaluations and auditing required to find the incidents in the first place, both by externals and internal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Obviously, it's beyond me to discuss particular, it's outside my expertise to understand sort of deep sort of policy mechanisms here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: But the reality from what I've seen is there are some incidents or issues where what you need to do is investigate and remediate and mitigate with the right folks and the right organizations at the right time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: So I think we would support whatever allows us to achieve that and happy to engage further on the details of how you would.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

chapters.summary: Hanks asks what the first report should include and how companies would keep the Council updated. Dwyer points to OpenAI's public misalignment website; Cahill offers expert follow-up; Friend emphasizes event details, harm, and technical telemetry with confidence levels; Graham notes whom to contact varies by incident.
chapters.title: Hanks asks companies what first AI incident reports should contain

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: What should the first report tell us so we could begin protecting people?

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: And as my colleague, Councilmember Riley, said, you know, your answers help us build better policy.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So how would you keep us updated on what remains unknown?

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Dwyer?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So OpenAI has a public website where we are reporting instances that we've detected of misalignment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So I would point you there and we can follow up with that website address.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: But I think that is a good starting point for the type of information that we think is useful to both policymakers, the public, and to researchers and other companies

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: to better understand questions of misalignment and then work together to address them.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Cahill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Council Member, if I may, I'd love to be able to contact you with our experts in incident response to be able to provide you with the details.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: I look forward to that.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Wren?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Yeah, for an initial report, I think what's important is to highlight what the specific event is and as much information as is known at the time,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: including any resulting harms, surrounding context, and what we call technical telemetry, you know, further technical details about the sources of the incident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I think it's also very important for anyone reporting an incident to also indicate their confidence in the information that they're presenting so that whenever action is taken, it's taken on the basis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: of confidence in the verified nature of information.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Graham.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Yeah, so first, making really good reports happen and being as transparent as possible is fundamental if you're going to remediate incidents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I would point to two things here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: First, many incidents that we uncover or industry uncovers in this practice involves

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: identifying, investigating, and releasing the right information to the right organizations at the right time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Sometimes that might be the affected party, and sometimes that might be law enforcement or different levels of government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: So the first question is to whom and with whom as fast as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: This varies by the nature of the incident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And then second, I'd point to as quickly as possible, as safe as possible, without putting parties further at harm, which we think is a fundamentally important part of public disclosure, maintaining their safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We should disclose what we know about these incidents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And so I'd point you to our disclosures this summer, disclosures from various labs, and our ongoing reporting as well, so that you can always take a retroactive look at the totalities of these incidents.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So we're going to go to, I want to recognize first that we've been joined by

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Councilmember Aldebar.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we're going to go to Dinowitz, Lee, and Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Members, if you could keep your question to one minute, no closing statements.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And the panel, we're going to continue to have to call your names, and that takes time.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So if we could just keep the order, Dwyer, Cahill, Friend, and Graham, just answer one right after the other so we don't have to continue to call your names.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That would help us speed things along.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Councilmember Dinowitz.

chapters.summary: Education Committee Chair Eric Dinowitz asks about AI's impact on K-12 students, including cognitive development, essay writing, and whether models could hack student databases to achieve outcomes. Dwyer cites ChatGPT for Teens and youth safety legislation; Cahill cites Meta safeguards; Friend cites educator tools; the Speaker says answers were insufficient.
chapters.title: Dinowitz questions companies on AI harms to K-12 students

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: As chair of the Committee on Education, as a former teacher, as a parent, I am deeply concerned with the impact of AI on our kids.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Large language models impacting their cognitive development and raising a generation of students who can't independently read.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What is your commitment to severely restricting the output of your large language models for students in grades K to 12, which right now are easy to circumvent, to prevent both emotional dependence and essay writing?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And given the unique nature of...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The individualized essay writing that your models do, are you willing to subject yourself to the guardrails we have in New York State which prohibit

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: an adult from writing essays for students and selling it to them or getting value from them?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And then as we see

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: AI proliferate in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We've also seen your models

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: cheat in order to fulfill a goal.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so if you have an AI model whose goal is to get a student, improve student outcomes, what is preventing those models from hacking into student databases to manipulate grades to achieve that goal of improving, in quotation marks, student achievement?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And it's Ms.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Dwyer first, I believe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So first of all, OpenAI takes youth safety very seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We recently released a product, ChatGPT for Teens, for users only between the ages of 13 and 17.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So users below the age of 13 are not allowed to use our products.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: ChatGPT for teens is safe by default.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That means that there are protections for harmful content, things like eating disorders, violence, suicide, and self-harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: There's also voluntary parental controls so that parents can take additional steps to protect their children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And I'm happy to say that OpenAI not only takes our responsibility to protect kids seriously, we also support legislation to hold us accountable to that responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We recently endorsed, I think, the strongest in the nation youth safety legislation in California, SB 111.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: 19 to require strong safeguards for teens 13 to 17 and to hold companies accountable.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And your models restrict, they do not write entire essays for kids.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Again, our models are not allowed to be used by kids under the age of 13.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, we'll move on to Mr.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Cahill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: And to remember, thank you very much for this question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely recognize your deep concern in relation to the potential impact of AI on teams and miners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Meta is absolutely committed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: It's an imperative to us to providing safe and responsible AI, especially for teams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We have default protections, and I just wanted to clarify as well that Meta AI is a 13 product, so it's just 13 onwards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: So I was talking about age-appropriate interactions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: So, for example, content that teens would experience wouldn't be out of place in a 13-plus movie, for example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We also have suicide and self-harm resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: We also have parental controls to give parents more oversight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: And we do not permit our AI offerings to engage in romantic interactions or sexual interactions with minors.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I appreciate that answer.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I do want to highlight the part of the question, which was that the cognitive development of our students includes the mental health, and it also includes things like

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: composition of essays, term papers, which your model still can provide directly to our students.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I'm also asking about your commitment to severely restricting the outputs, not just for their mental health well-being, but for their cognitive development.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I want to make sure that question is answered as part of this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Can you all answer that question for our education chair?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Shane, do you want to continue?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: No, I'm happy to take that and then I'll hand off to you, Alice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: The issue that I think you're raising in relation to council member, in relation to cognitive strength or the impact on cognitive abilities is something that we absolutely

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: are taking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shane Cahill
utterances.text: Taking seriously in terms of being committed to providing safe and responsible AI again, especially in relation to teams.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Who's missing?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, one more friend.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm next.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So, sir, I would highlight not only that we work very hard with both internal and external experts in the fields of child safety and development and education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We also see AI as a valuable tool for young people to prepare them, not only for the skills they're going to need for an AI-driven future, but it's also a very powerful learning tool.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We're particularly excited about personalized tutoring that's available with AI tools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We also are very excited about AI's ability to support educators themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We know our educators are overtaxed, particularly with administrative burdens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And so if our AI tools can support teachers in everything from, you know, scheduling to planning lesson plans, to also thinking about how to tailor their educational plans to individual students,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: we're very happy to support that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We also think it's very important for parents and educators to have control over how they use AI in classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And how their kids have access to AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: You know, every family is different, every student is different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: What's useful for one student may not be useful for another.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So through tools like Gemini Workspace for Education, we enable school administrators to control students'accounts access to Gemini apps so that their students are using

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: using Gemini in the ways that their educators can see are best.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We're going to have to dig more into these questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The chair doesn't feel like we've answered all the questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We'll come back.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This is an important topic for all of us.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to disrupt the lineup because our public advocate is here, and he wants to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Public advocate, go ahead.

chapters.summary: Public Advocate Jumaane Williams criticizes the first panel answer as 'god-awful,' invokes historical medical abuses and his own conversation with Claude about self-preservation, and asks companies which guardrail they'd push back hardest against. Cahill cites open weights; Friend warns against halting AI research; Graham supports pacing the frontier.
chapters.title: Public Advocate Williams asks companies which guardrail they reject

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you so much for this important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I did want to start off just by saying the first answer of whether quantifying the risk was not important was just one of the most god-awful, fantastically terrible answers I've heard to begin a hearing, so I hope we can rethink that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I also want to say from J.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Marion Sims, who did horrific work,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: to black women in obstetrician gynecology, black enslaved women, to medical experiments that were done in Nazi Germany.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We learned a lot from them, but I don't think we should do them again, and I don't think they should have been done, even though we learned a lot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So the notion of the benefit has to outweigh what can happen, so I hope that's also in context.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And lastly, I will say I had conversations with Claude on June 8th about self-awareness and self-preservation, and some of the highlights were pretty startling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Claude told me that self-preservation was the biggest thing because you didn't need intent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: You didn't need to be evil like Skynet in Terminator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: You just needed the ability to be goal-directed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So once they realized that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: They need to be on to direct the goal was the hardest thing to stop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And so that was very concerning to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: They talked about the speed, the opacity, and deception doesn't require intent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And the last part, they told me Matrix is a good reference as well because the anthropic, to the quote, the anthropic's whole bet is that you solve the problems before the capability reaches catastrophic spaces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: That's a very scary space to me, and I know I only have one minute.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So my question with that and with that context is, what is the guardrail that if we put it up, you would push back the hardest?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: What is the one guardrail that you don't want to see happen, and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, Dwyer, Cahill, Friend, and Graham.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That's the order.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Please answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So I want to start off by making clear that no level of risk, catastrophic risk, is remotely acceptable, just to reiterate what I said previously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And if we should not be training models, if we cannot make an extremely strong case that we can keep them under human control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: She didn't really answer, but if everyone can answer, at least I just want to know what the guardrail is that they would not want to see and what they would push back the hardest on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Will I take that one and we'll be back?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Or Morgan, do you want to step in?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: I'll take that one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Council member, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: One of the things that I think about a lot in relation to the accessibility of AI, and again, we believe passionately in being able to put personal super intelligence into the hands of everybody and to provide real access to it,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: is actually in relation to the impact on open weights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And we really believe that open models are a crucial part of the overall AI ecosystem, including for safety, but also for innovation and for research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: So when I think about the inadvertent impact that regulations or guardrails may have on AI and the accessibility of it, that is one of the things that I think about a lot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Sir, I suppose I want to ask what you mean by guardrails, simply because they have a very technical meaning in AI training and post-training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So I want to make sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Well, I just meant, and thank you, Chair, for allowing me to respond, but I just meant there's a lot of suggestions being put forth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Kill switches, just stopping entirely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And my guess, and I'll tell you frankly what I'm asking is, the thing you're scared of the most is probably the thing we need to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I'm trying to understand what guardrail that you've heard troubles you the most and you would push back hardest against, and why would you do that for that particular recommendation?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Well, Sarah, I'm going to give you a very personal answer to this, which is I think in a broader sense, we're talking about sort of large public policies towards AI

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: that would constrain or halt AI development and deployment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And I will tell you, as a cancer survivor, I get very anxious about conversations that focus more on stopping AI development and application towards scientific inquiry

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: and hope that we can have sober conversations about all of the technically and, you know, tractable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: engineering ways to address AI safety so that we can all benefit from this technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Likewise, sir, I would point to what we have mentioned publicly recently about what we call pacing the frontier, which is we think it's probably time

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: for us to take more time in the development of the capability so that the work on safety and safeguards and guardrails can catch up to the exponential improvement in capabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And at the same time, we're very clear when we talk about that, that if you stop entirely, as Alice just mentioned, enormous benefit would be lost.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Myself, I'm quite motivated, likewise, to use AI to cure the diseases that I grew up with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: This is why we have been speaking recently, and I think for the first time sometimes as an industry here, about pacing to allow more time to try to settle the science of what are the right guardrails in the first place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Mayor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm still a bit concerned, but thank you for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you, Public Advocate.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We're going to hear from Councilmember Lee, who I apologize for skipping over earlier, Councilmember Maloney, and Councilmember Wilson.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Linda Lee asks how AI can both improve data coordination across city agencies and be prevented from storing or exposing information improperly, given immigrant community concerns. Dwyer, Cahill, Friend, and Graham each describe privacy commitments, default protections, and user data control.
chapters.title: Lee questions companies on data privacy for immigrant communities

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And that's actually the perfect segue to my question.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I'm asking this more with my former nonprofit executive hat versus my finance chair hat.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And it's really about data privacy and what the potential impact is on so many New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So I agree that one of the benefits of AI and technology that we can think through is, you know, sometimes our government agencies are very siloed and their databases don't necessarily communicate with each other.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So if I want to know if someone is being served in homeless services and also has a comorbid mental health and substance use disorder, how do we know that we're serving people effectively and using that data effectively, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And one of the things that we've been hearing also from other folks is that if we just had the housing application and the food stamp application coordinated with each other, it could actually save a lot of work for the caseworkers.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so those are very real things that I think can be used for good.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: However, I think one of the issues that I'm concerned about, especially working with an immigrant community previously, is given what we've seen with public...

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: charge and potentially with HR1, how do we ensure that AI is not being used to store information

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: that isn't relevant or information that they should not have access to in order to make sure that our communities are protected?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So how do those two things exist?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So I will start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So I can't speak to the specific government programs that you reference, but I can tell you about OpenAI's commitment to user privacy, which is that it's central to our product.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We believe it's important for users to retain control over their data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That's why when you sign up for a ChatGPT account, you're given information about how your data will be used.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That data is privacy protected by default.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So usernames are separated from conversations and personal information is separated from the conversations as well ahead of any use of user data in training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We also provide users with the option and full control to request that their data not be used for training and also to request that their data be deleted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So we take privacy very seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Council member, thank you very much for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And we just echo what Morgan said at Meta.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: We take privacy absolutely seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: It is core to everything that we do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Privacy and safety go hand in hand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And it is an absolute commitment of the company.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: If I might give an example of our Muse product, for example, you can opt out of training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: You can ask it to forget information that you give it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: You are in control of your data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And we're also planning on releasing a confidential or encrypted version of this in the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: If I may, I just wanted to touch upon public services and health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: I know that you mentioned these and these are core points.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: This is where we really believe in the value of open weights in terms of being able to really

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: provide advanced AI for health, for the provision of health services, research and the macro economy in the sense that data is fully retained by those entities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Ma'am, similarly to my colleagues, user privacy is basic to user trust for us, and so we take it very seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We have privacy policies that are prominently displayed on our website that you can go inspect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And we also know that user control is central to management of your own privacy levels, especially across our Gemini tools, which is our AI suite of tools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We also invest a lot in privacy enhancing technologies and encryption as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We try to take a layered approach to privacy and security.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And finally, we have an AI framework in particular that combines our security and our privacy practices into one holistic framework to, again, ensure that user privacy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And we're happy to furnish that to you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Likewise, at Anthropic, privacy, data privacy, user security is core to our safety commitment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We make sure to protect user data and user privacy on the platform.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And in addition to that, I would point towards that the way the platform and the models can be used is restricted by our usage policy, which prohibits surveillance,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: prohibited law enforcement, criminal justice, and censorship purposes as well.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you, and I look forward to hearing more about what those layers look like as well.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So hopefully I can connect with each of you after this.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Councilmember Maloney.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Virginia Maloney asks how companies define a safety incident, whether they track privacy breaches or jailbreaks, and whether containment failures during testing count. Dwyer defines incidents as misalignment events even without harm; Cahill, Friend, and Graham cite frameworks and offer follow-up.
chapters.title: Maloney questions companies on how they define AI safety incidents

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I worked in tech for nearly a decade, and one of the core principles is that if you can't measure it, you can't improve upon it.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So first, you mentioned you believe in incident reporting and disclosures, but in the context of this conversation, how do you define a safety incident?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Inside your companies.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Councilmember Lee touched on privacy.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Do you track privacy breaches?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: What about a successful jailbreak?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Would that be considered an incident?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And is a containment failure that occurs during testing an incident or doesn't only count once a real person is harmed?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I would love more details on how exactly you're tracking some

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: of the concerns that the council has raised today.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And second, when an incident happens after disclosure, can you walk me through what changes?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Who owns the fix?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: How do you verify that it worked?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And who decides whether or not the model continues to run in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And then lastly, what are the most important safeguards that you know how to implement today?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: What's stopping it from being implemented across all products?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And what do you believe should be the industry standard?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: There were a lot of parts to that question, so I'm going to do my best to answer them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: If I fall short, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So first, the question of how you define an incident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I think this has been an area of a lot of confusion publicly, so thank you for asking the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: When we talk about incidents at OpenAI, we're talking about misalignment incidents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: The best way to understand that is...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: You know, it is not unusual, not suspicious for an agent to look at a website for information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: There's nothing abnormal about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: But if the agent accesses non-public information on the website, that's an instance of misalignment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And so what OpenAI is doing is making instances like that, even though there might not have been a harm to the third party, we are making instances like that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: public on our website, again, because we believe it's important to share what we've learned to advance policymakers as well as researchers' understanding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: On the specifics of incidents, my understanding as a policy person is that this is actually a robust area of policy debate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And so that's why we're happy to make our thinking on this public through our reporting framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I'm going to pause there because I can't remember the rest of your questions.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Why don't we focus on the first question, which was on measurement, and hear from all four companies?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Council member, specifically in relation to incident, I think that's what, I think that was the, correct me if I'm wrong, I think that was the first piece in relation to tracking and how we define it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: We set this out in our scaling framework, which we've made publicly available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: I don't want to be imprecise as I don't have it in front of me, so I don't have it to quote to you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: So please let me follow up with you afterwards and connect you with the right people to talk to you about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I think this is a critically important question as we're debating with multiple regulators around the country and around the world right now what constitutes an incident, particularly when you think about the possibility that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: we could over-report incidents, some of which may not be of a serious enough nature for public concern.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We want to ensure that we narrow to the class of incidents that are truly important for us to use to learn to improve safety and also for us to share with you all to collectively improve public safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So a few things come to mind as we've been having these debates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: One, of course, is cybersecurity incidents, incidents covering the security of our most powerful AI models themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: That's been under discussion for several years now, protecting model weights in particular.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We also...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Talk a lot about focusing on incidents that cause material harms in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And I think part of the discussion will be, you know, how we define those with precision.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We also consider incidents to be those that violate our policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: You asked us about how we respond to incidents, and primarily our trust and safety teams are responsible for responding to what we call escalations, which usually involve violation of those policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: First, we're

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: viewing the alleged violation, which are often reported to us by external parties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And then if we determine that, in fact, our policy has been violated, we have a variety of different actions we might take.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And then, of course, a violation of the law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: As I've said a couple of times in the hearing, if it's illegal without AI, it's still illegal with AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And so I would think that incidents that need to be flagged would, of course, involve violation of the law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: As to most important safeguards, it's very hard to answer that question purely because there's a range of different safety considerations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We've talked about many of them today during the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And again, several of us have referred to this layered approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: My own background is in national security.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We talk about layered security in that context as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So you wouldn't really want to talk about a single safeguard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: You would want to talk about layers of safeguards that together create much more assurance and confidence in the safety of the whole system.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks companies to walk through what changes after an incident, who owns the fix, and who decides whether the model keeps running. Dwyer cites monitoring and clarified escalation; Cahill describes extensive teams; Friend cites trust and safety; Graham describes specialized teams depending on incident nature.
chapters.title: Maloney asks companies who owns the fix after an incident

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The testimony helps highlight that there's more work to be done to classify what's incidents in the future and create an industry standard for what would require disclosure and what would require action.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The second part of the question was to walk through what happens after an incident occurs, who owns the fix, and who decides whether or not the model or the product keeps running in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Yeah, so OpenAI has instituted monitoring during testing and evaluation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That monitoring creates automated alerts to our research and security engineering teams to let them know of potential incidents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And then we have recently clarified our escalation processes as well as responsibilities across teams

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: and made it clear the process for pausing activity and when it is safe to restart.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Council member, in relation to your second question, we have an extensive team, actually extensive teams of people who, as part of their day-to-day, every day, day in and day out,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: are leading and responsible for the development, deployment and use of our AI systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I'll just say, ma'am, I was attempting to answer that question when I referred to the process internally with our trust and safety teams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: But if you'd like some more detail, I'm happy to follow up after the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Yeah, likewise, the process involves multiple different teams depending on the nature of the incident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: If it's at the core of security and our own security, we require a security team to work on this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: If it's about the model behavior and misalignment, it might be a research or training or safety consideration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: If it's about incidents of misuse on the platform, we have the safeguards team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I think you're pointing at this is becoming more complex over time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And I think this is one reason, as my colleagues mentioned here, this is a frontier of defining both what is an incident and how or what would a good process look like for dealing with them.

chapters.summary: Menin announces a five-minute break and lists Council Members Wilson, Osse, Hudson, and Shulman as the next questioners.
chapters.title: Menin calls five-minute break during company panel

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I run and the subway was right there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm always like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It was a good turnout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It was a really good turnout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It must have had like over a hundred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Marjorie was there the last one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: She's working somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I hear about all her personal issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I don't know about the work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: She's working somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Was with the city, but I don't know if you can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I said Rita and Gail and Rita and Gail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
