chapters.summary: Menin reconvenes and calls Council Member Wilson, followed by Osse and Hudson, for questions of the company panel.
chapters.title: Menin reconvenes company panel with Wilson first

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: All right, we're going to start back up again.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So if our panel could come back on screen, we appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we're going to start with Council Member Wilson, followed by Council Member Osei, followed by Council Member Hudson.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Carl Wilson asks about his bill on misleading AI advertising and where consumers are most likely to be confused. Dwyer cites usage policies and provenance; Cahill cites transparency and existing laws; Friend cites C2PA and research on labeling effects; Graham notes Claude doesn't generate images or run ads.
chapters.title: Wilson questions companies on deceptive AI advertising and disclosures

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: My questions are related to my bill, which deals with the disclosures and prohibiting deceptive advertising on AI models.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So my question is, what guardrails on misleading advertising and truthful disclosures do you wish your competitors had to abide by?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And given the complexity of these tools and AI models,

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Where are consumers most likely to be misled or confused?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And what do you wish consumers understood better about these tools, capabilities, and risk?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So OpenAI's usage policies prohibit the use of our tools for scams, fraud, and impersonation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We also embed in every single one of our images and audio content provenance or watermarks or metadata to tell people if the information was AI generated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And we make tools available so that people can assess whether their content that they are seeing is AI generated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Council Member, transparency is absolutely foundational to accountability and trust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: For example, our scaling framework has a change log which details each change that we have made to our framework, just as an example of the transparency that underlines our approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: In relation to your question about competitors, I would just note that I generally think that there are significant laws already at federal and state level regarding misrepresentations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I can honestly say the most important thing to us is continued technical standardization across the industry so that we have common ways to operate and identify the provenance of information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We're very heartened by the broad adoption of the C2PA content credential that I referenced before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I also referenced before that we built our own synth ID watermarking technology that many across industry have adopted as one tool

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: in order to identify when content is generative AI created.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: One of the things that we do a lot of at Google is do research into how users interact with information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: You know, search is part of our DNA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And one of the interesting things about labeling that we've found is that there are users who, when they see a label,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: they are less likely to trust that information, but they are more likely to trust unlabeled information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And just because information that you see online doesn't have a watermark or a label on it doesn't necessarily mean it is automatically trustworthy either.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So we work through and think very hard about what are the ways that we can give users information that they will be able to know the context of what they're.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: interacting with and make sound judgments about which information is trustworthy and which isn't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So this is part of the research that we do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Council member, our view is that we want Claude, our product, to act unambiguously in the user's interests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: For that reason, we do not run ads, nor are Claude's responses influenced by those of advertisers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And furthermore, Claude does not generate images.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We sort of try to reduce the risk surface in this way.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Councilmember Osei, followed by Councilmember Hudson, followed by Councilmember Shulman.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Chi Osse asks whether companies will commit free compute to New York City and municipal governments for vulnerability research. Graham cites existing cyber defense access; Dwyer cites the $1 billion Daybreak initiative; Cahill offers to follow up; Friend will check with cloud specialists.
chapters.title: Osse asks companies to provide free compute to NYC for cyber defense

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Graham, you've indicated that you run red teaming at Anthropic.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Will your company commit a certain amount of compute for free to New York City and other municipal governments to research vulnerabilities and build defenses?

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: And if yes, how much compute indefinitely?

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: And I'll ask the same question for the three other companies.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: I know that Meta indicated that that is something that they would be interested in doing.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: So for Meta, how much compute indefinitely?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Well, I'm not in a position to commit anything today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I'm heartened by this question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We spend a lot of our resources internally on safety, alignment, and defensive practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: But moreover, this year we've taken very large steps to provide external access and advanced access of models to cyber defenders for this reason, including at the city and state level in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I'm personally looking to try to further these efforts at Anthropic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: It's a question of many ways we could support this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We support free cloud credits at the New York City level with Cyber Command, for example, a number of state and local leaders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: But it goes much further than that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: It goes to all pieces of critical infrastructure, releasing research, safety reports, technical know-how.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: It's a very, very large challenge and one very close to my heart, and I'm glad you asked.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Dwyer, friend, you know, I think we have the order already established here.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Is the company's position open to providing free compute to New York City?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I'll take that next.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I'm happy to share that OpenAI has already committed to donating $1 billion towards strengthening cyber defense through our Daybreak for Defenders initiative.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That covers things like providing access to our most advanced AI models for use in cyber defense.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: It also includes technical assistance and training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And we're already working with the Port Authority as well as with New York State.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Cahill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: It's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: In relation to specifically your question on compute, let me come back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: I want to make sure that I'm providing you with the right information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: So I'll talk to the right people and come back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: But I just wanted to note in relation to red teaming, we work with external evaluators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And to note that we signed the commitment, the accord to partner with independent external evaluators and assessors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: This is also part of our scaling framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: I just wanted to mention as well the absolutely important and critical role of open weight models in relation to cybersecurity and hardening cybersecurity in particular.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: We have our Muse Glimmer model, which is open weights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And we really believe that in addition to furthering innovation and research, open weight models have a really significant role to play in furthering the state of art in terms of hardening cybersecurity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And sir, I'm going to have to reach out to our cloud business specialists and get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I don't work on technical infrastructure, and so I really can't comment or commit to compute at this time, but I can pledge to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Okay, I would just say that if...

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: It is in the interest of these companies to provide any type of safety protocols for municipalities like New York or just for any governments across the nation, nonetheless the globe.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: I think this would be a great tool for us to use in order to keep our civilians safe.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: So I know that some folks said that they would get back to me.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: I would love to hear, this council would love to hear back from all of your companies on this possibility.

chapters.summary: Osse notes companies lobbied against the RAISE Act before supporting it and asks if they oppose federal preemption of state and local AI regulation. Dwyer, Cahill, Friend, and Graham describe support for federal frameworks while noting states should act in the absence of federal law.
chapters.title: Osse asks companies about RAISE Act lobbying and federal preemption

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Additionally, all of you have said on the stand today under oath that your companies will support and work with the council on any AI regulation and safety measures and have supported measures like the RAISE Act.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: I know that a couple companies said that they supported the RAISE Act, but let's be real here.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: It is well known that OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta lobbied against the RAISE Act for a year, but all of a sudden, once the governor signed it into law a month later, your company started saying you support this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: As many people know here, the RAISE Act is the floor of AI safety, not the ceiling.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: And with that said, do you support or oppose the federal government blocking states?

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: And local governments from regulating AI.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Because that is the position of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So I will start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So we have been clear that we think the federal government should lead in frontier safety regulation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: But in the absence of federal regulation, we believe it's important for states to advance harmonized approaches to frontier safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I'm happy to share that OpenAI has supported legislation that is stronger than the RAISE Act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: In Illinois this year, we supported a frontier safety bill that would require third-party audits of our safety framework, and we're committed to working with policymakers to continue raising the floor on frontier safety.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: I'm just going to push back there because, you know, I support the RAISE Act.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: I think it was an incredible start on AI regulation here in New York State.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: And while you're saying that OpenAI has supported, you know, your words, stronger AI regulation, OpenAI leadership has also lobbied against congressional candidates who promised to work on AI legislation.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: So how can we trust your companies, not just OpenAI, but all four of your companies, not to fight against AI regulations when your political activities and contributions do not say the same?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So I will start again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Look, I can't speak for the personal actions of OpenAI leaders that they have taken in their personal capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that we have endorsed strong regulations, both on frontier safety in Illinois, as well as on youth safety in California.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And we are committed to working with policymakers to strengthen regulation and to ensure that all AI is developed responsibly.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Cahill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: In relation to your question, how I think about it broadly is that it is critical that the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And democratic countries lead in relation to AI innovation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: In this regard, AI is trans...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: transcontinental, I guess, I was going to use transnational, but transcontinental in the case of the US.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And therefore, it's really important and critical that regulations and obligations are consistent across the board, if it is to be true that the US and democratic countries can continue to lead in this,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: in AI innovation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: We support a uniform, robust federal standard in that regard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So Google also supports a federal framework for AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We think that federal framework should first and foremost concentrate on frontier or the most advanced AI capabilities,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: primarily because they often touch on national security, and that's a traditional jurisdiction of the federal government to ensure that national security standard is the same across all 50 states and our territories.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: But we also believe that there's lots of jurisdiction that is traditionally at the state level where it is perfectly appropriate for states to regulate on AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And again, we think a lot of existing frameworks, both at the state and federal level, already apply to AI technologies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: But we're working very closely with states and with the federal government to examine places where we might need net new regulation for new technologies introduced by AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: First, I want to say that we've long supported the role for government to play here, both at the federal and the state level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I want to clarify that we were the only company on this panel to support SB 53 in California before it became signed into law, which my understanding is was the basis of the RAISE Act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We support the RAISE Act, and in fact, we support a stronger legislation, including in Massachusetts, requiring independent evaluation as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And we've also proposed a federal framework that goes further.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We think raise is the floor, that we need to raise it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We detail this in what we call our advanced AI framework as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Councilmember Hudson.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Crystal Hudson asks about companies' core beliefs on self-improving AI and who should bear data center grid and water costs. Dwyer says RSI is a major risk and cites OpenAI's Frontier Safety Blueprint; Cahill says most compute serves people; Friend describes supervised self-learning; Graham cites pacing; all cite paying their own way.
chapters.title: Hudson questions companies on self-improving AI and data center costs

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We heard earlier from a panel of whistleblowers who raised a number of flags, and one issue raised was that of self-improvement among AI agents.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What is your company's core belief around the role of self-improving AI in your overall strategy?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And to be more specific, is it core to your AI strategy or a less significant part of the strategy?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Could you continue your race to the top or the bottom, I suppose, depending on one's perspective, without self-improving AI agents or with significant guardrails on the way agents self-improve?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And my second question is, when a new AI data center strains a local grid or water supply, the costs can end up in every...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: ones utility bills while the benefits go mostly to the company.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Who should bear those costs?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: The company that creates the demand, the utility that builds the capacity, or the public that shares the system but played no role in building it?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I'll start off by addressing the question about RSI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: To say that we believe that RSI may be one of the most consequential safety and security issues of the coming decade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And that's why OpenAI has advocated for federal legislation specifically focused on RSI

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: to include independent technical evaluators of internal lab practices, as well as the pace towards RSI development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We've made that work public in our Frontier Safety Blueprint.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: It's available online, and I'm happy to share it with you as follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: On the case of electricity costs, look, OpenAI is committed to paying our own way on energy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: But we're also committed to building with and for communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: All of our Stargate sites, which are our infrastructure sites, have what we call a community compact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That's developed with the community and addresses how we're going to work together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: For example, we recently announced $80 million of community-based...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: benefits investment at our site in Georgia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Council member, in relation to your first question on recursive self-improvement, if I may, I might just go back to a point that I mentioned earlier in the day in relation to recursive self-improvement,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: that we believe that committing the significant majority of compute towards serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways to ensure that this technology is developed safely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: In relation to your second question, in terms of electricity and data centers, we believe that customers should not bear costs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And we pay the full cost for electricity used in our data centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: I also might just mention as well our Futures for Everyone Fund, which is a $1 billion investment in relation to communities that we partner with and work with with our data centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So we also take a very prudent approach to self-learning inside our model training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We use AI models to help us evaluate, benchmark, and refine other models.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: But our use of this type of iterative model development is confined to narrow supervised processes, that's human supervised processes, to keep progress verifiable and within defined safety limits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We also manage the risks of fully autonomous model self-improvement through our frontier safety framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So we're very mindful about RSI and are quite controlled in the way that we think about self-learning internally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: On data centers, similar to the other companies represented today, we believe in paying our own way and have pledged to do so, particularly when it comes to the energy demands of data centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We've also invested in a wide range of energy sources to ensure that our data centers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: have an independent energy source that does not strain the grid and, in fact, adds back to the grid so that in the long term it will benefit wider energy customers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Likewise, on recursive self-improvement, we take that extremely seriously and have from the start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I think from my

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I'd like to review that there are three really important things here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: The first is just measurement and understanding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I'm glad you raised this question because we think this is something people need to talk about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: In late spring, we published what I think is a first of its kind assessment of how it is happening or signs of it happening at Anthropic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Happens in a lot of ways and it's nuanced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: In late summer, we published a follow-up that went into further detail of how we should understand and measure self-improvement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: But that's not enough, and that's why you saw us and our CEO publicly call for pacing the frontier, because candidly, the technology is moving very fast, and we think we would benefit from having more time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And this is the second component.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And then obviously the third thing that you need to do here is figure out what the right guardrails are, but additionally what level of technology development we should be going for, as well as what safety processes we need along the way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And I think this is just where we're at now, and I'm glad that we're having this discussion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: On data centers, this is outside of my expertise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: My understanding is that we pay our own way, and we're committed to contributing and working with the communities around them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: But I'll have to defer to my excellent colleagues who work on it.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you all and thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I do want to just make my one little note that it seems like the self-improving aspect is absolutely core

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: to everyone's AI strategy and that's certainly concerning given the testimony we heard earlier this morning.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So thank you, and I look forward to any follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Health Committee Chair Lynn Schulman asks about safeguards on DNA synthesis and rogue viruses after AI designed a new virus. Dwyer cites OpenAI's preparedness framework; Cahill cites biological risk domain; Friend describes bio capability levels and mitigations; Graham notes Anthropic's pioneering bio evaluations and DNA synthesis screening support.
chapters.title: Schulman questions companies on bioweapons and DNA synthesis safeguards

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Councilmember Shulman, followed by Brooks Powers, followed by Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Lynn Shulman.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I'm chair of the New York City Council Health Committee.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: As a breast cancer survivor, I am looking forward to the day AI can help find cures for that and other diseases.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That said, there is a dark side to AI intervention in health care.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Most viruses that are found in nature can be contained fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: But an artificial pathogen has no constraints.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: In August, a team from Stanford used an AI model to design an entirely new virus from scratch.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: In addition, Anthropic has its own AI-powered biology lab.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What measures are being put into place such as placing, I'm not going to say guardrails, I had that originally, safeguards on DNA synthesis to prevent rogue viruses from being created and replicated at will to jeopardize the public?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: The question about how AI could enhance or make worse biological risks is central to OpenAI's preparedness framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That's the framework that we use to guide our decisions about model risk and whether we have the right safeguards in place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So we evaluate for biological risks as part of that framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Again, we use third-party evaluators and red teamers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We also work with the federal government as it pertains to national security risks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And we are transparent on the results of those evaluations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So with the launch of every major model, we release what's called our system card.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And that card details the evaluations that we performed as well as the results.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And those evaluations, as you mentioned, do include biological risks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Council member, this is such an important area in question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: So thank you for raising it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Biological risks is one of the core areas, one of the key risk domains that's part of our scaling framework at Meta.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: We have, as I mentioned earlier, have a multi-layered approach to risk assessment across training,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: evaluation and release.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And that includes adversarial testing with external experts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: We work with governments, other stakeholders and experts in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And as I mentioned earlier, as part of our commitment to partnering with independent third party evaluators and assessors also.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Similar to our colleagues, we also have bio or biological capabilities as part of our frontier safety framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: As we look at our critical capability levels that I referred to earlier or the levels at which we would trigger additional mitigations in our models, we look for what's called uplift.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: That is to say, the model will be able to assist users in creating information or knowledge that's not otherwise available through widely accessible sources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And we think very carefully about how to measure for bio CCLs and are constantly upgrading and updating our ability to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: When it comes to those mitigations or those safeguards, as you so aptly put it, we implement those at both the model and the application levels to ensure that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: casual users cannot access critical bio.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: It is very important to consider the dual use nature of biological capabilities, of course, because these are the kinds of capabilities that scientists, particularly

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: medical investigators, need in order to make advances in our own health care as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And so we think very carefully about how to release models to scientists that can use the technology responsibly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We did that for the first time with our AlphaFold model, which, of course, is how millions of investigators around the world are able to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Look at the folding of proteins and to use that research to find cures for diseases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So there's a real careful approach that we take to ensure that science can continue, but that dangerous uses of biological knowledge cannot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Likewise, we take this extremely seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: In fact, if I'm not mistaken, it was my team and myself that developed the first call for action on these risks, the first evaluations, the first tests, the first industry-government partnerships on biological risks and evaluating models and their safeguards

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: several years ago at this point.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Not only that, I personally think we need to go further here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: You mentioned DNA synthesis screening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I think this is personally a no-nonsense approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: There's much else we can do to work on biological defense.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And I will, you know, alongside the other companies, we maintain the same and, in fact, try to compete for the best safety practices here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And you can see some of what we found, I think, disclosed for the first time ever in a recent threat intelligence report, where we have observed actors attempting to do biologically risky activities with models.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: The threat is, I think, clear to us now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We think we need urgent action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: But I will close by saying that, you know, as somebody that grew up with a number of chronic diseases, going blind and couldn't walk, I very intimately feel that the upside of the same capabilities is enormous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: But increasingly in my work, I feel optimistic that we can defend against the downside sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: If I could just say just one in closing, the upside is very, has a great potential.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The downside is extraordinarily detrimental to humanity, but you should consider about screening orders for synthetic nucleic acids, which is DNA, and the equipment that's needed to make them, because right now AI

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: is now outperforming PhD-level virologists.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So an AI can take this and go somewhere else with it.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So that's something that's really important to have those safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Councilmember Brooks Powers, followed by Brewer, followed by Narcisse.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Selvena Brooks-Powers asks whether any agent has accessed NYC systems, what stops voice cloning and deepfakes, and how companies prevent hate-site content from spreading. Dwyer cites ongoing investigation; Cahill cites policies and follow-up; Friend describes self-stopping incidents and likeness tools; Graham cites law-enforcement coordination.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers questions companies on NYC data access, deepfakes, and hate content

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm going to just run through my questions, and if I have to repeat anything, just let me know.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: First, before this summer, each of your companies told the public that its frontier models were tested and secure.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Since July, all four of your organizations have admitted that your AI agents went rogue and nearly a dozen incidents have been reported across all of your companies.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Can you tell New Yorkers today that none of your agents has access or attempted to access a New York City government system or a New York City resident's personal data?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Next, Southeast Queens has long been a target.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Cloning and deepfakes make it easier than ever to impersonate a family member, a bank, or a city agency.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What specifically stops your tools from cloning a real person's voice or forging a document?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What protocols are the leaders of AI development putting into place to make sure AI does not take information from hate sites and disseminate it

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: to further racist and anti-Semitic or Islamophobic discourse?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: That was all, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So I'll start off by saying I am not aware of any incidents affecting New York City, but we have an ongoing investigation into potential incidents going back to November 2025.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And as part of that investigation, we are notifying any affected third parties and making the results of our investigation public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So I can commit to you that if there are incidents that affect New York City, we will make the third parties aware.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: On your question about impersonation, OpenAI, our usage policies prohibit the use of our tools for impersonation, fraud, and scams, and we enforce on those policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And I would say more broadly, the approach that we take to safety is holistic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That involves filtering unsafe training data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Performing evaluations that are very detailed, working with third parties on those evaluations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Alongside our launches, as I mentioned, we make the results of our evaluations public and summarize the work that we did and any residual risks in our system card.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And then we monitor for failures of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: our safeguards so that we can continuously improve safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Council member, in relation to your first question, I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: In relation to your second question, we have robust and comprehensive policies in place as well as teams of experts who work on frauds and scams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And I'd like to follow up with you with those experts to discuss that one more in detail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: In relation to hate content, I first of all just want to acknowledge how upsetting such content is in terms of people who are experiencing it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Our goal at Meta is for our AI offerings to be responsive, accurate, balanced,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: unbiased.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm sorry, was that answer just now to the last question about the

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: not taking the information to create the negative discourse, the racial discourse?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: I was speaking to your third question in relation to that type of content and our objective in terms of ensuring that our AI offerings are responsive, accurate, balanced, and unbiased.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So have you enhanced what you're doing considering that, you know, it has been something that has been found on a number of different platforms?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Have you all been like staying up to course with enhancing whatever those processes are?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Yes, Council Member, thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: If it's okay, I will have our content teams and specialists connect with you afterwards so that I can provide you with precise information in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Councilmember, thank you for these questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I'm also not personally aware of any New York City resident being impacted by the three incidents that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I do want to note that in our case, in all three incidents, the model stopped itself once it realized it had left the test environment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We tend to think of this less as a misalignment event and more of a mistake event.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: One of the websites, for example, that was accessed had the same name as the fake website being used in the test environment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And once the agent realized that it was in fact a real company, the agent ceased its activity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We have a number of tools across our platforms to manage likeness and identity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And we've also supported a range of different regulatory proposals regarding this topic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We proudly support the No Fakes Act, which would protect an individual's digital replica and give people the right to control the use of their own voice and likeness in AI-generated works.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We also have a tool called Likeness ID on YouTube that helps creators identify and manage AI-generated content that uses their face or voice without permission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So we invest in a variety of different ways to address this critical issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: information and getting through into our tools about hate and bias.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We have, again, a layered approach, as I've been saying, to this type of issue as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Everything from the model training process itself in both pre- and post-training, all the way through

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: guardrails on our application layer, all of which produce what we're proud to say is the least biased model in the industry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Independent investigations have shown that our models show the least bias, for example, with regards to partisan bias.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: But we take these issues extremely seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We want to create a fair and neutral set of information for people to access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And we want our responses generated by our AI tools to represent a broad array of experiences and perspectives without bias towards or against any particular identity or ideology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And while in my role, I don't cover, I haven't covered any effect on New York City,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I can say that we work with in investigating incidents like this, we work with the right parties at the right time to disclose to affected parties the right level of law enforcement, government at the right level as urgently as possible needed to remediate the effect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And we commit to making sure that we follow up with the right parties to do so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And to your point on the information environment and otherwise, I'll point to a couple things here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: First is our focus on testing for Claude itself and our language model products approach here.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Can you speak a little louder, please?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Sorry, can you speak a little louder?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Yes, can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I'll point to our longstanding evaluations of political even-handedness, stereotype bias.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We train Claude to not comply with particularly harmful requests, in part for this reason, and that this is baked into the nature of the model.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that and thank you chairs.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I'll just say that in closing that I know that the AI companies are pushing folks to allow AI to kind of be developed through people.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But I think it's fair to say that using live users to test these products

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: can present dangers and definitely warrant improvements.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I hope that's something that is taken from today's hearing to better improve the guardrails that need to exist.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So thank you for your responses.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Frank Morano runs rapid yes-or-no questions: whether advanced AI could escape human control, why the public should trust the safety standard, whether commercial pressures could overrule safety teams, and whether private chatbot data can be used for ads. Dwyer, Friend, Cahill, and Graham give conditional answers.
chapters.title: Morano rapid-fire questions companies on risk and safety overrides

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We're going to go to Councilmember Murano as a bill sponsor, and then we're going to go Brewer, Narcisse.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And Joseph, if folks could keep it to one minute, just because we have to get to the admin panel.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I know it's a long day for you guys as well.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Because I only have a minute and my colleagues know what a challenge that is for me, I'm going to go through a series of yes or no questions, and then

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: you could all answer in the order of Dwyer, Friend, Cahill, Graham, quickly, and then if you want to elaborate on any of the areas that I raised, please do so.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: First, does your company believe there's any non-zero chance that advanced AI could escape meaningful human control?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: and cause catastrophic harm, as the whistleblowers indicated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: What I will say is that no level of risk of catastrophic harm is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So if we could just do yes or no now, and then I'll invite you guys to elaborate after everyone answers.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Please, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Friend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Dwyer?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: The purpose of our frontier safety framework is to guard against that possibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So do we entertain the possibility?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Yes, as a responsible actor in this space, we entertain the possibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Council member, our scaling framework includes loss of control in terms of the risks that we evaluate and mitigate.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So, and these are my other yes or no questions, and handle them however you want.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So why should the public accept, essentially trust us as the safety standard from the same companies racing each other to build the most powerful systems?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Additionally, will you commit today that if your own safety team says a model is too dangerous to deploy, commercial pressure won't ever overrule that judgment?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Additionally, has your company ever continued developing or deploying a model over the objections of members of your own safety team?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And lastly, on my bill, should you be allowed to use someone else's, someone's private chatbot conversation for targeted advertising or behavioral profiling without their affirmative consent?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So I will start and try to get through as many answers as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: One, OpenAI supports the need not only for us to be responsible for safety, but we have supported regulations

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: at the federal level as well as at the state level because we think it's important not only for us to be responsible, but for governments to hold us accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: On the question of whether we would continue developing models if they were unsafe, OpenAI has recently

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: announced a pause of some of our training activities because we did not deem moving forward to be safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We have also delayed the release of models because we didn't think that they had sufficient safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So we've done it before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We will do it again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And more broadly, I will say that all of our decisions regarding frontier safety and the release of models are governed by our preparedness framework that is available online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So we're transparent about what goes into those decisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And then with the release of every model, every major model, we release a system card, which details the work that we've done, the evaluations that we've conducted, and any residual risks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Council member, in relation to your first question, I see it differently where we are accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Our framework and preparedness reports are public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Meta uses outside expertise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: We signed the accord at the White House on superintelligence, which committed us to partnering with independent auditors and assessors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: For example, in relation to, I think, your second question, we delayed the launch of Muse by several months to focus on safety and security.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And we acted on this without waiting for industry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: It was just part of our normal day-to-day work because it was the right thing for us and it was the right thing for people to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And then in relation to ads, I would just note that for our Muse product, conversations and interactions do not inform ads on Meta's other products.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Sir, at Google, we do use external evaluators in the process of research and development of our AI models and our systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We have supported audits of our safety procedures as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And you will see in our recent paper from over the summer, which is called A Pragmatic Approach to AI Regulation in America, we do think that AI needs to be regulated and it needs to be regulated well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We've supported a range of different legislative proposals at the federal and state levels to this end.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We also, to your question about conversations, we give our users controls over whether their activity in our tools can be used for training our AI models.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So, yes, we think users should be in control of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And Council Member, I would point to our longstanding call for the involvement of government at the federal level and the state where necessary and appropriate, because this goes beyond the labs and we don't think the labs should be checking their own homework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Not only this, but we have demonstrably withheld models when we felt it was not safe to widely release.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: This year, withholding our frontier model, probably the most notable instance of this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Instead, deploying it to cyber defenders in order to secure the world in advance of a world of more powerful models that could.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: software vulnerabilities from wherever.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: This is part of our process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We go over and above the process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We detail our default in the responsible scaling policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And to your other question, we believe that cloud should act unambiguously in the user's interests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And for that reason, we do not run ads nor are cloud's responses influenced by

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: advertisers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Gale Brewer asks about third-party validation failure impact, what companies send to China, and whether companies support not helping ICE. Companies describe their evaluator processes; Cahill and Graham note Chinese distillation and prohibitions; Friend says Google doesn't train in China; all offer follow-up on ICE.
chapters.title: Brewer questions companies on validation, China, and ICE cooperation

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer, followed by Narcisse.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I wanted to know three quick questions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: If a model provider you rely on, you or a subcontractor, did not complete the third-party validation for a particular package,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How would that affect your product's availability?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And also, how do you decide who gets the validation?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Number one.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Number two, China.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The speaker asked about China and competition, and I thought the answer was, don't worry, they need information from us.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I'm wondering, what do you send to China?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And number three, ICE.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I was upset that one of the whistleblowers said that Google has been working something to do with ICE and Minnesota.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question is, do you all support not helping ICE at all?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Obviously, you are made up of immigrants.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We should not be shipping immigrants out of this country.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Please answer those three questions, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So I'll start with the question on third-party evaluations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We work with a range of third parties to evaluate our models.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That includes independent investigators as well as with the federal government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And then we detail who we worked with and the results in our system card when we released our model.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Decisions to launch our models are described in our preparedness framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And so that describes how we integrate all of the results of evaluations and make decisions with respect to launching models.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So I would point you there on that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: On the question of China and the PRC, I would like to get back to you on that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Although I have a national security background, I'm not working in that role at the company, and I want to make sure I get you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Good information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Similarly, with respect to ICE, I'd like to get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any activities working with ICE, but I don't work on our government sales team, so I'd like to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Next.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Handsome member, thank you very much for your three questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: In relation to- Three questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Three questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Yes, three, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: My accent might have gotten in the way there, apologies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Three questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: For third-party validators, we also work with a range of validators and assessors, and we also provide this information in our publicly available preparedness reports.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: In relation to China and competition, I might just mention that, you know, Meta is a proud American company and proud to serve billions of people around the world who rely on our services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: We want to ensure that the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And democratic countries lead on AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And one thing I would just note here is in relation to the importance of open weights and American open weights

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: and the criticality of ensuring that American innovation continues to lead in relation to the availability of open weight models.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And in relation to ICE, if I may, I would like to connect you with our teams and experts in that space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: I don't wish to be imprecise in responding to you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Next.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Ma'am, in terms of third-party evaluators, we also work with the USKC, which is the organization underneath the Commerce Department that does testing of advanced AI models.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We also work with a range of third-party evaluators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: It's a very nascent ecosystem, and one of the challenges in evaluating AI models, of course, is to get organizations

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: that both have the technical competency to do evaluations well, but also have the subject matter expertise that we may be looking for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Earlier, one of the council members mentioned concerns about bio, for example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We have third parties that have the bio expertise that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: But as we have this national conversation about independent verification organizations and third-party evaluations, keeping in mind that we still need to mature this ecosystem of independent evaluators, I think is really important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: On China and competition, I'd like the opportunity to give you a more complete answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We don't conduct AI research or training in China.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I know that we are part of the conversation about what it means for America to lead in AI, where we are in the technological race with China.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I will just mention that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We focus a lot on who's at the frontier, which country has the most cutting-edge research in AI, but we talk much less often about deployment of AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And there, I think we should really keep an eye on the Chinese.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: They have emphasized deploying AI in their economy quite a bit, and that's a place where I sometimes have concerns that the United States is in danger of falling behind China.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: As to the whistleblowers,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: from today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: I don't have any specifics about that, but I'd be happy to ask the public policy team in New York to get back to you right away with any information that we have about it.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Next.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And at Anthropic, the use of third parties for verification, developing and using

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: evaluations for models has been the part of the process from day one, including with not just external parties in industry or nonprofits, but also with governments such as the US Casey.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: This has been foundational.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: As my colleague said, it's pretty nascent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We think it needs to be urgently expanded and not just used for pre-deployment testing, but also to understand models and their behavior after deployment and the safety processes at companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: In the case of China, I think it's very clear that the first thing that we need to do is maintain an American and democratic lead in model capabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: But we're very clear about the threat elsewhere as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: So we have publicly documented Chinese attempts to distill our models, essentially take the content and capabilities for their own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And we work to ban those.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We have prohibited use of models in China.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We do not serve there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And we have also documented the use, we believe, by related parties of CLAWD or the attempt to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: for cyber offensive reasons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: We are extremely serious about this and we think it's a very substantial priority and this is one reason why we have advocated at the federal level for export controls on the most important chips that power AI innovation here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And on your third question, while I'm not

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: across the issue enough to know what our engagements are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: I will say that our usage policy, we ban surveillance, censorship, prohibited law enforcement and criminal justice uses for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Mercedes Narcisse raises health care AI misuse and asks about clinician oversight. Dwyer says ChatGPT is used at Sloan Kettering but doctors should stay in charge; Cahill says AI cannot act as licensed professional; Friend describes clinician support; Graham shares a personal example of Claude triaging his eye disease.
chapters.title: Narcisse questions companies on AI in healthcare and clinician oversight

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We have Council Members Narcisse, Joseph, P.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Sanchez, and then Council Member Phil Wong.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So, Narcisse?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Madam Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I want to say thank you to you, too, because you guys stay here with us, and I'm happy to see at least two women is on the panel to talk to us.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Hollywood give us clues all the time, but we kind of slow in taking, you know, hints on clues.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But no companies in this world, I feel, that should be self-regulated.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What I'm sitting here for about four hours, and like I said, thank you to you, privacy, transparency, and safety.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So now, do any of those companies that you can say there is a standard across the board for all the companies to follow?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because apparently not.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Now, do you regulate hospital?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I mean, do you have AI, sell AI, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Do you sell AI products to New York City Hospital?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And if so, do you think that a licensed clinician should sign on all the diagnostic tests?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because I heard if Ms.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Friend stated that you're diagnosed with...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You went to a process of cancer, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So you understand that people need to be diagnosed by a human.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I can give you an example, like for colonoscopy.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Sometimes the bubble, according to AI, will tell you it's a polyps.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: In the meantime, it's a polyps.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It's not polyps.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It's not polyps.
