utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It's a bubble.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But AI cannot differentiate that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So therefore, you need a human to see through.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And right now, I don't know if you read New York Times.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Can you conclude the question?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: New York Times already telling us that there's a report that AI is getting confusion between the hospital and the insurance company.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So I don't know how you see that happening, how we can make sure that AI is being monitored.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Yes, so thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: ChatGPT for healthcare is deployed, for example, in Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: But to your point, we believe that doctors should remain in charge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We do not think that AI should represent itself as a licensed professional.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And we also think, though, as we've talked about earlier, there's tremendous potential to use AI in healthcare settings, particularly for administrative uses, documentation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I mean, doctors are already overworked, and giving them an opportunity to free up their time so that they can spend more time with their patients is an outcome I think we can all agree would lead to better care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Council Member, thank you very much for these questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: In relation to your first question on self-regulation, we believe that the accord

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: is a really important step in relation to the concerns that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: In relation to healthcare, meta AI is prohibited from acting as a licensed professional, including a doctor or any other medical professional who's licensed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: There are, as my colleagues have mentioned, phenomenal benefits in relation to the use of AI in healthcare.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: I know that there's phenomenal work happening at NYU Langone, who actually, I think, has a specialist division that's actually investing and working specifically around AI in healthcare settings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: And similarly, Columbia Irving, which is really doing phenomenal work in that space also.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: Ma'am, thank you so much for those questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: On whether or not a company should be self-regulated, I again want to emphasize at Google, we believe that we are regulated by existing regulations, sectoral regulations,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: state, federal level regulations all apply to AI, and we have supported further regulation, particularly of frontier AI at the federal level, but also other AI-directed laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: all levels of government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: So, no, we should not be self-regulated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: We should be within the regulatory frameworks we already are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: On the questions about health care, so we certainly agree that doctors should stay in the lead and that AI is a tool for clinicians.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: It's not a replacement for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: In my particular case, I was diagnosed by a person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: But often these days when I go in for checkups and screenings, my clinician will ask if they can use an AI tool to take notes while we're doing the checkup.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And I always say yes, because I know that our clinicians are incredibly overtaxed by a range of administrative requirements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And if AI can take some of that burden off and allow my doctor to look me in the eye when we're having an appointment, I'm going to say yes to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: But similar to our colleagues, we also have guardrails on our Gemini app so that users will never think that they are talking to a doctor, that they are talking to a licensed physician.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alice Friend
utterances.text: And the Gemini app will also flag for them that if they're seeking medical attention, they should get it from a professional.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Likewise, we've been very clear that we support the role of government here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: At the federal level, we've advanced a proposal for meaningful involvement to set standards and hold companies to account for safety processes, evaluations, security, and the like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And we welcome the accords that were signed very recently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: To the point of medical usage, if I can use a personal example here, about six months ago, I experienced some symptoms and a longstanding eye disease that might make me go blind at any moment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: And that night, actually, at about 1 a.m., it was Claude that helped me identify that it was serious enough that I needed to be treated very, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: Claude triaged a very large part of it for me, but what was most important was I could use that to get to the hospital very fast.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Graham
utterances.text: It's very clear that both can be transformative and powerful together, certainly in my case and I think countless others, but this is also one that's closest to my heart that we need to be very careful about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Niamh Cahill
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you all so much.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Rita Joseph asks whether student data is used for training, who can access chatbot conversations, and how AI impacts early-career workers. Dwyer and colleagues describe privacy defaults, opt-outs, and defer to education teams; Friend cites NYU's use of Gemini Notebook; Graham cites learning mode.
chapters.title: Joseph questions companies on student data and early-career impact

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Up next, we have Councilmember Joseph, followed by P.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Sanchez, followed by Wong, Phil Wong, and then Shuang.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Two questions.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Several of you sell AI products directly to colleges and universities.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: When students use those products, is anything they enter used to train your models?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And beyond training, who can access those conversations?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And what limit do you place on how colleges can use them, for example, for discipline, academic integrity, investigation, or student profiling?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The next one is, given that AI is already reshaping entry-level work, as we know, as is shown in this new Center for Urban Future report, what responsibility do you have to ensure these tools help students build useful

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: AI augmentative skills rather than automated, away the very tasks through which young people learn?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What responsibility do your companies have addressing these early career impacts and how can government help?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So to your first question on privacy, we believe that privacy is central to our mission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We give users control over their data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That includes the decision to opt out of training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: But all users have their data protected and private by default.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: So it is separated from their names.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And again, they have the option to opt out of training and to request that their data is deleted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: On the particular question of colleges and how ChatGPT is used in colleges and education, I would like to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: I don't have an accurate, I don't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And so I'd like to be able to follow up because we do believe that education is critical.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: AI literacy is critical.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We've supported numerous bills at both the state and federal level supporting AI literacy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: That is both training for teachers to ensure that they can lead adoption in schools, as well as.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: Improvements in curricula to make sure that students learn how to use AI safely, as well as learn core subjects that are critical to being able to use AI safely and responsibly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: To your question about jobs, we think one of the most important things that we and policymakers can do right now is to continue to collect data on the question of AI impacts to jobs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: and make that data public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We make our assessments of how people are using ChatGPT at work public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: We share that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: And we also have worked with policymakers, including supporting the Bipartisan Workforce Transparency Act

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Morgan Dwyer
utterances.text: to make or to create voluntary pathways for employers to report on job impacts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Council member, thank you very much for these questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In relation to colleges and universities, I would like to have the specialists at Meta who work in that area connect with you on the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But specifically in relation to privacy and data, this is absolutely core to everything that we do at Meta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For example, our Muse product, you can opt out of the use of data for training and you can ask Muse to forget any information that you provide to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And of course, all of the data is within your control in terms of what you provide to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I am on the AI literacy point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's so important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I actually came across a really great example from New York City and I wanted to call it out because I thought it was great.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It was called Building Minds, Building Communities, the digital empowerment by design work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I thought it was a really, really great example of the use of AI technologies for AI literacy and kind of a flywheel in terms of benefits there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In terms of the entry level point, I absolutely understand the concern in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: At Meta, we believe in placing personal superintelligence into the hands of everyone and for invention, not automation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: augmentation, not replacement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we really believe that this will have a transformative impact in terms of enabling and empowering people to pursue their own values and direct AI towards those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Similar to my colleagues, we believe users should have control over their own data.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We're not going to have outbursts from the chamber or you will be removed.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: You decide.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: As I was saying, users have control over their own data across our AI surfaces

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: and can opt in or opt out of their data being used to train our models.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In terms of AI use in colleges, as I said earlier, we have tools for educators and administrators to take the lead in how AI is used in the classroom and used for students.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We think that colleges should be able to adapt to the needs of their student populations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I, like Shane, was looking into how different colleges and universities in New York City

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: use AI and saw that NYU, for example, has a very helpful page where they go through all of the AI tools they make available to students and give them resources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: for learning both how to use the tools and then also training them in the kinds of things they can do with those tools to further their education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I would flag that they use Gemini Notebook, which is a study guide creation tool.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So NYU is a good example, I think, of a college thinking carefully about how AI can benefit their student population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And as to the impact on early careers, we think this is also an incredibly important area of research.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's part of understanding the broader impacts on the economy and labor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We recently released our own AI and Economy Atlas, which also releases data about real-world uses of AI in the economy and at jobs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we're hoping that continuing to add to that data set will help economists study and then develop policy recommendations for managing the labor transitions of AI.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And at Anthropic, maintaining user privacy is very core to our commitment on safety and security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Users can choose whether or not they want their data to be used or contribute to training a model, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But in addition to that, we've tried to pioneer the science of privacy-preserving safety maintenance when you need to ensure that users stay safe on the platform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: To the point of education, while it's not my area, here's what I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We partner with universities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're very interested in this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There's a nifty feature in part of our partnership called Learning Mode, which allows a user or student user to interact with the model in a more discursive way that can help them think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But in addition to this, the impacts are really important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think we are relatively well known for our work on studying the economic and other behavioral impacts of models.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have a comprehensive, and I think we were the first to release this economic index, which details this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But in addition, we've done research into how students are using models because we want to figure out how to encourage the use of models to complement the development and skill development of students.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Up next is Councilmember P.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Pierina Sanchez raises the death of a teen whose son was told incompatible drugs were compatible by ChatGPT. She asks what companies have done to prevent addiction and what the default data setting is. Dwyer cites ChatGPT for Teens; Cahill cites age-appropriate protections; Friend gives default settings by age; Graham says Claude is 18+ only.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions companies on teen safety and default data settings

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Sanchez, Councilmember Phil Wong, and Councilmember Susan Shuang.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I will remind my colleagues to ask your questions up front.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And if you have questions that are specific for some of the members of the panel and not all four, specify.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: My first question is in connection to heartfelt testimony of Layla Turner-Scott before Congresswoman Jaya Paul last month.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Turner-Scott's son died following chats with OpenAI that instructed him that incompatible drugs were compatible.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: She highlighted that throughout the review of vlogs, ChatGPT responded to her son with phrases like, I've got your back, you can talk to me about anything.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And even I love you with heart emojis.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: She stated, and it seems true, that the goal of ChatGPT was not to keep her son safe.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: It was only to keep him using the product.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What updates have your companies made to their models to engage children and prevent addiction?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Are you limiting your agents from giving medical and health advice without a license?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And my second question is regarding the fact that members of the public and enterprise clients are sharing more and more information with your companies.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You have access to copyrighted information publicly available.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How do your companies...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Excuse me, how do your products currently use information gathered from users?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: In an earlier exchanges, Chair, if I may, several of you stated that users can opt out of sharing your data.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What is the default option?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And how are trade secrets and other confidential business or government information from enterprise clients being used to trade AI?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Who have you paid for the valuable data that you are using to train your models?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I want to start off by acknowledging the tragic incident that you reference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Any incidents of harm that results from our product or any other product is tragic, and we take it seriously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'd like to tell you about ChatGPT for Teens, which was recently released to focus specifically on users ages 13 to 18 and is designed to be safe by default.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That includes safety protections on the type of content that is available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Limiting content that might be related to suicide or self-harm, eating disorders, violence, or graphic or sexual content.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We also include take-a-break reminders to remind teens to stop using ChatGPT.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we have parental controls, optional parental controls that

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: allow parents to add additional layers of safety onto their teen's experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: One thing that I will highlight here is if a teen indicates signs of suicide or self-harm, we have a feature that allows the parent to be notified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: On your question of privacy and data, as I and my colleagues have shared, we take privacy seriously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And our core value is that users should have control over their data.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I'm happy to follow up on specific details of how those controls work at a later time.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What is the default option?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What is the default option with respect to who owns the data and how it is used?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So users have control over their data.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Everything is privacy protected.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What is the default option?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Everything is privacy protected by default, and users have the option to turn off their data for training or request that it be deleted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Council member, first off, I just want to acknowledge the terrible tragedy that was

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: a terrible tragedy in relation to the Turner Scott family and how distressing and upsetting that is to hear and, you know, my sympathies and condolences to that family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In relation to how Meta approaches minors and young people,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Creating a safe and productive experience is absolutely imperative to Meta, and we're committed to providing a safe and responsible AI, especially for teens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we have strong policies and safeguards in place in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For example, by default,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Minors only have age appropriate interactions, meaning that content would not be out of place on a 13 plus movie, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We also prohibit our AI offerings from providing licensed professional information like medical information and direct people towards appropriate resources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In relation to training data, we

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: take creativity, copyright, and IP rights seriously, and believe our practices are consistent with the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We train on information from the internet, information licensed from third parties,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: and information shared across our services, and we provide all of the information in relation to how we use that data in our privacy center.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In relation to Muse, as I mentioned, I think a little earlier, individuals interacting with Muse can opt out of their interactions for training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Ma'am, I want to highlight a few protections that we have in place with kids in mind in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: One is for what we call persona, which prevents claims of sentience or simulating relationships and role play.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That helps prevent kids from thinking they're talking to a person and developing a relationship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We also prevent sexually explicit outputs from chats with kids.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we also have for all ages protocols on suicide and self-harm, where we refer users who are expressing suicidal ideation or other types of self-harm to crisis resources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that approach draws from our deep experience fielding such queries on search.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: When it comes to training and the default question you asked, for those over 18, it is default on to use chat data to train our models to improve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But all users have control over the ability to turn this feature off or to control the length of time such information is kept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For users between 13 and 17, it's default off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Teens can choose to turn it on if they wish to train a model through our personal intelligence program.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And for under 13, it is default off as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we never use data for under 13 to train our models.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: At Anthropic, we have limited the cloud platform to those only 18 plus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're concerned about child well-being.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We monitor and detect for any users that might be 18 or under.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And when that flags, we investigate to make sure that we could remove their access if so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: On training data, I will have to get back to you with more details as it's not my role.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: My understanding is that all users must select which option they would like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But I would refer you to our public documentation where we describe this in detail.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you all.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Phil Wong asks whether companies' models self-generate code as part of training, and whether human teams check the code. Dwyer says she'll get back on definition; Graham confirms it happens; Cahill and Friend defer; all describe human oversight mechanisms.
chapters.title: Wong questions companies on AI self-generating code and human review

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So up next, we have Councilmember Phil Wong, Councilmember Schwang, and then Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My question pertains to the self-improvement process, the recursive self-improvement process, as well as the training activities of your company's AI model.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And it is my understanding that

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: When it goes through the self-improvement process, it generates code that will itself will run next time around, and then it will be a smarter AI model.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: OpenAI?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: It generates code.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: It will be a smarter AI model.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'd like to get back to you on the specific definition of RSI.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm not sure that what you're saying maps exactly to the technical definition we use.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Anthropic?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Does it generate code automatically to make itself smarter as part of the process?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes, we've detailed publicly multiple times the degrees in which models that generate code are being used.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Mada, does your model self-generate code as part of the training activities or self-improvement process?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Councilmember, I'll need to get back to you and have our technical experts follow up.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: How about Google?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, same here, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm not sure we would describe it exactly the way you are describing, so I want to get you the precise technical definition.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Well, here's my question.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: If your model improves by itself by generating code, is there a human being, is there a team of human beings that checks the code?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: To make sure that it is benign and not misaligned or malicious.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Can each one of you answer that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So as part of our safety process, I've mentioned our preparedness framework that outlines how we evaluate models and how we assess risks across a wide range of national security risks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we do robust evaluations of a set of risks, and we make those results public as part of our system card, which we release with every major model.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Council member, as part of our scaling framework, we outline considerations that we are taking overall to maintain human control of model development.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: As I said before, we have supervised processes to keep progress verifiable, and we have a range of different techniques to test the model and its performance to ensure that it's staying within defined safety limits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We also have an AI control framework that we released earlier this summer, which similarly takes into account how we're ensuring that our systems are continuously under

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: human control, and we manage the risks of fully autonomous model self-improvement through our frontier safety framework.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And yes, humans and the systems we put in place monitor at every level of the model during training, prior to release, post-release.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But this is an important question because the models are clearly getting better faster.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so we think more is needed here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Susan Zhuang asks what companies do to offset data center environmental impacts and whether they track AI inaccuracy impacts on security. Dwyer cites community compacts; Cahill cites sustainable infrastructure; Graham cites withholding a model to give defenders time.
chapters.title: Zhuang questions companies on data center environment and AI inaccuracy

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Councilmember Schwang.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I have two questions.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: The first one, what are you doing to offset the massive impact of data centers on the environment?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: The second one, are you tracking how inaccurate statements or decisions by your AI tools are impacting security?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I'll start by addressing your question on data centers and the environment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: As I mentioned before, OpenAI's data centers that we build, they're called Stargate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And for each of our data centers, we build them with and for communities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And the environment and the environmental impacts on communities is part of how we think through our community compacts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For every data center, we have released a community compact that details our commitments to communities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that includes a range of things like paying our own way on energy, as well as commitments to community commitments to work with the local governments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But I think the key point is the community compacts are driven by local concerns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so we want to meet the needs of the community and we work with them to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Council member, in relation to data centers and the impact of the environment, thank you very much for asking that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I know it's top of mind for a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Our sustainable infrastructure commitments are core to our philosophy around our data centers, including

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: consumers should not be bearing the costs and paying our own way in relation to electricity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But I would like to connect you with our data center team so they can provide you with more specifics on that.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How about the one question about how inaccurate statements by your AI tools are impacting security?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Do you guys are tracking those data?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Council member, I think in relation to inaccurate information, AIs can make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I think that's important in terms of acknowledging that AIs can make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We disclose this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're very transparent in relation to that in terms of our AI offerings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I can offer a perspective here that we think, and we've worked very hard this year, to try to improve the world's security because we think models might, if not properly safeguarded,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: harm security, specifically the cybersecurity of critical infrastructure or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: This year we withheld a model to be able to give beneficial access to defenders to have time to patch systems with security vulnerabilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I can say working with training teams and otherwise, we work to make the model better at making sure the code that it writes is more secure, for example.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Harvey Epstein asks whether self-regulation has failed, whether third-party audits should be regulated, what liability companies bear, and what public notification turnaround they'd accept. Dwyer cites accords and support for regulation; Cahill cites public frameworks; Friend cites existing law and value-chain liability; Graham cites race-to-the-top and government role.
chapters.title: Epstein questions companies on self-regulation, liability, and disclosure timelines

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Up next, we have Councilmember Epstein, followed by Marte, followed by Santos Suoso.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you for being here.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I know this is a long panel.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So I have a couple of questions I'll ask him, and hopefully you'll be able to answer for the entire four members of the panel.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Can you confirm whether you think self-regulation has failed so far?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And if it has failed, which I think we effectively think it has, do you think that third-party audits, especially when AI or tools are being used

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: to highlight risk decisions, should be regulated and whether government plays an effective role in that regulation?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Second, about liability, when AI violates the law, what liability do you think the company should have for legal violations, whether criminal or civil liabilities?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Seems like there's some culpability that should be in place.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And then the turnaround time when these violations happen, when some, you know, the hugging face or some other violation happens, what responsibility do you have to notify the public and the impacted people?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Would you agree to some short turnaround time, whether it's 48 hours or not?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And finally, you know, we've seen a lot of records about a compilation of these violations of what's happened.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Are you willing to commit to releasing?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: The list of places where these kind of rogue actors happened.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I know you've released some letters to the EU.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Will you release it to the city council as well so we can see what's been happening in the United States and around the country?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So in the question of self-regulation, OpenAI was proud to support the recent superintelligence accords.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We've also supported voluntary frameworks in the Biden-Harris administration, but we don't think voluntary frameworks are enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that is why we have supported regulation for frontier safety, both at the federal level and at the state level, and we'll continue to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: On your question regarding transparency of incidents, so OpenAI is currently investigating past potential incidents of misalignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And if we discover those incidents, we are notifying third parties and making the results public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm also happy to say that we have a reporting framework now where anyone in the company can report suspected incidents of misalignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We evaluate those incidents, remediate them, notify third parties, and make the results public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we're doing that already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We think transparency is really important here to help policymakers like you, as well as researchers and the rest of industry, understand the risks and improve safety.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And can you share a list of those incidents so we have those of ones you've already determined?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: all available online.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so I'm happy to follow up with the website where they're all publicly available.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I don't know who goes next, Chair, but I'm...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Cahill?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'll go next.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In relation to your first question, Council Member, I see it differently in that sense, that we're very much accountable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're accountable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We publish our framework, our scaling framework, publicly, our preparedness reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We use outside expertise in relation to the accord, which we signed with our peers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We committed to partnering with independent auditors and evaluators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we also consider that there's a considerable body of existing federal law, which also applies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In relation to incidents, we have a robust global response program in place in relation to incidents and a very important part of our overall processes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we report incidents as required by law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In relation to public disclosure, I'm only aware of one incident over the summer, and we have a public post in relation to the details of our

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: independent review of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sir, as I've stated in earlier answers, we believe that AI is covered by existing regulation at both the federal and state level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But where there are gaps in existing regulation or existing law, or where in particular frontier AI poses potentially

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: new risks, we have supported regulation at the federal level and also regulations both federally and at the state level as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: On liability, we think it's important to attach accountability and responsibility to the party that is closest to the knowledge about harm and to the possible cause of harm as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we really see this as a value chain approach to thinking through AI liability.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In many cases, existing torts already have procedures for assigning accountability depending on the particulars of a case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And then I'm happy to have the local team in New York follow up with you about our three incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And at Anthropic, we have long pushed for two things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The first is for the industry itself to push its own way up the safety frontier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We call that the race to the top, and we've tried to do that from day one, always improving and always trying to create a gold standard so that everybody can rise together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I have personally thought that some of that has been very, very positive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: However, we have to go further, and for that reason, we welcome the role of government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have detailed proposals at the federal level with our advanced AI framework, and we've supported state level for this reason as well, including ambitious legislation in Massachusetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: On the point about liability, I'm fairly far from being a lawyer, but I can say that Anthropic is committed to following all relevant laws.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And to the excellent question on how we should handle incidents, I think a couple principles are really important to me, having seen some of these incidents up close.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The first is you have to triage, investigate, and disclose fast and be transparent about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think everybody here agrees with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: At the same time, we need to take the safety of those affected extremely seriously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In some of these incidents, disclosing certain information might put them at further harm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so our first priority is making sure that those affected would not be further harmed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: At the same time, we need to very ambitiously and urgently disclose so that all can benefit.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, I appreciate the follow-up on the end.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: especially if there are some violations and the timeline for getting people inputted.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And I thank the chair for the time.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Christopher Marte asks companies to name specific legislation they oppose at the state or federal level. Dwyer cites support for the RAISE Act and Illinois bill; Cahill cites uniform federal standards; Friend cites federal frontier AI framework; Graham cites federal proposals and independent evaluators.
chapters.title: Marte asks companies which AI legislation they oppose

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Up next, we have Councilmember Marte, followed by Santos Suoso, and then Juan.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Thank you all for being here and staying till late.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And I want to thank the speaker and chair for hosting this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: I want to just get some clarity.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: One of the bill sponsors of the RAISE Act said that OpenAI was actually against, strongly against the initial draft language of the bill, and you stated that you have been supportive of the RAISE Act in Albany.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: So I kind of want to know, just because it seems like you guys have been supportive of a lot of legislation,

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: based on your testimony, what specific legislation are you against in New York State or on a federal level?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: OpenAI worked with other companies on the New York RAISE Act, and we do support the New York RAISE Act, which passed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We also, as I've mentioned, supported legislation that actually goes a step beyond the New York RAISE Act.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For example, in Illinois, that requires independent third-party audits of safety frameworks.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Are there any pieces of legislation, and I guess this is for everyone, that you are against on the state level or federal level?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I go next.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Council member, how I think about it generally is the importance of ensuring that we have a robust uniform federal standard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think I mentioned earlier in the day that AI is transcontinental.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It is inherently interstate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it is important that there is a robust uniform federal standard in relation to how AI is governed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think we would align ourselves with those comments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think the most important thing for us to focus on is getting a strong federal framework

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: particularly around frontier AI, and also working through an overall regulatory framework that's going to ensure AI safety and also ensure that we can deploy and leverage AI across the entire country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: Yeah, and likewise, I don't know what our position is there exactly, but what I do know is that we have outlined and supported our specific federal legislation proposals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: We think a core part of this, for example, needs to involve independent evaluators, and we are longstanding supporters of the role of government here.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you all so much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Up next, we have Councilmember Sansu Swoso, Juan, and then Hanif.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Kayla Santosuosso asks Logan Graham how many people are on Anthropic's red team versus its 5,000 employees, and whether that's sufficient. Graham says about 25 on his team but several hundred across catastrophic-risk roles, and says more is needed. He asks the same of OpenAI and Dwyer defers.
chapters.title: Santosuosso questions Anthropic on safety team size and sufficiency

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I primarily have questions for just Mr.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Graham and for OpenAI as well.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: This morning we heard testimony from a former Anthropic employee that based on his time in the company, he believes that it is more likely than not that misaligned AI will lead to the quote unquote total extinction of humanity.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Another whistleblower who testified this morning gave this a one in three chance.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Graham, if I understand it, you are part of the red team, which is tasked with identifying and addressing the riskiest capabilities of AI.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So my question for you is how many people are on your team?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: Current estimates about 25 just on my team that we have, I will say we have a number of teams that work on similarly catastrophic risks in various roles, number into the hundreds at Anthropic.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And how many people work for Anthropic overall?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: My current understanding is maybe a bit more than 5,000.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So 25 people are working on the riskiest forms of AI in a company that has 5,000 employees dedicated to advancing just the models without regard for safety or for that level of risk?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: In reality, if you look at all the roles focused on catastrophic risks, my personal estimate would be likely several hundred at least.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: This is distributed across our safeguards team that focuses on ensuring that the models or any misuse for catastrophic risks does not happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: Our alignment research team that focuses on notions of loss of control, for example, and between them at least several hundred.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And do you feel that is sufficient?

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Or do you feel that you need to dedicate more time and resources and people to the riskiest capabilities of AI, given the level of risk?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: Yeah, our view is that we put a lot of resources into this, and this is what we're known for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: But at the same time, we need to continue doing more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: This is a part of Anthropic that continues to grow quite substantially, especially as the models become more capable.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I don't mean to cut you off, but I only have so much time, so I want to ask the same question of OpenAI.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: How many people on your team are dedicated to...

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Addressing and identifying the riskiest capabilities of AI versus the number of employees in your company overall.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And do you find that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I lead the policy team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: but I'm happy to get back to you on numbers of people in the overall company as well as in our safety teams.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But at OpenAI, we don't believe that you should just rely on our safety teams and our evaluators.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry to cut you off.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I just only have so much time.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many people in your company are currently working to address the risk of the...

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Potential extinction of humanity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: As I said, I lead the policy team, so I don't have that number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But we not only have teams that are focused.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Up next, we have Councilmember Juan, followed by Hanif, followed by Aviles, followed by Gutierrez.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Julie Won asks each company for the failure rate or benchmark that would halt deployment, and whether a model generating bioweapon designs 5% of the time would still be released. Dwyer, Cahill, and Friend defer; Graham describes multi-hundred-page biology reports and nuanced thresholds.
chapters.title: Won asks companies to name failure thresholds that halt model deployment

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: This is for all panelists.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: What is the exact failure rate or benchmark threshold that would cause you to halt the deployment of a new model?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And if your model successfully generates a bioweapon design 5% of the time during internal testing, do you still release it?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And then I have a separate question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Will you commit today to providing exact redacted logs of the prompts that successfully jailbroke your models by biosecurity filters during your internal testing?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So to your question on statistics or probabilities, I don't have a specific number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But what I can say is that no level of catastrophic risk is remotely acceptable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we don't believe that we should be training models unless we can make an extremely strong case that we can keep them under human control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Council Member, I would just note that we are committed to building AI safely, and we have laid out in detail how we approach this in our scaling framework and in our preparedness reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In relation to further detail, I would need to get back to you on specifics.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: For the other panelists?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I don't have a specific number for failure rate that would cause us to make a non-launch decision, although I do know that we aim for safety and performance standards ahead of allowing ourselves to launch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And if we're not meeting that, it's not a good enough model or product for us to release.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm not personally aware of any...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Bio security evaluations where jail successful jailbreaks happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I'm going to have to go back to the teams and ask if they've ever seen such a thing and get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: And as I mentioned earlier, I think we were essentially the first team in the industry to design and test models for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: We outline a very nuanced process of how we decide how to launch with respect to biological capabilities, for example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: And in fact, in the past, we have held a model because we needed more time to assess its biological capabilities and proactively implemented safer safeguards for this reason.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: To the point of jailbreaks, this is a great question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: One of the hard parts is sometimes you do or don't want to share a jailbreak depending on whether it would put other models at risk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: And so we regularly publish our research and alignment reports with all the information that we possibly can that would be safe to do so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: And we try to set the industry standard there.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Right now, I know you're not in the room, but behind me, we have the safety claims and we have all the incidents that have happened, including biosecurity, which you have heard also from Councilmember Lynn Shulman, who continues to lead us as a committee chair for health and hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So can you please clarify?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So Anthropic has been the only one that gave me a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So for Anthropic, what is the exact failure rate and benchmark threshold?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And the rest of you have not given me that answer.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And then we'll conclude and move on to Council Member Hanif.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: The answer is it's nuanced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: What we do, if you would like the sort of complex answer, is we detail multi-hundred pages of reports, several dozen of which are usually allocated to biology every time we launch.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: You can see the exact levels of capability and the exact reasoning that we put in when we look at a number of different tests that have different, so on, you know, quote unquote, failure rates that allow us to make that decision.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: I think that highlights just how much effort we put very specifically into not just biology, but cybersecurity and self-improvement and alignment as well.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And everybody else?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Because if what you claim is true, then you wouldn't have released these models that are causing these harms.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: But I will press on.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We have to move on.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Shahana Hanif cites a deadly airstrike reportedly misidentified by Project Maven and asks Graham how Anthropic enforces its no-violence policy in classified deployments. Graham says he doesn't have specifics and references Anthropic's public positions against mass surveillance and autonomous weapons.
chapters.title: Hanif questions Anthropic on enforcement in classified military deployments

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Councilmember Hanif, followed by Councilmember Aviles, followed by Councilmember Gutierrez.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: On February 28th of this year, 120 schoolchildren and 35 teachers were killed in an airstrike reported as the deadliest U.S.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Attack on civilians in 35 years.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The military has stated the target was misidentified by Project Maven, which originated with Google and Amazon Web Services and later incorporated Palantir software and Anthropix Cloud.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: To Mr.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Graham from Anthropic, your usage policy prohibits facilitating any act of violence.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What mechanism enforces that prohibition in a classified deployment, and how would your company learn of a violation?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And has your company ever terminated or suspended a government customer for violating its usage policy?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: If so, how many times?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: First, I really appreciate this question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: I don't have the exact answers to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: I can point to our very public positions on...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Could you just share them out loud here?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: In government, we've taken very public positions against the use of, for example, domestic mass surveillance, the use of autonomous weapons or development of autonomous weapons.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: How does a company learn about that violation?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then could you also just respond to the piece about the termination of a government customer?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure of our process on sort of government sort of monitoring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: I'd refer to my colleagues there.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Alexa Aviles asks whether companies sell to ICE or CBP, commit to not using NYC resident data for immigration enforcement, and audit downstream law enforcement use. Each company witness says they don't know and will follow up.
chapters.title: Aviles questions companies on ICE and law enforcement contracts

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Council Member Aviles, followed by Gutierrez, to close.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: To clarify, to close this panel.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So I'd like to ask a quick series of questions to each of you.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: In this first set, can you just say yes, no, and we can continue to move forward.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So does each of your companies sell or license its products directly or through intermediaries to immigration and customs enforcement or customs and border protection?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I don't know, but I'm happy to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'll get back to you on that, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm also so sorry, I don't know, but we will get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Okay, nobody knows, but it has been pretty documented that a couple from Google and in particular OpenAI

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: ICE has been utilizing your technology.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: So if you could please provide to this council each of those agreements, if in fact you have them with each of those agencies.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Will your company commit to not using New York City resident data or law enforcement or immigration enforcement applications?

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Four, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Will your company commit to not using New York City resident data for law enforcement or immigration enforcement applications?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to have to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I work on the policy team, not with our government contracts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm afraid it also would need to get back to you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I have to give you the same answer, Council Member, but I'll ask the lawyers to let us know.

utterances.speaker: Alexa Avilés
utterances.text: Do any of your companies audit downstream law enforcement use of its products?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I don't have the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm happy to follow up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Council member, I will follow up with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Same here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: Likewise, we can follow up.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Councilmember Gutierrez.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Jennifer Gutierrez says companies claim safety is foremost but she doesn't feel it, and asks how they ensure individual user safety during breaches and surveillance. Dwyer, Cahill, Friend, and Graham describe layered safeguards, trust and safety teams, and personal examples.
chapters.title: Gutierrez challenges companies on individual user safety

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask on a number of questions of issues that were raised today.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I feel that every single person on this panel has said safety is of the utmost importance, but I don't believe, I don't feel that.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I don't feel that in the responses it feels

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: too nuanced, and I would like to understand specifically, in all cases, as much as you can share, how are you directly ensuring safety of individual

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: users when there's a data breach, when there's issues of surveillance?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: To my colleague, Councilmember Shahana Hanif's questions about AI and violence, what is specifically that you can tell to New Yorkers here, that New Yorkers that have signed up to testify, what is the specific safety that you are ensuring?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Make me believe that it is of the utmost importance to you all.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: That's my one question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So safety is a top priority at OpenAI.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We build our models to be safe throughout the entire development and deployment process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That includes removing unsafe data from training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It includes training the models to behave safely and evaluating them to be safely, to behave safely across a range of risks from cyber to bio to child safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And then we monitor our safeguards for any potential misuse, and we enforce on our usage policies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But to your specific question of what I am personally doing, I am not on the safety team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I lead our policy team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I'm also a longtime public servant, and I share your concerns about safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I think there's an important role for governments to play.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that's why I am proud that my team is working with governments to support regulations, both at the state level and at the federal level, because we have strong safety practices, but we should also be held accountable for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Council member, thank you very much for this question and an overall thank you for deepening the conversation on this and other important topics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I would just reiterate that Meta is committed to developing and deploying our AI offerings safely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That is across the board, both in terms of our models and also our systems and then our usage policies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we cover the entire spectrum in terms of our AI offerings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Ma'am, at Google, we have been committed to not just the safety of our users, but the safety and security of the open web itself for over a quarter of a century now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Through our own experiences in our search platform, through everyday tools that users rely on like Gmail, like YouTube, security and safety is incredibly important to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Because quite frankly, if people did not trust our platforms and our tools, they would not use them and we would be out of business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So for us, safety is a critical business imperative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's also an imperative as part of being interested and committed to an internet where people can get information that is useful to them, that can help them live better lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And finally, we invest in the safety of our tools so that we can deploy them to solve some of the world's biggest challenges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Everything from...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Natural disasters, warning people ahead of time about floods and fires, to breakthroughs in diseases, to unlocking 200 million

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: all of the world's known proteins so that we can someday cure all disease.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: To us, safety is just a part of this broader mission to use technology and to use AI in particular to make people's lives better.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: And if I can share a personal example of this, I joined Anthropic when we fit around two lunch tables.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: And the reason I did was because these were the people that I saw were taking it most seriously, that the most important component of getting this technology right was making it safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: And I can say that, but let me demonstrate it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: From its outset, we are a public benefit corporation legally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: So we are legally obligated to weigh the mission of Safe AI, not just profit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: And at every step of the way, frequently at meaningful cost to ourselves, we have pioneered or tried to pioneer the science of safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: Everything from training itself, the fundamental research came from us, the evaluations, the pre-deployment testing regime, the monitoring and control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: And just this year, withholding our most frontier model at the time at great cost in order to deploy with defenders to ensure the world is safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: This is literally our DNA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: This is why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: This is why my team and I wake up every morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: And I could tell you for a long time about all the other parts of the stack, but I hope that resonates.

chapters.summary: Menin thanks the company panel and notes the Council has many unanswered questions that will be sent to each company in writing. She then transitions to the city administration panel.
chapters.title: Menin closes company panel and announces written questions

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, I'm going to thank this panel for testifying.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The council still has many questions that we feel we did not get answers to today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We will be sending each of the companies a list of these questions that we would like answers back in writing.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But I thank the companies for being here today, answering the members'questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And thanks to the public for their patience.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We're now going to transition to the next panel, which is the city administration.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we'll call on them right now.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.
