utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, please remove them from the chamber.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Menin calls the administration panel: Sarah Milstein (OTI), CJ Dixon (Cyber Command), Benjamin Krakauer (NYCEM), Sam Levine (DCWP), and Carlos Ortiz. Council staff swear in the witnesses.
chapters.title: City administration witnesses sworn in

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Now we will move on to hear from the administration.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And today we will hear from Sarah Milstein, Deputy Commissioner of Strategic Advisory Services at OTI, CJ Dixon, head of the New York City Cyber Command,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Benjamin Krakauer, First Deputy Commissioner of New York City Emergency Management Department, and Sam Levine, Commissioner of the New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please rise your right hands.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you swear or affirm to tell the truth and respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Graham
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Commissioner Sarah Milstein?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Head of Cyber Command, CJ Dixon.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Deputy Commissioner Benjamin Krakauer.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: I just want to acknowledge that it was yes.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: And Commissioner Samuel Levine.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You can begin with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: And Deputy Commissioner Carlos Ortiz.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: I apologize, and Deputy Commissioner Carlos Ortiz.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein

chapters.summary: Sarah Milstein introduces herself as OTI Deputy Commissioner overseeing the Office of Algorithmic Accountability and Cyber Command. She announces OAA has been formally established with six new positions in the FY27 budget and hiring underway.
chapters.title: Milstein describes establishment of Office of Algorithmic Accountability

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Good morning, Speaker Menon, Chair De La Rosa, and Council Members.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: My name is Sarah Milstein, and I'm the Deputy Commissioner for Strategic Advisory Services for the Office of Technology and Innovation, OTI.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I'm joined here today by my colleague, CJ Dixon, OTI's Deputy Commissioner of New York City Cyber Command and New York City's Chief Information Security Officer.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I'm also joined by Samuel Levine, Commissioner of the Department of Consumer Affairs and Worker Protection, DCWP, Carlos Ortiz, DCWP's Chief of Staff and Deputy Commissioner for External Affairs,

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: and Benjamin Krakauer, First Deputy Commissioner for New York City Emergency Management, NYSOM.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: In my role at OTI, I oversee both the Office of Algorithmic Accountability, OAA, and New York City Cyber Command.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We appreciate that the Council is holding this timely hearing about the risks of AI technology.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker, for getting representatives of the companies that develop, deploy, and

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: sell AI tools to the general public to speak to the capabilities, limits, and risks associated with these systems at this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: As a representative of OTI, I'm here today to provide information to the Committee of the Whole about how we serve the city's technology and cyber defense needs and to address the proposed legislation that potentially impacts the administration.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: For those unfamiliar with our work, OTI's core mission is to use technology, data, and design to make the city work better for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We achieve this through a wide range of digital products, infrastructure, data systems, and shared expertise.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: In other words, we use technology to help agencies make every New Yorker's experience of city government better.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: For our discussion today, we can speak to the work we're doing around agency use of algorithmic tools and our cybersecurity program.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: To touch briefly on the AI arm of OTI, I'm pleased to share that the Office of Algorithmic Accountability, OAA, has been formally established and six new positions have been created in the FY27 adopted budget to staff it up.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: The hiring process for those roles is actively underway.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: The OAA's duties include analyzing algorithmic tools submitted by agencies to determine whether there is risk that the proposed tool could result in discriminatory decision making, conducting and publicly reporting on pre-deployment assessments,

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: creating and maintaining a public-facing platform for submission of comments, establishing a protocol with the Department of Investigation for receiving complaints from the public,

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: promulgating rules establishing basic compliance standards that all agencies must meet in developing, procuring, deploying, and using public-impacting artificial intelligence,

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: and reporting the results of pre-deployment assessments and audits conducted by the office.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Overall, the office is progressing as planned, and we remain focused on building the capacity needed to carry out this work effectively.

chapters.summary: Milstein addresses Intro 161 on algorithmic tools and city employment, calling it duplicative of the broader Local Law 25 workforce study already underway. She describes OAA duties including pre-deployment assessments and rulemaking.
chapters.title: Milstein gives OTI views on Intro 161 and the workforce study

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I will now turn to the legislation on today's docket that would impact OTI.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Introduction 161 of 2026 would amend annual reporting on algorithmic tools to include their impact on city employment with a focus on potential changes to funded agency positions, salaries, and duties.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: OTI is currently undertaking a study on the impact of algorithmic tools on municipal employees pursuant to Local Law 25 of 2026.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: This study will provide insights into the extent to which algorithmic tools, including artificial intelligence, impact city employees and the administration of their duties, including their hiring and work functions.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: While we agree that it is important to examine the impact of AI on our workforce, the bill as written would not produce new insights beyond those in the larger, more expansive directive of Local Law 25.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: The next three bills involve New York City Cyber Command.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: This office plays a vital role in protecting and defending the city and its residents from the impacts of cyber attacks.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: On a day-to-day basis, we provide 24-7 security services and assist agencies in bolstering their cyber maturity.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We work collaboratively with agency partners, as well as state, federal, and private entities to safeguard the essential services and data New Yorkers depend on daily.

chapters.summary: Milstein explains Cyber Command's role protecting city infrastructure and raises concerns with Intro 2602, saying neither OTI nor Cyber Command has private-sector regulatory experience and deferring to DCWP on enforcement.
chapters.title: Milstein raises concerns about Intro 2602 third-party validation

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Our core mission is to make New York City the most cyber resilient city in the world, and we take this extremely seriously.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: New York City is a target for cyber attacks with a technology landscape that is unparalleled among other cities and states.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: This requires a unified, comprehensive defense against constant cyber threats.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Our key duties include setting information security policies and standards for the city, directing the city's citywide cyber defense and incident response,

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: deploying defensive technical and administrative controls, and providing guidance to City Hall and agencies on cyber defense.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: In my fairly new role at OTI, it is a privilege to work with our staff and our agency partners in furtherance of this critical mission.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: New York City Cyber Command's alignment within OTI has placed the team in a strong position to monitor and respond to wide-ranging cyber threats.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Cybersecurity is continuous work.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: In my role, I'm confident we can continue to adapt to a constantly evolving threat landscape.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Simply put, New York City Cyber Command has a 24-7 apparatus in place to defend the city's systems from malicious attacks, regardless of the threat.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: the origin.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: With that in mind, pre-considered introduction of 2026-2602 would make it unlawful to market, offer for sale, sell or deploy an artificial model, an artificial intelligence model

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: in New York City that has not received third-party validation or does not have a technical capability to be shut down by a human operator.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: The bill would require the director of the Office of Cyber Command to promulgate rules regarding what the third-party validation, assessments, certifications, and disclosure would entail and the qualifications for third-party validators.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: To be clear, Cyber Command's core mission is to defend the City of New York's infrastructure from cyber attacks.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We are not subject matter experts on the qualifications for an entity to be considered a third-party validator.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Further, neither an OTI nor Cyber Command have experience regulating the private sector in the way that this legislation would require, and neither would be the best choice to lead this regulatory regime for consumer products.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We defer to DCWP to speak about the private sector policy and enforcement piece.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: To that end, DCWP supports the intent of this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: They recommend including robust record-keeping requirements to better allow the agency to conduct affirmative enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: They also note, based on conversations with advocates and sister agencies, that the administration is not certain about the availability or ability of such businesses.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We look forward to hearing from those stakeholders.

chapters.summary: Milstein categorizes AI risks using NIST definitions, distinguishing cyber attacks on AI systems from AI-induced harms. She notes Intro 2601's 24-hour notice requirement conflicts with existing breach protocols and state SHIELD Act rules.
chapters.title: Milstein on NIST risk categories and Intro 2601 concerns

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: holders today, including on whether initiatives like this one could help spur a market for such services.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Pre-considered introduction of 2026 to 601 would require the Office of Cyber Command to establish standards and procedures for contractors to identify the occurrence of a reportable AI safety incident.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: To take a step back, I'd like to lay out how AI risk and incidents are categorized according to the National Institute for Standards and Technology, NIST.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Under AI under attack, AI cybersecurity incidents are traditional cybersecurity compromises where the AI system is the target, for example, data poisoning or jailbreaks.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Misuse or malfunction, AI-induced incidents, would be harms resulting from the use or failure of AI aside from a cyber compromise.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: In this category, the AI system itself behaves exactly as it was built or trained, but the real-world outcome causes harm.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: These incidents are not cyber attacks.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We understand the Council's intent here, given the publicized instances of AI systems operating outside the bounds of their intended use.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: As I noted earlier, the risk landscape is constantly evolving, and we are continuing to evolve our strategies to keep the city's infrastructure safe.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: But not all threats related to AI systems are necessarily cyber attacks, and the legislation as written does not address that.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Cyber Command would be a critical stakeholder in this discussion, but it is important to emphasize that we need to work with our stakeholders.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: state and federal partners to address these issues holistically.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I also want to provide further context on breaches of security generally.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Agency disclosure of a breach of security in any form is governed by Section 10502 of the Administrative Code.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: There are extensive protocols for interagency coordination in the event of any breach of security.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: These protocols are aligned with the New York State Stop Hacks and Improve Electronic Data Security, SHIELD Act.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Current law, policies, and protocols are in place for incidents described in the legislation.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Further, the threshold of 24-hour public notice is inconsistent with current law and would compromise the city's investigation of a cyber incident.

chapters.summary: Milstein addresses Intro 2606 on emergency response plans and Intro 2605 on civilian enforcement. DCWP supports 2605's intent but raises staffing and expertise concerns and suggests partnering with the Attorney General's whistleblower portal.
chapters.title: Milstein addresses 2606 emergency plan and 2605 civilian enforcement

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Pre-considered introduction of 2026-2606 would require the Office of Cyber Command,

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: in coordination with NYSIM, to develop or update an emergency response plan concerning AI system-related threats to New York City's infrastructure, operations, public health, and welfare.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I'd once again like to emphasize that there are laws, policies, and protocols in place for breaches in security, regardless of actor.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: However, we are happy to discuss more broadly with Council how we already coordinate with NISM to coordinate and engage with partners to restore services.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Finally, I will provide DCWP's feedback on the remaining legislation that would impact the administration.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Pre-considered introduction to 2026-2605 would allow any person to submit a complaint to DCWP alleging that a person or entity has violated certain provisions of law related to artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: DCWP strongly supports the intent of this bill to establish a civilian enforcement structure for AI violations, especially given widespread reporting that concerns being raised by AI companies' employees are being ignored.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: However, there are fiscal and operational concerns with the volume of complaints that the agency would receive and the resources and expertise required to handle each individual complaint.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Therefore, the administration believes it would be important to coordinate closely with mission-aligned enforcement agencies at the state level.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: The New York State Attorney General just recently announced its secure whistleblower portal for New Yorkers to report unsafe and illegal conduct related to AI technology.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: This could be an opportunity to partner on this existing program to more effectively enforce complaints on behalf of New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Milstein says DCWP has concerns about Intro 2599 on chatbot data privacy, citing deep technical requirements outside the agency's scope, and that the administration is working on chatbot rules. She says DCWP supports Intro 2603 on advertising disclosures, noting false advertising is already prohibited.
chapters.title: Milstein on Intro 2599 chatbot bill and 2603 advertising

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Pre-considered introduction of 2026-2599 would impose requirements and restrictions on companies that provide chatbots, including requirements related to data security and privacy,

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: the right of chatbot users to access their own data, and restrictions on how chatbot providers can use chatbot user data.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: DCWP has concerns about this bill.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: While we support Council's goal to better regulate companies'deployment of AI chatbots and believe the approach taken by this bill is sound,

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: the implementation and enforcement of this bill's data security and privacy requirements would require a deep technical understanding and investigative ability that is outside of the agency's scope.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: To be clear, DCWP is committed to regulating harmful practices, including relating to chatbots, that fall within the agency's investigative ability.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: To that end, the administration is working on rules related to the use of AI chatbots to better regulate this space for consumers.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: The administration is also invested in supporting the New York Attorney General in their efforts to rein in data abuses, for which this bill may serve as a model.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Pre-considered introduction of 2026-2603 would require any advertisement that promotes an artificial intelligence AI model in the city to disclose whether such a model has undergone validation by a third party.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: It also would prohibit any such advertisement from including any materially false or misleading statement regarding the safety of an AI model.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: DCWP supports this bill to require disclosure of third-party validation of any advertisement of an AI model.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: However, as mentioned above, the administration is not certain about the availability or abilities of such businesses, and we want to be clear that any advertising that uses false or misleading statements is currently prohibited under the city's consumer protection law

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: and will be enforced with the full scope of DCWP's authority.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We look forward to working with council to ensure the law includes effective enforcement mechanisms and to continue addressing issues within DCWP's scope of work as it relates to AI.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Thank you for the time.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: This panel will now take questions.

chapters.summary: Menin asks about OpenAI's October 1 letter recommending the city coordinate with frontier AI firms on cyber escalation. CJ Dixon says Cyber Command follows the NIST framework and has met with Anthropic but not OpenAI since he joined in May, and says protocols have not changed much.
chapters.title: Menin asks administration about OpenAI cyber coordination letter

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I've got a number of questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So OpenAI sent the City Council a letter on October 1st recommending that New York City better connect

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: its existing cyber and emergency management capabilities, and I'm just reading from the letter, with the escalation, containment, and recovery capabilities of frontier AI companies.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So has the city of New York this year met with OpenAI, Anthropic, or any other frontier AI company to discuss how the city would coordinate with them in the event of a serious AI-related cyber or public safety incident?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to defer to my colleague, CJ Dixon.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: So I would like to note that New York City Cyber Command follows the NIST cybersecurity framework for all of our cyber programming.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: That is everything from identify, protect, detect, respond, and recover.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: The basic first principles in cybersecurity have not changed, even with the advent of artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: And we have been in conversations with various frontier models about how we may integrate their tools and software to better enhance the functions that we already deliver to the city.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: So in reference to your question, yes, we have been in conversation with the frontier AI companies to enhance the way that we perform cybersecurity.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: However, those basic cybersecurity controls have functionally remained the same.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So you've met with OpenAI and Anthropic in particular?

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: We have met with Anthropic.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: I have not met with OpenAI since coming on board on May 5th.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Are you planning on meeting with OpenAI?

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: Only based on that, only...

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: Dependent on our needs right now.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: We do not know definitively if there is a valid reason for us to meet with any frontier AI company.

chapters.summary: Menin expresses concern about Dixon's statement that protocols haven't changed given rapidly escalating AI. Dixon clarifies AI cyber attacks exploit the same software vulnerabilities but the city must react faster, with constant evolution.
chapters.title: Menin pushes Dixon on unchanged cyber protocols

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I guess I'm just concerned by the statement that nothing has changed in your protocols given that we're now dealing with a rapidly escalating technology that as we certainly heard today and we've been hearing now for

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: couple weeks to months that there are serious safety concerns.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I just want to get an answer in terms of what proactive steps is cybersecurity taking to meet with some of these frontier companies and ensure that our systems are safe.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: Acknowledged.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: And it does not mean that we have not changed our protocols.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: Some of the risks inherent with artificial intelligence are unrelated to cybersecurity.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: In those situations where an AI model presents a cybersecurity risk, those AI models will still exploit the exact same software vulnerabilities that are inherent in computer technology as they've always been.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: So our protocols have not had to change to address the fundamental issues inherent in computer technology, only the speed by which we must react in a cyber attack.

chapters.summary: Menin raises the resignation of AI czar Jihao Chen, reportedly in frustration over unfilled positions, and notes the Office of Algorithmic Accountability was supposed to be operating by June. Milstein says the law took effect in December, funding came in June, and the director announcement is imminent.
chapters.title: Menin questions Milstein on AI czar resignation and OAA delays

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I am concerned by news that City and State reported on Friday that the AI czar, Jaihao Chen, who is our chief technology officer, resigned, I think, a week to a week and a half ago.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And reports saying that he resigned in frustration that a lot of positions were being not hired or being held up by OMB.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And that relates to my second question, which is Councilmember Gutierrez, I think she's still here, yes, and I passed bills last year

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: to create the Office of Algorithmic Accountability.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And so it appears that Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Chen's resume

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: from what we're reading in the press was related to that and the fact that that office was supposed to be up and running by the city in June, but it is not up and running.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And in fact, in your testimony, you said you're now posting for the positions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's now October.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Jihao Chen served as director of AI and ML at OTI for two and a half years.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: He did important work in the previous administration to help define and understand AI use throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: He's been very helpful in getting new OTI administration up to speed, and we wish him the best.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We are very excited to be staffing up OAA.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: The law went into effect in December.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I was brought in this summer to help stand up the office.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We got funding in June in the FY27 budget.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: And we've been actively working to hire for the roles, for the director role for OAA, and look forward to announcing something quite soon.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We're really grateful to the council for having stood up, for having helped us stand this up.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I think the work is going to be excellent.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It just seems that this is an inopportune time for his resignation, and I am concerned that

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The office was under Councilmember Gutierrez's bill, supposed to be up and running in June.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In addition, the companion bill, which...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's my bill, which we passed a year ago, required OTI to engage in rulemaking around this Office of Algorithmic Accountability.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But OTI did no rulemaking whatsoever, so it did not comply with that bill.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Instead, OTI issued updated guidance, ignored the rulemaking process.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: There's been no proposed rule, no public hearing, no public comment period, and no adoption into the rules of the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, speaker.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So OTI is fully compliant with the law.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: The rulemaking piece of the law had us this year submit the initial

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: the initial, I don't want to say paperwork, but the initial points for our rulemaking and the actual rulemaking will happen in this fiscal year.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We are also fully compliant with Local Law 35, which was brought under the Office of OAA as part of the December 25th

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We've been in the process of fulfilling that report for five years.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We've done it on time for five years in a row.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: That's the law that requires agencies to disclose their use of public impacting algorithmic tools.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: And we're on track now for

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: for on-time reporting for March of 2027.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So we're really excited actually doing that work, very proud of it.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We just last week sent out the email to all of the city agencies to kick off this reporting cycle and are holding on this Thursday the orientation meeting that gets everybody rolling.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, I mean, just to clarify for the record, we don't believe that's in compliance at all.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The office was supposed to be up and running in June.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm sure Councilmember Gutierrez will talk about her bill, but the office was not up and running in June and was supposed to do the rulemaking.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: When do you feel then the law department will be, you mentioned law department, when can we expect to actually see the rulemaking?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This is in the March 27 deadline?

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Menin asks what prevents city employees from entering confidential data into AI systems like Copilot. Milstein says the Microsoft contract prevents training on city data and that data is HIPAA and criminal-justice compliant and securely hosted.
chapters.title: Menin questions Milstein on confidential city data and Copilot

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So what safeguards are currently in place to prevent city employees from entering

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: confidential private city data, whether authorized or unauthorized, into AI systems such as Copilot that are being controlled by outside corporations?

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Our contract with Microsoft, which runs Copilot Chat, prevents them from using city worker data to train their models.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: The way they host data for us also ensures that we're HIPAA compliant.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: CRI-S compliant, that the data is kept carefully and securely, that there isn't risk of the data being leaked either to Microsoft or to the public.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So you can confidently say that no private or confidential city data has ever been obtained by an AI company and then used to train an AI model?

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I'm confident that our agreements with Microsoft prevent them from taking such actions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And does OTI currently measure the impact that AI tools are having on the city's workforce?

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Per local law 25,

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: of December 2025, we are engaged in a workforce study to understand the impact of algorithmic tools on city workers and automated employment decision tools.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: And we will be having, we will have results from that to share next year.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa notes her Intro 161 would require annual reporting unlike Local Law 25's one-time study, and asks about workforce impacts. Milstein says the study is defining 'impact' but that displacement numbers and subcontractor impacts will be part of the research.
chapters.title: De La Rosa questions Milstein on Intro 161 and workforce impacts

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to pass it over to Chair De La Rosa.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And just continuing on on that same question, you all testified that my legislation, my Bill 161, basically does the same thing as Local Law 25.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: One, we look forward to seeing the report.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Local Law 25, to my knowledge, requires a one-time report that's going to come out of that study.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: 161 is more comprehensive and is requiring that report to be updated yearly.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And as this technology is evolving, in my opinion, hence why I put the bill forward, you know, more

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: consistent reporting is going to be needed, especially as we begin to see how the workforce is impacted.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Before I was a technology chair, I was the labor chair.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We have a wonderful labor chair in the House, and I'm grateful to her leadership.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: But this is an issue that impacts not only organized labor, but I also see it as an issue where we're leading.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The nation really and how the workforce will react to this evolving technology.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And so is there anything that you can share with us right now on where the workforce is and what those impacts will look like?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I know you're working on the study, but is there anything you can give us forthcoming?

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So the initial stages of the report are in part about determining how we even define impact.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: It's a pretty broad term and could mean many different things.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So we're in the phase of determining that now so that we're able to produce a report that's really meaningful for city workers.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We certainly support the intent of your bill.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: be interested in further conversation about the annual nature of the reporting.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Some of the information that we're looking for, for example, is, I think, an important question.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: How many funded agency positions, for example, will be eliminated due to the use of these tools?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The agency vacancies has been something that this council has really been looking at, especially as we look at civil service reform across the board and bringing people into municipal service.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So, you know, we do want to understand sort of displacement and what that looks like for the workforce.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We want to also understand reduction of hours over time, which this council has not been shy about questioning the administrations, past administrations and present administrations about.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We also want to know about subcontractors, right?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: There's a ton of city contracts that are in play right now and we want to know what the impacts are.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So I look forward to continuing this conversation with you all and building on what we will see from the report of Local Law 25.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa raises worker protection concerns. Milstein points to New York Civil Service Law 8010, which establishes a moratorium until 2028 on transferring duties to AI and protects collective bargaining rights and civil service status.
chapters.title: Milstein cites Civil Service Law 8010 worker protections

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I also want to say that while my bill doesn't specifically speak to worker protections,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: this council does believe that worker protections are important, especially as we look at that displacement and what could happen, right?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We just questioned the companies for the better part of the day about whistleblower protections.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: and what happens when this technology gets out of control.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So we want to understand how those protections are also extended to municipal workers.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Do you have anything in place right now that protects our city's workforce?

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Because this is a little technical, I want to make sure I get exactly the right information, which is that the New York State

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Civil Service Law, Section 8010, establishes a moratorium on discharge, displacement,

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: or the transfer of existing duties and functions currently performed by employees of the New York City and the New York City School District to an artificial intelligence system until 2028.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: The Civil Service Law also stipulates that the use of AI shall not alter existing collective bargaining rights, terms of employment, or civil service status.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Further, existing collective bargaining agreements may offer employment protections beyond 2028.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So with that law in place, we have a little bit of time, and we really appreciate the intent of this law and the fact that it gives us in New York City a little bit of time to figure out

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: how we understand the potential for displacements, for de-skilling, for the use of subcontractors that might be displacing other city workers, and the sorts of things you were raising.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So I really appreciate that question.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Great.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa previews her bill creating a civil service AI title and asks about interagency AI coordination. Milstein describes OTI's Local Law 35 reporting work, with 56 agencies participating last cycle, and ongoing research on risk assessment and accountability.
chapters.title: De La Rosa questions Milstein on interagency AI oversight

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So we'll continue that conversation.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I also want to...

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: give you a preview, I have a bill that creates a civil service title for AI within our city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And one of the things that I'm curious about is like this interagency communication around AI.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Can you speak to us?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Where are you right now when it comes to each of the city agencies and evaluating where the agencies are in terms of the use of AI internally?

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So one of the privileges that we have at OTI as the agency that runs the reporting for Local Law 35 is that we learn from agencies throughout the city how they are using algorithmic tools that have

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: direct public impact.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: And in the process of collecting that data, we have a fair amount of contact with agencies to be able to learn more

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: and to establish relationships with them so that we can also serve as advisors to them and understand their challenges as this technology unfolds.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: In the last cycle, last year, we had 56 agencies participating.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Our first hearing as technology chair was around surveillance.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And one of the things that we pretty much grilled these companies about was about self-regulation.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And I think from the tone and tenure of this council, we don't believe in self-regulation.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: However, we've given the grace to our city agencies to self-report the use of AI.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I want to ask you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And I understand that OTI is not an agency that's going to impose penalties on other agencies for not reporting.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: But there is a specific concern that my colleagues and I have around self-reporting, especially when it comes to the NYPD's reporting of surveillance technologies.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: This council has had many hearings on that.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I wonder, you know, under the Office of Algorithmic Accountability, what accountability tools will be put in place to make sure

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: that we are properly regulating the use of surveillance technology in the NYPD and other technology?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You know, this council held a hearing just in June around the Department of Education and the use of AI.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So what are some of those tools that we can look forward to seeing?

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for that question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So in advance of having full-time staff at OAA, we have been doing research to understand some of the types of

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: risk assessment and risk management that organizations like ours can do in a situation where self-reporting is what we have been relying on.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We're a little bit early to say how we would implement that in the city, but we are very actively

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: hiring for a director who understands that set of problems and can help us figure out how we come up with effective risk assessment and management that includes

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: you into city agencies, perhaps beyond self-reporting.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks how prepared the city is for autonomous AI-driven attacks, and whether a kill switch should live in Cyber Command. Dixon says the city provides 24/7 detection and response regardless of whether attackers are human or AI, but that a kill switch is technically infeasible in distributed systems.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks Dixon about autonomous attacks and kill switches

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And of course, we will continue that conversation.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I did want to ask you, how prepared would you say we are

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: for enterprise security system for autonomous AI-driven attacks, not just attacks by human, but AI autonomous attacks.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: How prepared do you all feel we are as a city?

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I'll let CJ Dixon answer that.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: And that is a great question, and I will acknowledge that this is a very dynamic environment.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: It is always changing.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: That's just the nature of technology.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: New York City Cyber Command, however, provides 24 by 7 detection and response capabilities through our 24 by 7 security operations center.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: We have provided that service to the city since the establishment of New York State Cyber Command.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: We provide that service whether or not the attacker is human or an artificial intelligence-based attacker.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: That attacker would still attack the exact same vulnerabilities in the system, and therefore we would still respond functionally in the same manner.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: We would just have to do it faster.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: We continue to evolve with the technology, and we will continue to do so with the best of our ability as the technology continues to evolve.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The speaker, rightfully so, in my opinion, asked the companies about the possibility of a kill switch and where that kill switch should live.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Do you have any opinions if the kill switch should live in Cyber Command?

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: I agree in principle.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: with the idea of a kill switch.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: I will say there are some technical barriers that would prevent a

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: kill switch as conceptualized living in any agency within New York City, whether that is New York City Cyber Command, OTI, or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: The reason being is the technical reality for these models is they are deployed on distributed systems, on distributed architecture.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: In order to truly

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: With a singular button or with a kill switch or anything of that concept for that to actually work functionally, we would need to be able to coordinate across multiple stakeholders that are not actually regionally co-located to be able to turn off everything at the exact same time.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: New York City Cyber Command nor OTI does not have the authorities or the technical capability to do that.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: And this runs us up against a similar challenge that we've had with other kill switch bills as it relates to computer technology in general.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: As this technology gets more distributed, it gets harder and harder for any singular solitary entity to turn it off specifically.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: That is not to say that there is not technical means by which a group of entities with the legal authority to do so

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: could not disconnect a given model from a given function, but in this particular case, we agree on principle, but it would not be able to be implemented at New York State Cyber Command in practice, not with the technical barriers that are in place.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sure there'll be more on that.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: In your opinion, should AI control be recognized, a recognized cybersecurity specialty?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: If so, what should be the training and curriculum included in that?

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: I do not believe every function related to artificial intelligence is necessarily going to be a cybersecurity specific challenge.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: There are some intersections between artificial intelligence and cybersecurity as a particular domain.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: And when those

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: two domains interact, that is where certain things should fall within cyber command and a cybersecurity professional's purview.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: And that is any instance of a cyber attack or cybersecurity, regardless of if the perpetrator is a human or an artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I just want to ask one follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: How many people are working in cyber command right now?

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
Julie Menin
utterances.text: And how many vacant positions do you have?

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: I will need to go back and find that exact number for you, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Please provide, if you could please provide that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We'll do.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks DCWP Commissioner Sam Levine what AI misuses harm consumers most. Levine cites voice cloning scams against seniors, algorithmic price fixing, surveillance pricing, and an attitude among AI companies that they bear no responsibility for downstream consequences.
chapters.title: Levine tells De La Rosa about consumer AI harms DCWP is seeing

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I have a question for our DCWP.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Commissioner and team, what types of AI misuse are you seeing that harm consumers that you're most concerned about?

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: It's great to have the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: opportunity to be here.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: We're concerned about a wide range of misuse, whether it's people using voice cloning technology that these AI companies make fully available to scan our seniors,

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: whether it's grocery stores using AI technology to fix prices or to personalize prices, something that the speaker has introduced a bill to prohibit.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: We're seeing widespread misuse of these tools.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: And the other thing we're seeing across the board is an attitude by these AI companies that they bear no responsibility for the downstream consequences.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: I have to just say, Chair, I was struck by the final answer I heard by the witness for OpenAI, who when asked a basic question about AI safety, responded that she works in policy, not safety.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: How are you running a company like OpenAI set to go public introducing trillion-dollar tools and you don't have safety as part of your policy division?

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: Deeply disheartened by what we heard at the hearing earlier today.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You should have heard their first answer.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: It went something like, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: There were a lot of I don't knows, and on behalf of the admin, we hope to give you more fulsome answers.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks if DCWP is sufficiently staffed and whether a private right of action would help. Levine supports a private right of action and warns AI companies will run to Washington seeking federal preemption once the city acts.
chapters.title: Levine supports private right of action on AI harms

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, and we look forward to engaging with you in that more broad conversation as well.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: In your opinion, is DCWP sufficiently staffed to combat this AI misuse?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And would adding, in your opinion, a private way of action, a private right of action, strengthen the ability to enforce against violators?

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: I'll be candid.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: I feel that even as under the Mamdani administration, we are adding to our ranks, I believe we are capable of taking on.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: many of the misuses of AI, whether that's DoorDash using algorithms to underpay its workers, something we remedied in the largest labor enforcement action in history, whether it's companies using AI to

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: harm consumers through surveillance pricing, we're strongly supporting the Speaker's bill on this.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: I think we have strong tools.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: That said, no enforcement agency, and I've worked at the state, federal, and municipal level, will ever have the resources to take on every possible misuse of this technology.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: That is why, Chair, I would strongly support a private right of action, as contemplated by a number of these bills, to give ordinary people, workers, and businesses the opportunity to hold these companies accountable.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: I can guarantee you, though, these companies, as soon as the city does that, are going to run to Washington asking for preemption.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: Regardless of what they might be saying at this hearing, what really speaks is where their lobbying dollars are going, and that is to D.C.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: Congress asking to hit delete on all of these city and state AI safety laws.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner and team.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Jennifer Gutierrez asks Milstein about the OAA report cadence and DCWP's implementation of Local Law 144 on automated employment decision tools. Levine says 144 has flaws because audits aren't required to come up clean, and the administration issued a policy statement on existing laws.
chapters.title: Gutierrez questions administration on OAA reporting and Local Law 144

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'm going to pass it on to my colleagues, Councilmember Gutierrez, followed by Aldebar, followed by Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Good to see everyone.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: My first question is for Deputy Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Going off of the speaker's line of questioning regarding the Office of Algorithmic Accountability, can you share, I know,

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: You said you're excited about this report.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: You're setting up an orientation meeting.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It feels like not a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I guess what can you share before the report is scheduled to be released?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What can you share about the cadence of how often you're going to be able to meet?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do you expect the report to be released on time?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: This is not a reflection of you, but I really felt like the previous administration under the previous OTI leadership.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Was delayed in many things.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And we certainly don't want compliance to be one of those things.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So if you can just share with me a little bit about the cadence, how many people, you said the funding you got in June, how many people will the office be able to employ where you are in that process currently?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: That was it for you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I had a question for DCB, but I can come back.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And then for DCWP, I just wanted to ask if you can share a little bit about how the implementation of Local Law 144 is going, the automated deployment decision tools.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Just wanted to see how the implementation of that law is going.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And that's it.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: Let me start by 144.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: I think this was a really well-intentioned bill to regulate the use of automated decision-making systems for hiring.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: I think it does have some flaws, though, especially in that it requires companies that use AI systems for hiring to conduct audits.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: It doesn't actually require that those audits come up clean.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: That's really a civil rights question.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: That is why our administration...

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: put out a policy statement last week on behalf of DCWP, Commission on Human Rights, and Tansy and Limousine, making clear that existing laws apply.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: But I do want to circle back to a broader point that this hearing reveals, which is that bias in decision-making produced by AI systems is a very real concern you're addressing.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: These companies would like an exemption from the law.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: The companies that testified earlier want to assert that if decisions are made in a black box, nobody can be held accountable for it.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: I applaud this council's effort to actually impute responsibility for these harms to the companies making billions of dollars on it, and we would be very happy to work with the council to work on a

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: revised, expanded, strengthened, automated decision-making bill that places the responsibility to remove bias from hiring where it belongs.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And do you think that the...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are there instances where the harm is happening amongst the city agencies using these tools?

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: I don't believe that I would defer to OTI and to those in hiring.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: I don't believe that the city is using AI tools to sort resumes, but I would defer to others in the administration.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: I can tell you in my agency, we have people reviewing applications.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: Just as starting in January when delivery workers get deactivated, we have people reviewing that.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: When consumers file complaints, we have people reviewing it.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: We are a big believer in our administration that the people of New York should be served by the people of the city government.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Part of the package of bills that the speaker mentioned that we passed last December on Christmas was to get the city and to get OTI to report on those AI tools that every city agency is reporting on.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So we'll know soon enough.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But please, Deputy Commissioner, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for the question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So I think there's a couple of reports we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I want to give a little bit of context.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Local Law 35 is the report that requires agencies to tell us about the algorithmic tools they're using that have public impact.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: And that report we have delivered on time every year for the past five years.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: The process for it kicked off last week, and we'll be collecting data over the course of the next few months with the plan to publish it in March of 2027.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We have all the indications that that will come in on time as it has in each of the past five years.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So we're feeling good about that.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm just referring to the report from Intro 199.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I was just referring to the report required by Intro 199.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So that's the package of bills from last month.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We are, the director of OAA, which we hope to be able to announce quite soon, will be primarily responsible for the additional reporting that will be required in March of 2027.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: And in part because we have this good experience internally understanding process with Local Law 35, we think we're in a good position to move quickly on the additional reporting that will be due in March of 2027.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And you said announcement.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do you have someone already for the role?

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We will have an announcement, and I hope you'll have an announcement about the announcement.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Shirley Aldebol asks where OTI is in hiring the six new OAA positions and the challenges. Milstein says a director announcement is expected in a week or two and that finding people with both AI expertise and city systems knowledge is difficult.
chapters.title: Aldebol questions Milstein on OAA hiring delays

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We have Councilmember Alderball, followed by Maloney, followed by Juan.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair and Speaker Mannion.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So you said the hiring process for the six new positions that were created in the adopted budget are actively underway.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Like specifically, where are you in the process?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: How many people have already been hired?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: how many people are left to be hired, and what have been the challenges in being able to hire people quickly?

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for the question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So we hope to be announcing a director for the office quite soon, in the next week or two.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: And we are in the process of defining the additional roles so that they can be brought on quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We certainly are challenged to find people who have the right combination of AI expertise and understanding of city systems to be able to hit the ground running.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: That has been a little bit of a challenge.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: But we do have, I think, bringing in a strong leader is going to help us draw good people who are going to want to do this work with us.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: If I may, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Part of the role is to analyze algorithmic tools submitted by the agencies to determine whether there's risk that the proposal could result in discriminatory decision making.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: What is your office doing or thinking about in terms of protecting the city's workforce as AI develops and evolves and

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: you're kind of like the gatekeeper?

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: for the question.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So in parallel with some of the risk assessment that we can do with the software, we are doing the

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: research associated with Local Law 25, which has us researching how algorithmic tools are impacting algorithmic tools and

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: automated employment decision tools might be impacting city workers.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: And I believe that we should have results from that in 2027, and we'll have a much better sense of the landscape of how workers in the city are impacted.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Virginia Maloney asks what NYC's AI government wins are, whether OTI's generative AI guidance is binding, and how the city handles procurement of fast-changing models. Milstein cites Microsoft and Adobe as approved tools and says she'll follow up on win examples.
chapters.title: Maloney questions administration on government AI wins and procurement

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Councilmember Maloney, followed by one, followed by Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: As we all know, generative AI technology is changing how we communicate, work, and how businesses operate.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And the same could be said of our government offices, both how we work and operate, either officially or unofficially.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So I want to know how New York City agencies are adapting to the new reality.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The first, on the opportunity side, there are plenty of examples of government wins of adopting useful technologies for the public good.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: In Connecticut, they have real-time translation in 80 languages for these kinds of public meetings to increase accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: In California, they automatically check permit applications against 18,000 pages of building code.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: in order to speed up reviews.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So my first question is, what is our equivalent win in New York?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And if we don't have one yet, what's the plan to identify those opportunities?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And the second question is around oversight.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: If I may wrap up, OTI published generative AI guidance for agencies last December.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So as we're exploring these opportunities, is that guidance binding or is it advice?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: What happens if agencies ignore that guidance?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Has OTI been prescriptive about a list of generative AI or agentic AI tools that have been reviewed and approved for city use, that are use cases that the city officially supports?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And then how are we thinking about procurement when these models are constantly iterating and changing every few months and when new, every few days truly, and when new technologies are being introduced?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Thank you for those questions, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I'm so glad you brought up the question about wins because we're really interested in both effective and responsible use of AI, and I think effective would cover the wins.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I don't have a perfect list here, and I'd like to follow up with that because we'd really like to represent the agency as well.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: In terms of tools that we have approved, broadly there are two sets of tools that OTI approves.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: centrally Microsoft Office Suite and other Microsoft tools, and that includes their Copilot chat, and some of their other tools have AI features built in.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: And we also have a central license for Adobe Creative Cloud, and many of those

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: tools have AI features built in.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Other tools, other software tools that are used by agencies are reviewed for the most part on a one-off basis by OTI,

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: and we are still determining the best way to move forward with that process to make sure that we are managing, identifying and managing risk

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: appropriately.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I think your question about procurement is an excellent one and part of what we have started to research ahead of having staff at OAA, we've started to talk with

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: various experts in risk management to understand some of the ways that we might think about risk in an ongoing way.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: When traditionally all kinds of procurement has, like there's a gate at the beginning for various concerns, and then it's rolling.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I think you're right, that's not appropriate for this situation, and we should have more to discuss on that in the coming months, but it's an active question that we have as well.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Council Member 1, followed by Hanks.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Julie Won says city agencies are using non-approved AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and NanoBanana Pro for public-facing work and asks about data privacy in city contracts.
