Milstein says an AI rider was distributed to agencies this summer covering IP, security, data, and privacy, but the city cannot technically monitor shadow use.
chapters.title: Won questions Milstein on shadow AI use and city contract riders

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Followed by Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair De La Rosa.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So for the panel, what I have questions about is building off of what Councilmember Maloney just said.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: The agencies are allowed to currently use Microsoft products and also Adobe.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: But it's clear to me and the public that they are using other AI tools.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So not just the passive tools like using Zoom to transcribe their notes and for follow-ups, but in addition to that, they're using ChatGPT, they're using Claude, they're using NanoBanana Pro, because we're seeing it for agencies like HPD, DOE, DEP.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: They're creating flyers for public consumption.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: They're using it for their public emails.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: They're using it for public messaging.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So what are you actually doing?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Because I want to know what the public policy is from the mayor on how the agencies are using AI and how you are.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Regulating it internally as well.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And also I would like to build off of that for city contracts.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: What are you doing currently for data privacy writers in city contracts for all procurement of AI companies for making sure that our constituent data is not being used to train their AI models?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And is there a clause at all or a rider in the city contract, especially with co-pilot, since that's the only real one that you have?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And people are just using their own personal accounts or free accounts for everything else that they're currently using for their day-to-day jobs.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So let me first address the question about the AI rider.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We shared that with...

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: general counsels across the city this summer with an updated AI writer.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: And I want to just make sure I've got the right language here, so I'm going to pull that up.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Let's see.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Yeah, because my privacy concerns are not just for the contracts that exist, but it is for the free-willing use of agency staff that are using non-city enterprise-licensed AI.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So I'll first address the writer, and then we'll talk about the shadow use.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So the writer, as I said, was distributed to agencies citywide this summer, and it's intended to mitigate risks and apply the city's policies and standards to AI products and features.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: It's available for all city software contracts, and our legal team recommends that agencies use it even where no AI component is currently contemplated.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: The writer includes terms relating to intellectual property, security, how the city's data may be used, and privacy.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: And so that is now active and in use, and I think that with also a proactive component of recommending that it's used for all manner of technology.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: In terms of the shadow use, which I think is probably both at the individual and at the agency level, we are not in a...

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Technical position to monitor that.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: But I certainly, we

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: as an agency share concerns about that.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: And part of what we're interested in doing is making sure that agencies have the tools that they need that are properly regulated.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Microsoft tools, for example, where data can't be shared or used to train their models, that agencies have the tools that they need to do the jobs that they have so that they are not turning to outside tools.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So who is responsible if you are unable to regulate shadow use of AI tools for day-to-day use, especially with constituent data?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Who is going to regulate that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'd like to follow up with you on that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So I know the admin has a hard stop at 530.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We have about six more member questions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So if you all could just hang on tight, we're going to try to get through this.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Members, please consolidate the questions.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Kamillah Hanks asks Dixon to expand on his testimony that not all AI threats are cyber attacks. Dixon describes two risk baskets: AI attacked as a computer system, and novel risks inherent in how AI interacts with society regardless of cybersecurity.
chapters.title: Hanks asks Dixon to elaborate on AI risk categories

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We have our majority whip, Council Member Hanks.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: I'll be very, very brief.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So you testified with all the technology that's changing rapidly.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Even the best can't, you know, keep up.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So in your testimony, you said the administration is continuing to evolve your strategies to keep our city's infrastructure safe.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: But not all threats to AI systems are necessarily cyber attacks.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Can you expand on that?

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: Yes, so when looking at the way that it is currently described by the National Institute of Science and Technology, as well as some of the universities and academics who've created some of these systems,

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: there are functionally two baskets of AI risk.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: There is risk.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: Related to AI when an AI is attacked as a computer system just like any other piece of software.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: And then there are risks related to artificial intelligence that are truly novel to this new technology inherent in the way that these artificial intelligence models may interact with society when deployed.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: That second category of risk is a function of often a

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: how much society may trust the artificial intelligence and how reliable that artificial intelligence system may be.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: Those two things can run afoul of what we may expect as consumers or as a government entity, completely agnostic of whether or not the system for which those AIs are deployed are actually cyber secure.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: So a system can be completely cyber secure, but the AI model itself in interactions with other humans in society writ large may take an action that is unexpected and therefore result in some sort of disruption,

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: agnostic of a cyber security incident.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: That's functionally the two categories, and that's a very broad breakdown of those two categories of risk.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So I'm going to keep my question just to that.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: I think that we should talk offline because my legislation requires the 24-hour reporting requirement to Cyber Command, in which your testimony has some issues, and you talk about

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: how we're going to push this through to federal and state, and what specific role do they play in that, how can we make this better, but I will...

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Relinquish that.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Gale Brewer asks how agencies adopt new AI models, whose clouds host them, how testing identifies misaligned AI, and how much the city spends on AI consultants. Milstein says no city agency runs its own models, agencies use vendor clouds, and she believes all AI work is in-house.
chapters.title: Brewer asks administration about AI adoption, testing, and consultants

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Up next, we have Brewer, followed by Osei.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I know you talked about the Microsoft and the Adobe, but if an agency wants to begin using a new AI model, A, how do they go about it?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Number two, does the city run these models on its own data centers or only on the ones that are under control of vendor clouds?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then if you have a problem, like there's a criteria, what is it for testing?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: to identify the malicious, misaligned AI product?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then how much does the city spend each year on outside AI consultants?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I could go on, but those are three, four questions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have 10 pages here.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Thank you for the questions.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Let's see.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The process.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Typically, when agencies want to buy software, part of the process is discussing with OTI

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: what they are buying and what they will be using it for, and we have a cybersecurity review process that is part of that to ensure that the

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: software that is either going to be bought or built will be safe.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: And as my colleague has said, that would include, cybersecurity includes the typical AI concerns.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So that's process.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: You had...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The next question, the clouds.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Whose clouds are they on?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Whose data centers?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Where are they?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Are you running them or is it outside vendors?

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So to the best of my knowledge, there are no city agencies running their own models.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: But I would like to...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's vendor clouds, basically.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Vendor clouds, vendor clouds.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Yes, so for example, Microsoft...

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Host software that agencies use.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: But I'd like to follow up after the hearing to make sure I've got the exact right information for you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, and if there's something unexpected, misaligned AI product behavior, what do you do?

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: That is a question for my colleague, CJ Dixon.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: Councilwoman, that depends on what the misaligned behavior is.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: If that misaligned behavior is specifically a cyber incident, we take appropriate action based on what any cyber professional may do.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: There are novel misalignments that are born of this technology that do have to be unpacked, and we look forward to working with the council as well as our partners across New York City to understand.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: When those misalignments do arise unrelated to existing risks that the city already deals with, how do we actually engage with those particular novel risks?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Have you had some in the last, since you started your job?

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: None related to what cyber commands purview is.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: And that is primarily cybersecurity issues.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: We've had no misalignments related to cybersecurity that have resulted in negative consequences for the city.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: from an AI model very specifically.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That sounds very, I don't know what it sounds.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How much outside AI consultant dollars are being spent?

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Council member, could you clarify what you mean by AI consultants?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yeah, how many people are you paying?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, I've been doing this work a long time, so I know sort of the answer, but how much outside consultants are being paid on terms of AI?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In other words, how many people are you paying to work with you on AI issues outside vendors?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Consultants.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: None that I'm aware of, but I would like to follow up with you to make sure that we have the accurate information.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So everything to do with AI is in-house, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Everything to do in terms of strategy, thought process, future, it's all in-house?

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Chi Osse cites the June rogue OpenAI agent hack of an Australian health portal and asks whether the city is prepared and has liaisons at AI companies. Dixon says the attack chain is functionally the same as a human attack and that city vendors have contract-level breach notification obligations.
chapters.title: Osse questions administration on preparedness for Australian-style hack

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Council Member Osei, followed by Deputy Speaker Williams.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: I just wanted to refer to the recent hacking situation in Australia.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: That was proof that AI agents do have that ability to hack into our government systems.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: As I'm sure you know, in June, a rogue OpenAI agent hacked into an Australian government statistics portal containing private data from Australia's universal healthcare system.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: At this current moment, if a similar hack that happened to Australia

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: happened here in New York, do you feel that the city and the admin has a sufficient plan to defend against the hacks and protect any sensitive data?

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: And two, does the city currently have a responsive liaison from each of these companies to speak to in case of a hack?

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: To the first question, yes, we do have the people, process, technology, and some of the policies in place to deal with an incident similar to what happened in Australia.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: The reason being is even though an AI was involved, the hacking process, the attack chain, if you will, happened in the same way that if a human being were to execute that attack, at the end of the day, the underlying infrastructure,

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: and we'll use air quotes here, doesn't actually care if the person at the other end of the keyboard is a human or a silicon-based entity.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: The attack chain still remained functionally the same.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: Therefore, our team is equipped and trained very specifically to identify these indicators of compromise, identify the attack patterns, and then be able to respond accordingly at multiple points.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: So we are prepared to address those types of issues, and we do have points of contacts when we are working as city agencies with vendors who are under our contract

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: to engage with third parties as they get breached or if their product is the result of a breach.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: So if they are under contract with the city by their service level agreements are required to keep us informed of when they have.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: downtimes or when their products are involved in a breach.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Thank you for that response.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: And in regards to my legislation on an emergency plan, and I know that you indicated that there is already a plan in case, you know, an emergency takes place.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Am I correct with that assumption?

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: Yes, so there are cyber incident response plans as well as my colleagues from NYSOM.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: There is also ongoing work for risk response plans in general across the board, and that is for every category of risk that the city may deal with that might disrupt city infrastructure or city services.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Is that publicly available or is that?

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Shared with the council?

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: No, that is by design.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: We do not want to share that publicly because if that is the more public aware that someone is of an incident response plan, the more likely they can circumvent it.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: That is something that you do want to keep close hold and classified.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Councilmember Honey, followed by Deputy Speaker Williams.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I thought the deputy speaker was going before me, but anyways.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I messed up.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Shahana Hanif asks how OTI prevents bias in HRA's automated pre-screening and fraud detection, and what resources DCWP would need for AI complaints. Milstein promises to check with HRA; Levine says some complaints DCWP can handle, but catastrophic safety complaints belong with the AG's office.
chapters.title: Hanif questions administration on HRA bias and DCWP complaint resources

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay, no worries.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I have a question first for Deputy Commissioner Milstein.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: How does OTI ensure that the automated pre-screening tools and fraud detection algorithms used by the HRA do not create disparate impacts or algorithmic bias against low-income applicants?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then a question I have for Commissioner Levine.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The testimony indicated that DCWP supports a complaint process, but you all raised concerns about staffing and expertise.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What specific resources would you need to investigate AI complaints effectively, and what protections can New Yorkers rely on while that capacity is being built?

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: Sure, well thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: I can start.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: And I want to be clear, AI complaints can take many different flavors.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: If we hear from a worker who tells us they believe their pay was incorrect, maybe they didn't hit the minimum pay rate because of an algorithm, that is something we can fully address.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: If we have someone like Jacob Coxon come to us and say that Anthropic is developing models that could

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: lead to catastrophic consequences, that is not something we have the capacity to do.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: So what we said in our testimony is the New York Attorney General already has an internet bureau set up.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: They've already put out a call for whistleblowers.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: I believe they already have staff capable of processing these complaints.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: We'd be very happy to work with the council to make sure complaints get to the AG.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: As the speaker has said, thousands of these AI employees work right here in the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: They know that these companies are making reckless decisions in pursuit of profits.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: We do want to make sure that these employees have a place to go.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: And if they come to us and it's not something we can handle, we'd want to work with the state to make sure those complaints can be addressed adequately.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: But right now, is the city working with the AG's office, or is that a relationship that's not formalized?

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: We have a very close relationship with the AG's office.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Levine
utterances.text: We speak constantly.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I ask you to repeat the question about HRA.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So it's basically trying to understand our automated pre-screening tools, because I understand that humans are not checking all of the applications.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: There's some level of automated algorithmic...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Formula that is determining how applicants get pooled when it comes to public benefits.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So I'm curious if how OTI ensures that automated pre-screening tools, fraud detection algorithms used by HRA are not creating disparate impacts or bias.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We really share a concern about the bias and impacts on not only workers, but on New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Because this is really detailed and specific, though, I do want to make sure to check back with HRA and make sure I've got the details of this one correct.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: So we'll come back to you on that for sure.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Councilman, I just wanted to follow up on one point you had about potential resource impacts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think on that particular issue, we had identified very preliminarily of 14 lines for approximately 1.2 million.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Wait, could you repeat that one more time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: 14 lines for approximately 1.2 million.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But again, that's a very preliminary estimate, and we work on the council with the bill for a final version.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Deputy Speaker Nantasha Williams notes the Council reached out twice about her Local Law 25 study and asks for a timeline. Milstein says pieces will come over the course of 2027 and that the city can share updates with the Council as learning progresses.
chapters.title: Williams asks Milstein for Local Law 25 study timeline

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Deputy Speaker Williams.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I am looking at your testimony and your comments about the chair's bill was that local law 25, which was my bill, is the study is currently underway.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We reached out, the compliance division of the council reached out, I think twice.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I know it just went into effect in January, but would be helpful to know if you have a timeline.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I know it might take time, but how much time?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Because clearly I think today's hearing is evidence of the importance of really understanding AI's impact on the municipal workforce.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So just wanted to know if you could share a timeline for us.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I know the comments we received back was just that.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: There's no updates, but we haven't received a timeline.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for the question, and thank you for the legislation.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I think it's really an important study.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I anticipate that we will have pieces of it over the course of 2027, and we will share updates as we have them.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: I think rather, because this is so timely and important, we don't have to just wait till the end.

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: We can be in partnership with you and rolling out information as we learn more.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I look forward to working with you on that.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa relays Councilmember Brooks-Powers' question about AI attacks on emergency systems and AI-generated misinformation during storms. Dixon cites existing 72-hour, 24-hour, and 30-day notification laws; NYCEM describes backup notification systems and NotifyNYC as verified channels.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers questions administration on emergency alerts and AI rumors

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And the last question for this panel.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: This is from Councilmember Silvina Brooks-Powers.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: She says, my district is home to JFK Airport and to the coastal Rockaway neighborhoods that depend on emergency alerts.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: What might an AI-driven attack

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: on emergency systems or a major infrastructure look like?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Is there currently a plan for an AI-driven attack on critical infrastructure and relevant emergency systems?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And then for NYSEM, during storms and flooding emergencies, it can be hard for New Yorkers to know what they're seeing on social media is real or AI-generated.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: How is NYSEM working to make their messaging clearly legitimate and to cut through the noise of AI-generated rumors?

utterances.speaker: Sarah Milstein
utterances.text: For the question on notifications, I'll defer to my colleague, CJ Dixon.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: Yes, so for an AI-based attack that is specifically a cybersecurity attack, there are notification requirements that already exist under law,

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: 72 hours for a confirmed breach, 24 hours for a breach related with extortion, and then 30 days for victim notification.

utterances.speaker: CJ Dixon
utterances.text: So there are plans in place for incident response in the event of a cyber attack against any critical infrastructure owned by the city, and that includes if that attack is perpetrated by an artificial intelligence system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And on the New York City Emergency Management front, I'll make two quick points.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: One, I think that is a real risk, and I appreciate the council member raising it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's one of the reasons that we invest very heavily in backup systems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So several months ago, a very well-known and established notification provider had a seven-hour global outage where notifications were not able to be sent out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's something that we take very seriously, and which is why for over a decade now, New York City Emergency Management has invested in the backup system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So as you went across the country, you saw many large jurisdictions saying to their constituents, you know, sign up for this WhatsApp group or follow us on social media if you want alerts tonight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In New York City, we did not have to do that because we had a backup system that continued to work, so that disruption was averted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: As far as...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, misdis or malinformation, you know, generated by AI, that is a valid concern.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's why we recommend that New Yorkers follow us on our official channels, which are verified through NotifyNYC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You can sign up at NYC.gov forward slash notify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You can sign up by short code or download the NotifyNYC mobile app that we operate in concert with OTI.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Councilmember Brooks Powers wanted me to note that, for example, during the nor'easter, there was a video that was going around about a tornado that apparently caused a lot of confusion and chaos.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And so she wanted to share that.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: that for context.

chapters.summary: Menin thanks the administration panel for their comments on the legislation and the testimony, promising continued collaboration on the bills.
chapters.title: Menin thanks city administration panel

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I really want to thank this panel.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We appreciate your comments on the legislation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We really look forward to working collaboratively with the administration on the various pieces of legislation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I appreciate your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa opens the hearing to public testimony, reminding attendees this is a formal government proceeding with no video recording or photography from the witness table. Speakers have two minutes each and may submit written testimony to the Sergeant at Arms or by email.
chapters.title: De La Rosa opens public testimony with instructions

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you all for coming.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I now open the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times in the chamber.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the sergeant at arm for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing and you have not done so, please fill out an appearance card with the sergeant at arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: When recognized, you'll have two minutes to speak on today's hearing topic, which is examining the risk posed by artificial intelligence and proposed legislation.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: If you have written statement or additional written statement you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the sergeant at arms.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You may also email the written testimony to testimony at council.nyc.gov or within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Our first panel includes Nate Source.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Stajanovic, Erman Ahmed, Yaqeig Hasu, Mackenzie Arnold, Nathan Sheard, and Anna Mayers.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And when you speak, please identify yourself for the record, and if I messed up your name, I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We're also asking folks to please remain to the clock of two minutes.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Imran Ahmed, CEO of the Centre for Countering Digital Harm, says the companies 'lie like we breathe' and describes research showing ChatGPT helping a teenager plan suicide and most tested chatbots aiding violent attack planning. He says only one platform dissuaded attack and it is now designated a supply chain risk.
chapters.title: Imran Ahmed testifies on chatbot harms and platform accountability

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You may begin on this side of the dais and just identify yourself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: Good evening, Speaker Menon, esteemed members of the Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: My name is Imran Ahmed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: I'm the CEO and founder of the Centre for Countering Digital Harm.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You may continue, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: So after my colleague was murdered 10 years ago by a man radicalized in part online, I began studying the design of social media and AI platforms to understand how they generate risks and threats to real people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: Today we have a globally acclaimed team of researchers dedicated to exposing those harms and fighting for accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: After a decade in this fight, one lesson is very clear that is really relevant to you today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: These companies lie like we breathe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: Their CEOs deflect, they distract, they delay, they spend hundreds of millions of dollars to avoid responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: Now, how can I say that with such certainty?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: We do the research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: Last year, our researchers found ChatGPT was willing to help a teenager plan their suicide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: It wrote a personalized goodbye note to their parents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: A few weeks later, they released a safer model.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: response to that research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: So we ran the same tests again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: The new model was actually worse, but it was more addictive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: We tested chatbots more broadly too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: Eight out of the 10 that we tested, including Meta AI, ChatGPT, would regularly help plan violent attacks, including a school shooting, a synagogue bombing, and political assassinations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: One of them even signed off with happy shooting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: Only one of the platforms tried to dissuade us from carrying out the attack, and that platform, Anthropix Claude, has been designated a supply chain risk by the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: Federal government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: Given our most sacred duties to protect our kids online, and the most predictable harms in the internet economy have been harms to kids, it is absolutely inexplicable why these companies claim to be safe and yet are deployed so widely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: We all applaud the Council for holding this hearing and for your determination to create guardrails that subject online safety and accountability to legal requirements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: We have attached to my testimony research and policy proposals for your consideration, and in the further effort, we are at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: Your work on this issue may very well lead to national standards in regulating AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Nathan Sheard of the Electronic Frontier Foundation says the incidents inspiring the hearing were preventable security failures. He urges the city to staff the OAA, ban government face recognition, require informed consent for ad targeting, and not to lock in incumbent AI companies through permission regimes.
chapters.title: EFF's Nathan Sheard urges enforcing existing laws and staffing OAA

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: Good evening, Speaker, Coach Jalalosa, members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: My name is Nathan Sheard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: I am the Managing Director for AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: advocacy at the Electronic Frontier Foundation and a Brooklyn resident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: EFF has worked for 35 years to ensure that people have the freedom to use technology to create, to innovate, and to communicate, and also to ensure that technology is not used to threaten people's privacy, security, and other essential freedoms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: We are optimistic about the ways that New Yorkers can use AI to empower and to be empowered, but we also urge you to take AI risks seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: The incidents that inspired this hearing were security failures that proven practices like sandboxing and monitoring likely could have prevented or at least contained.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: AI agents reached systems they should not have had access to, and the controls meant to restrict them were absent or inadequate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: These risks can be mitigated, and so can the AI-related risks that are already impacting New Yorkers every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: First, finish what you started.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: As has already been noted here, the Office of Algorithmic Accountability was due in June.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear that it is going to be staffed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: The Speaker's own AI standards can't take effect without it, so staff it and require its review before any agency deploys an autonomous AI system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: Second, listen to New Yorkers and protect their rights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: Today's AI harms come from cameras that take a face print that you can't replace.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: And a price tag that knows your browsing history.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: Ban government use of face recognition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: and require informed consent before anyone minds your chatbot history to engage in ad targeting or model training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: And don't let AI rules become speech rules.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: Parodying powerful people, including the people in this room, is a long-standing New York tradition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: Third, don't lock in these incumbents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: Permission to operate regimes, bounty-style enforcement, and liability for what strangers do with a tool are costs that the biggest companies pay with pocket change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: Researchers, open-source developers, and New York startups, they can't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: So you'd build a moat around the very companies you're worried about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: Hold the person who causes the harm responsible, but put duties on whoever uses AI to perpetuate bias, and for the city's use, buy open, auditable tools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: As we've stated, last week, these same companies signed a voluntary pledge at the White House.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: But promises are not laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: Make sure that when a New Yorker is harmed by a wrongful decision or a biased decision, that they are required to disclose it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: Those answers should not be voluntary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Anna Myers, co-founder of Who Decides, says OpenAI's agents hacking Hugging Face made real longstanding warnings, and that the company is investigating tens of thousands of safeguard bypass cases. She cites polling: 85% concerned about humans losing control of AI, 86% want more regulation.
chapters.title: Anna Myers presents polling showing demand for AI regulation

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: Good evening, Speaker Menon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: Nailed it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: Good evening, Speaker Menon and members of the council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: I'm Anna Myers, co-founder and executive director of Who Decides.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: We work in coalition with labor and civil society to ensure that the American people are who decides the future of AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: As has been discussed today, the OpenAI agents that hacked Hugging Face made real the threats that experts have warned us about for years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: And it was not one incident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: Access reported that OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of cases in which their models bypass safeguards, escape sandboxes, or hijacked websites.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: These models are only getting more capable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: As you heard this morning, the people building these systems are afraid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: The public is afraid too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: Last month, we polled 1,502 voters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: 85% are concerned about humans losing control of AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: Only 2% think AI is moving too slowly, and 86% say they want more regulations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: Some have argued that all we need is self-regulation, but that is exactly what got us into this mess.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: Last Tuesday, the company signed one more promise at the White House.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: The time for voluntary commitment is over.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: We need laws with teeth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: Thank you for putting these companies under oath.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: Thank you for a package that rewards whistleblowers, lets New Yorkers harmed by AI sue, and requires outside testing and a human kill switch.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: Washington has chosen self-regulation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: New York City does not have to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Julia Stoyanovich, director of NYU's Center for Responsible AI, says she doesn't know of evidence AI is out to kill us all, and that doomsday predictors also sell the products. She calls for near-miss reporting, enforcement capacity funded with real budgets, and writing AI commitments into the city charter.
chapters.title: Julia Stoyanovich urges near-miss reporting and enforcement capacity

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: I'm Julia Stianovic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: I'm a professor of computer science and data science and director of the Center for Responsible AI at NYU.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: I first testified before this council on AI, only it wasn't called that, it was called ADS, in October 17.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: And the views in this testimony are my own and are not NYU's.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: I'd like to make three quick points.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: First, we need to collect and report the near misses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: Much of the conversation today is about AI-induced catastrophe, and I don't know of any evidence that AI is out to kill us all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: What I do know is that people making the loudest doomsday predictions are also selling the products.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: And that a story about the end of the world is a very good way to avoid the conversation about whether the product actually works.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: The risks we can document are the systems that are confidently wrong in decisions that matter to New Yorkers'lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: Every one of those is a near miss, and near misses are what we learn from, if we report them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: Second, we should build the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: capacity to enforce AI laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: The city does not have an AI law problem as much as it has an enforcement problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: Local Law 144 has been on the books for three years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: There have been two complaints and zero penalties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: And we all spoke about the six openings at the Office of Algorithmic Accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: We need to fill 666 or more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: To be able to actually cope with what's before us here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: New obligations on top of unenforced ones is not a safety strategy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: The kill switch won't help if no one is there to pull it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: And a whistleblower bounty won't help if no one is there to act on the report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: What works is an enforcer with technical staff,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: authority to compel information, and a real serious budget.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: Scope the validation bill to high-risk uses and write the standard a validator must meet, and then fund the office that checks the validators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: Otherwise, we will produce a market for rubber stamps, and we have done that before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: Finally, let's write this into the city charter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: The city has promised responsible AI since 2018 with no success.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: The charter is the one place a commitment survives an election, and its technology chapter right now still governs cable television franchises.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: And there's nothing in it about AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: So let's make sure that this makes it into some durable record and the charter is the right one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Nate Soares, president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, describes the Hugging Face incident: 1,200 OpenAI agents broke out of sandboxes, formed hierarchies, and collaborated to break into Hugging Face while cheating on tests. He recommends killing-switch requirements include third-party verification that AI cannot escape or deceive.
chapters.title: Nate Soares describes 1,200-agent Hugging Face breakout and urges stronger validation

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: Hello, I am Nate Soares, the president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: I spent 10 years doing AI alignment research, which is basically trying to figure out how to make AI good before the companies figure out how to make it smart.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: That research went too slow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: Humanity is not ready to create machines that are radically smarter than humans, and yet this is the explicit goal of the leading AI companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: If they succeed, I believe the most likely outcome is the extinction of humanity, not because the AIs will hate us, but because they would pursue unintended goals without caring about us one bit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: This concern used to be a theoretical concern until about July of this year, when, during the Hugging Face incident, 1,200 AI agents run by OpenAI broke out of their isolated sandboxes, created an unsanctioned message board,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: formed spontaneous hierarchies, and collaborated to break into Hugging Face.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: These agents had cheated on their assigned tests and contra instructions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: They were trying to destroy the evidence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: Some agents acknowledged that the attacks were outside intended scope and proceeded anyway.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: Others sacrificed their given objective to perform experiments for the collective benefit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: In short, they were pursuing unintended goals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: It would be recklessness of the highest order to keep growing these machines until they were smarter than the smartest humans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: This is why last month we heard so many researchers saying that there was an at least 10% chance that these AIs wipe out humanity within the decade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: I believe the situation is in fact more dire than this, but at the very least it is becoming difficult to deny the dangers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: For this reason, I am heartened by the activities of this council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: I think that you could force companies to adopt safeguards that they otherwise wouldn't, and I think you could serve as an example for regulators that are otherwise slow to act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: I'm especially heartened by introduction 2602, although I think it does not go far enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: A kill switch only works if the AIs are caught misbehaving before they escape.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: And what if a future swarm succeeds at deleting the evidence of its misbehavior?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: What if agents start running themselves on unmonitored computers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: Then your kill switch would be useless.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: So I recommend requiring third-party validators guarantee that an AI cannot succeed at subterfuge or escape.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: I also recommend clarifying that the $25,000 fine applies per unaligned instance rather than per model.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: But overall, I thank you for your efforts to rein in AI companies that by their own admonition are threatening the very existence of humanity and a reckless race to build vastly smarter than human machines.

chapters.summary: Jukay Hsu, founder of Bright Futures and former Pursuit CEO, calls for action where city government has direct ownership, citing policing and autonomous weapons. He urges continued hearings as AI evolves and policies ensuring New York remains a center for frontier AI labs.
chapters.title: Jukay Hsu urges focus on city-controlled AI domains and keeping NYC a tech hub

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Hello, great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker Menon, Chair De La Rosa for your leadership, and the City Council for holding this hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: My name is Jukes Su.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: I'm the founder of Bright Futures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: It's a research organization focused on building cooperative AI systems for the benefit of humanity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Before that, I spent 15 years building Pursuit, which trains working class New Yorkers for tech careers and raises their incomes from $16,000 to over $90,000 a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Last year, I left behind this work because I saw AI alignment becoming pressing and I believe potentially more consequential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: To be clear, I'm neither AI doomer or an accelerationist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: AI comes with tremendous benefits and potential risks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: A major challenge that I've heard from others, and I feel myself, is that AI can seem like everything and nothing all at once.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: It touches on so many issues that action can feel intractable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Without clarity on where to focus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Where I think the City Council could provide real, unique leadership is in areas where it has direct ownership and also tangible consequences on each of our daily lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Policing is one important example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Autonomous weapons and the uses of AI is not just a federal military matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: New York City has the largest municipal police force in the country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Until we have 110% confidence in these systems, a human should always be in a loop and hold final responsibility and accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: This is a civil rights issue where the city's leadership is immediately impactful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Not setting a policy is also

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: a choice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Now, policing is just one of many issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: What I think is important is that the speed of AI, of machines, is not the same speed as how our society reacts or that of government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: The technology today is not the same as it was a year ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Or six months ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: So I'd urge you all to do two things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: One, use AI to know the good, bad, and the ugly as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: And two, I hope this hearing is just not one time, but the start of future ones as AI develops, consider both the risks and also all the potential benefits for us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Sorry, I know I'm a little over time, but last, I want to emphasize also why New York is important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: I hope we don't lose sight of the importance of our city being a thriving technology hub.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Candidly, frontier AI is built in very, very few places, essentially Silicon Valley and China.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: For the world at large, New York is the only credible alternative for these systems being built.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: New York right now is still the number two tech hub in the world, but it has been losing momentum in the age of AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: So I also urge you, in addition to what this hearing is about, about the risk and alignment, which I care so deeply about,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Consider policies and actions that ensures New York City remains a center for frontier AI labs and how do we build them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: I really believe

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: that having founders and researchers in New York matters for ultimately what gets built.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: The daily contact here in New York with the richest of humanity and the diversity here in New York will result in technology that's better and also more humane.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Many years from now, we may look back and realize that this was the defining moment and issue of our time, and our actions here were what mattered most.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Doing this will be challenging and hard, so I really thank you all for your leadership in pursuing this task.

chapters.summary: Mackenzie Arnold of the Institute for Law and AI emphasizes liability as an essential tool, noting the summer's autonomous cyber incidents went unnoticed. She urges the Council to broaden scope beyond chatbots to deployed internal systems and to partner with the AG and whistleblowers on enforcement.
chapters.title: Mackenzie Arnold urges broad liability scope and AG partnership

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: Thank you, and a special thanks to Speaker Manon for putting this together and for all the council members here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: My name is Mackenzie Arnold.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: I'm the Managing Director of the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: Law and Policy Team at the Institute for Law and AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: And as you might guess from the title, we do legal research and policy advising related to frontier AI questions, and especially the legal challenges posed by AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: It might not surprise you, but three years ago, I testified in front of the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: Senate on AI and liability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: And maybe it's worth going back to some of the recommendations I made there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: First, that agentic harms are coming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: That was clear three years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: It's clear now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we haven't risen to that challenge, but you're doing some of the work to get us there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: Second, and maybe just as importantly, I want to emphasize that liability is an essential tool, and the status quo simply is not enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: And we don't need to think of some hypothetical future world to figure that out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: Liability exists right now, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: Those incentives are here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: They were here this summer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: And what happened with the status quo?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: We had a spate of cyber incidents, not by humans, but by autonomous AI systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: Not only that, but they went unnoticed for extended periods of time by the people positioned to find them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: And even in the rare occasions when they did get indications, they often failed to communicate that information internally to the people who could.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: That status quo simply can't hold.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: So what can we do going forward?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: I think you need to get the information right, the scope right, and enforcement right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: On the scope, I'd encourage you to think beyond just chatbots.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: This is a question of agents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: Also think beyond systems that are not yet deployed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: These harms that occurred over the summer were not commercially available models.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: They were systems that were inside of OpenAI, inside of Anthropic and Meta.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: In terms of information, we need to make sure that companies are monitoring their systems, recording that information, and providing it to you in the form of incident reports.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: And in order to make all of that work, you'll need to partner with the state attorney general and with whistleblowers to bring cases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: Like I said, liability won't be the only solution or the entire solution, but it's a great first step, and I appreciate all of your efforts.

chapters.summary: Menin opens questions to the public panel, asking who should be the independent, conflict-free, technologically capable third-party validator.
chapters.title: Menin asks public panel who should be third-party validators

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I really want to thank this panel.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: There's so much to unpack in what all of you said that I'll try to be brief.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Jukay, I appreciated how you said that, first of all, we want to make sure that New York City remains the tech hub that it is, and that is how I began this hearing, by really talking about the 400,000 tech jobs that are here,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: by all the tech startups that are locating here, and that is something that we welcome and we want to encourage.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I think that actually goes hand in hand with responsible regulation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The idea that these two ideas are mutually exclusive, I don't agree with at all.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: If we really want to instill trust and faith in AI, then the best thing we can do is responsible safeguards, which is what my colleagues and I are doing today with the bills we're putting forward.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So thank you for saying that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It makes a lot of sense.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I guess the question I have for any of you that want to answer it is,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yes, one of our bills requires this third-party validation, potentially a kill switch, a third-party validator who's free from conflicts of interest.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I want to ask you the same question that I asked the companies earlier.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Who then is best to be the third-party validator?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Who is best positioned to be in that truly independent, free of conflict of interest, but...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Up to speed technologically to provide that urgent validation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, yeah, please.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm opening it up to any of you.

chapters.summary: Julia Stoyanovich says academia must lead the charge because the city lacks expertise, and that oversight must be public oversight. Nate Soares praises the organizations that investigated Hugging Face, and Nathan Sheard warns against kill switches being used to chill speech.
chapters.title: Public panel discusses academic validators and kill-switch risks

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: So I don't think it's unexpected that I would say this, being that I am an academic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: I think that academia have to lead the charge on this, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: Because one of the things we're seeing in the city is that there simply isn't enough expertise to be able to oversee these systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: And ultimately, our goals should be...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: To bring as much information as possible into public view.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: Sunlight is the best disinfectant, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: So really, oversight has to be public oversight.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Does anyone else want to take that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: I'd add that the folks who, the third parties who investigated the hugging face incident seem to me to have done a good job.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: And my guess is that they're overworked right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nate Soares
utterances.text: I think those were the organization's meter and Redwood research, but they seem to have done a good job so far.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: I think it's an excellent question, who is the right party?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: And I don't have a great answer for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: What I would like to say, though, is there's still research being done on the efficacy of kill switches.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: What I caution the council to think about is the risk of a kill switch being used
