utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: as a tool to chill on popular speech.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: And so really thinking through to make sure that as we think about the ways that we want to provide the right protections for New Yorkers, that we're also not building tools that in the future could be used to harm people's essential liberties.

chapters.summary: Imran Ahmed raises the dirty secret that civil society research is often funded by platforms, and calls for public funding. Jukay Hsu argues many parties can play a role and that power will be dispersed beyond frontier labs, which complicates expert reliance.
chapters.title: Ahmed and Hsu discuss validator funding and broad expertise

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: If I can make a brief point on who could do this work, being realistic,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: To date, civil society studying social media and AI platforms has had one dirty secret, that most of its funding has come from the platforms themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: So Meta and Google were enormous funders of extremism research, of safety research on their own platforms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: And when I would meet, and we don't take their money, when I would meet with their CEOs, they would say, the CEOs of the civil society bodies which were funded by them, they'd say, we're not allowed to say that they haven't done enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: We can always say they could do more, but not they haven't done enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: So there are real compromises there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: In Europe or the rest of the world, and you can hear from my accent that I actually grew up in Britain, that the government would fund this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: And when it comes to giving a body the resources to have the speed and creativity to be effective in dealing with the fastest moving technology

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: in human history, I cannot think of a non-governmental source of funding that would be sufficient to get it to scale fast enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: So the question for New York City and New York State, which is a substantial economic unit, the budget of New York State is one quarter that of the entire United Kingdom, one state alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Imran Ahmed
utterances.text: It does have the economic capacity to do so, and I think you would have to seriously think about whether or not you're willing to put some public money towards creating an institution that's able to operate with the speed, resources, and creativity to be effective.

chapters.summary: Mackenzie Arnold notes there may be only a dozen people capable of this work, suggests relying on academia, private parties, and the public, and urges the city to send a clear market signal requiring audits for city contracts without being overly prescriptive.
chapters.title: Arnold urges the city to send a clear market signal for validators

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: And yeah, I agree with these kind of comments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: It's such a tough challenge and totally agree with you that New York can be both.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: And I think people are looking for answers that's not so black and white and realize the reality of this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: You know, that's such an important question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: You know, I think who can be third-party validators?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: I think it's yes and and for everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: The labs are doing a lot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Like you heard, Anthropic is investing a lot into this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: There are many more people going to AI alignment and safety research, which is so important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: I think the one thing that's challenging is going to be, I think the things are, like everyone said, moving so quickly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: I think everyone can be a judge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Experts today, like yesterday, six months ago, is not the same thing as today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: And what's really going to happen is that you all can also be the judges by using this, like what makes sense and what doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: A lot of it's, I think, common sense, hopefully, in the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: And then the last point I kind of make to that, even though that seems counterintuitive about who are the experts, where we all can play a role, we have agency, is that in the future, it's not just these five, what we call frontier labs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: All the companies here in New York are fine-tuning their own models.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: We all may have our own very powerful models in the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: So actually, beyond the frontier labs, part of the challenge may be actually, you know, your student researcher downloading a model and uploading it and fine-tuning it to create capabilities or test things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Or, you know, a company to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: inadvertently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: So I think it's a much broader set of things than just relying on experts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: I think, again, that is important, but I think we need to really widen the scope around that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: This is not a technology where it's going to be nuclear weapons controlled by a dozen states.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: These will be as powerful, but we will have use and access to that, and I don't think that's going to stop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: If I can jump in with just one last thought.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: I want to pick up on the yes and approach because I think this is right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: I was just talking with someone the other day who works at one of these evaluators today, and they joked that there were dozens of entities that could do this, and by that they meant a dozen people, not a dozen different companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: I think we'll need to rely on both academia and private parties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: I think we'll also have to rely on the public, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: A big part of incident reporting is revealing some of that information to the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: One of the only times I've ever been happy with Twitter was this summer as people were arguing over the incidents and we were starting to get a better idea of what happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: One note of caution I'll add is that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: One way this goes wrong is that the few potential evaluators that there are get tasked with many different things, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: And there's a chance that New York should lead on this and that they should also coordinate with the state and with California and others and not be overly prescriptive in the exact sort of analyses that need to be done by the entities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: Where you can be exceptionally helpful is in sending a clear market signal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mackenzie Arnold
utterances.text: So requiring that these audits or validations be done in order to get contracts with the city or things like that.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks whether the panel has concerns about open weight models and how to defend against bad actors. Nathan Sheard says open models let researchers evaluate tools, and the city should use existing laws to pursue harmful actors rather than relying on incumbents.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks panel about open weight model risks

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I have two questions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The first one is for anyone in the panel who wants to take it.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Do you have concerns related to open weight models being available?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And if safety features can be eliminated from open weight models, how do you defend against bad actors who use them?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: I can start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: I think one of the things I think about when we're thinking about open weight models is that we do want the ability for researchers and startups and potential future competitors to be able to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: develop tools and resources and also so that we can be able to evaluate these tools and see how they really work, which is difficult with the closed models.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: But then it certainly does lend the question then of how do we make sure that the proper protections are in place and I think

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: We have some of the tools to do that already.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: When an act takes place that is potentially harmful or threatening to New Yorkers, their freedoms or physical safety,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: pursue, use the laws that we have now to pursue the people who are engaging in those activities, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: So rather than try to create, look to the incumbents, the powerful corporations to put in the protections that will keep us safe,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: use the existing laws that we have to be able to keep people safe and really look at who are the people that are creating the harm and use the things that we have in place to pursue justice and protection and security there.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks Stoyanovich, who is skeptical of the catastrophe narrative, what harms matter most to New Yorkers. Stoyanovich describes auditing a hiring personality profile system that gave inconsistent results based on file format, and cites the MyCity chatbot advising businesses to break the law.
chapters.title: Stoyanovich details documented AI harms to New Yorkers

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I do have a direct question for Dr.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Stajanovic.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I hope I didn't mess that up too bad.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I know you said you seem skeptical of the catastrophic narrative around what's occurring, but you still have concerns about possible harms.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Can you describe to us

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: based on your expertise, what are the harms that are most relevant to New Yorkers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: Thank you for this question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: So we are running these systems in the city, in the public sector, in the private sector, and we have seen in New York very specific harms that come from deployed systems and with very consequential decisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: So in my own work, I did an audit of a hiring system that claims to construct a job seeker's personality profile, a bunch of numbers from their resume or social media feed, like

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: a Twitter feed at the time or a LinkedIn profile.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: And these systems are complete nonsense, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: For the same job seeker, if you change something, like the file format of their resume, it's going to give you a completely different personality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: So we need to actually be looking at whether these systems even work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: I think that that should be just stop one of anything before we worry about existential risk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: We had a similar scenario with the MyCity chatbot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: I mean, we all have heard about that fiasco where the city spent half a million dollars, conservatively speaking, on a bot that advised small and medium-sized business owners to break the law, which was quite problematic, speaking with the city's authority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: So I really think that we need to be looking at cases such as these ones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: Where there are very

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: known risks and start there and clean up our own house.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you for that and I want to thank you all for your answers and insights.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We have three members on stack, Councilmember Osei, Councilmember Hanif, and then Councilmember Maloney to close this panel.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Chi Osse asks Anna Myers whether harms to children, workers, consumers, and catastrophic risks conflict. Myers says it's a 'yes and' and the public should be central to decisions. Asked what Americans fear most, she says they feel they have no say.
chapters.title: Osse asks Myers whether AI harms conflict with each other

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Myers, there are a lot of issues in AI.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Currently, we hear about the harms that it has for our children, workers, consumers, and the coming threats of catastrophic risk.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Do any of these issues conflict with one another, and which should we address, if not all of them?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: This is a yes and question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: This is, we cannot silo these into separate scenarios.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: Kids, workers, consumers, catastrophic risks can all be addressed in parallel to each other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: Just like the council has done a great job with their bill package of covering multiple things at once, we need to resist the urge to fight against each other on whose bill is more important at times or what we're protecting at times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: When I worked on the RAISE Act, we were working on C2PA at the same time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: There's no reason for us to stop the protections of catastrophic risks while at the same time working on transparency data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: The most important question we need to have right now is who is making these decisions, and it shouldn't be five CEOs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: It should be the American people and the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: electeds that they voted for.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: And based on your conversations and polling, what are Americans most worried about when it comes to artificial intelligence?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: Yeah, right now that they don't have a say in it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: It's no accident that we named our org Who Decides.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: It's time for the American people to have a say in it and our polling showing that they feel that they are not a part of the conversation and that this is happening around them and they want to be in it.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Councilmember Hanif, followed by Maloney.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Shahana Hanif asks about safeguards against surveillance targeting identity or political activity and whether her Ban the Scan bill is important. Stoyanovich strongly supports it and calls for a proper data protection regime; Sheard emphasizes irreplaceable biometrics and chilling effects.
chapters.title: Hanif questions panel on biometric surveillance and Ban the Scan

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you for your expertise, and this is for everyone on the panel.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: As AI and facial recognition technologies become more powerful, what safeguards should cities put in place to prevent surveillance tools from being used to target people based on their identity, associations, or political activity?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Would legislation like my ban the scan bill, which would regulate and prohibit biometric surveillance in places of public accommodation, provide an important safeguard?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I'm particularly interested in your assessment of Madison Square Garden owner James Dolan's use of biometric surveillance to identify and exclude individuals.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: Anyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: So absolutely, I'm very supportive of your bill, and I think that we have a lack of data protection in this city, in this country, in the state, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: And data protection is a tremendously important issue, and because of how convenient AI tools are,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: people very often voluntarily give up very private information about themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: So I actually have in my written testimony that's much longer examples of AI assistants being marketed that essentially people give access to their calendars, their children's

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: biometrics, the schedules, all of the school contact information, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: So we really need to educate the public about

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: the benefits, but also the risks that data sharing poses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: And we need to establish a proper data protection regime in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: There's no way around it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: So as I mentioned in my statement, I am very concerned about the, and EFF is very concerned, about the risks connected to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: the collection of biometric data like face prints that can't be replaced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: If I lose my driver's license, I get a new driver's license.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: I lose my social security or my license plate gets out, I can replace those things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: I can't replace my face.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: And the risk of government use of face recognition technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: So far, I...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: outweighs any benefit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: The way that it will chill our ability to engage in protests, to engage in free speech, to be able to associate with freely and to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: search new ideas, healthcare, the risk that we'll be able to document like where we go into healthcare, how we move around the city, is considerable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: There's no way to separate that risk from government use of the technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: I think Illinois has a good model on how we can respond to private use of the technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: You know, we definitely don't want to be in a situation where people are being persuaded or otherwise not being informed about the way that they're

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: biometric data is being collected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: So by making sure that we have that the only time that that, but we also want to make sure that researchers are still be able to use the technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: The ACLU years ago used face recognition on a number of Congress people and they built a, and was able to show how it was

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: how easily it misidentified people, especially black, brown folks, women, older folks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: And so that kind of research and use can be really helpful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: But we need to make sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: So how do we protect people from the harms but still allow that research and other consensual use to be done?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: And I think, again, that model of making sure that people have informed, written consent about how the technology is being used and how the data is going to be stored and that they can only be used for the ways that have been explicitly approved by the individual whose

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: data is being collected is a way that we can make sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nathan Sheard
utterances.text: sure that people are, that we can mitigate the risk and it is only used in ways that people are very, are in an informed, consensual way agreeing to.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Councilmember Maloney.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Virginia Maloney asks whether foundational AI work happening in San Francisco is a problem and what New York's advantage is. Hsu says New York should both welcome companies and work on alignment; Stoyanovich calls for New York to invest in responsible innovation, upskilling, and enforcement capacity.
chapters.title: Maloney questions panel on New York's AI advantage and workforce

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I chair the Council's Committee on Economic Development, and I want to see technology companies, including AI technologies, build and hire here, and wanted to refer to some of the testimony earlier about that.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The four companies that we heard today have offices here, but the foundational AI work and that research is happening mainly in San Francisco.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Is that a problem?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: What is New York's AI advantage to grow that industry here?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And the second part of my question is on workforce development, and in particular, Pursuit did work on reskilling.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So I'm curious if you can speak to entry-level tasks that have been replaced by AI versus reskilled by AI, and the path from junior to senior, and the role or responsibility that the city plays

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: in helping people through the AI transition that's coming.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: and anyone who wants to speak.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Yeah, maybe I can speak quickly to both things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: I mean, on the second point, yeah, reskilling is so important, as we heard from everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: The city, I hope, plays a critical role here, and I hope you and others will continue to kind of address that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: It's so challenging right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: We don't know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: There's recent reports of how it's affected so many entry-level jobs, but that's going to continue to change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: It's not obvious what it is, and hence this might be unsatisfactory, but I hope just continued monitoring and understanding and engaging is so important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: But I think there are some obvious things, like autonomous vehicles will be coming to New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: I don't know if that's one year, five years, or ten years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: It's safer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: People trust it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: And so thinking about something like that, can New York City take bold leadership around what's going to happen to our 200,000 drivers and couriers so that they get reskilled and transitioned in the future?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: And I think there's so many opportunities to do that where the answer, I mean, there's an obvious thing that's going to happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: So how do we tackle that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: And then the first, yeah, I do hope.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: So many technology companies here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: I think that's how we build great stuff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: That's how we have growth and safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Alignment is so important, as we all agree here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: So I think part of it's a tone with all of you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: People want to live and build in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: And so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Also, you all can consider as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: I think what Mayor Bloomberg did, such a great job with tracking, is to make New York feel like a place where tech companies can grow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: Just showing up, talking about it, welcoming it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jukay Hsu
utterances.text: So I hope we can do both things, and you all both do that, working with the companies, new companies, and also think about alignment and work with them to address this, because we need the industry also to address this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: If I may add to this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: So the deputy commissioner of OTI, when she spoke, she uttered the phrase that I find really upsetting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: And that was, she said that we need effective and responsible innovation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: And the effective part of this would cover the wins for us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: But that is really not the kind of a position that New York City should be taking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: Our position should be that the wins should come from responsible innovation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: And this is our angle here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: And this, I think, is the kind of industry that we can and should build.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: We really are uniquely positioned as opposed to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: San Francisco to do this, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: And we always have been leading in at least proposing regulatory instruments for automated decision systems, AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: For us to actually develop an industry, we need to understand that we have to invest, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: And, you know, following up on what one of the people at the table here said, we have a pretty substantial amount of money here at our disposal that we could put towards responsible innovation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: Towards upskilling, towards making sure that the public's literacy is raised, right, so that we can all regulate and oversee this space together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julia Stoyanovich
utterances.text: So really, New York City should invest in responsible innovation, upskilling, literacy, and building enforcement capacity and oversight capacity in-house within the government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: Yeah, I think New York is a tech city, and we need to resist the urge to compare that we're not that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: I used to work in VC that invested in enterprise tech.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: We are a growing tech industry and the labs, those four companies are here working.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: They will grow slowly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: It's an affordability issue as well, and we can't narrow it to just that we're not tech welcoming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: And I think the mayor is doing a great job at that, and the city has a lot of opportunity to focus on the whole conversation and not just we don't see enough tech people moving here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Myers
utterances.text: This is a great tech city, and tech is only growing here.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa thanks the public panel and calls the next panel of state and international officials, including UK MP Jess Asato, Assemblymember Alex Bores, and state Senators Gounardes and Gonzalez.
chapters.title: De La Rosa calls state and international officials panel

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And I want to thank this panel for your expertise.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And this is not the end of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: This is the beginning.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The speaker has tasked us to continue to hold hearings with the different committees on AI in all of its sort of expansiveness.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So thank you so much for being here.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I want to call up the next panel.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: As we do this transition, I also want to remind anyone who has not signed up to speak to please fill out a card with the sergeant at arms.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: In this panel, we have our state colleagues and our colleagues from around the world testifying on this panel.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We have the Honorable Jess Asato, who is a UK Parliament member and has flown in specifically for this hearing, so we want to thank her for being here.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We have Alex Boris, current Assembly member.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We have Andrew Ganardis, Senator.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We have Kristen Gonzalez, Senator.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We have Clyde Bernal, Assembly member, and we have Jordan Wright, Assembly member.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We're going to begin this panel with Senator Gonzalez.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Whenever you're ready.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Honorable Jess Asado, you could also join this panel, please.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And thank you for being here and flying all the way in from the UK.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: State Senator Kristen Gonzalez says AI is not inevitable and New Yorkers are already harmed by surveillance, chatbots encouraging self-harm, and algorithmic bias in hiring, healthcare, and housing. She describes her rights-based bills including the New York AI Act and data center moratorium work.
chapters.title: Senator Kristen Gonzalez testifies on rights-based AI legislation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: Great, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: I want to thank Speaker Menon and the New York City Council for your attention to a, if not the, major policy issue of our time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: I am New York State Senator Kristen Gonzalez, representing the 59th Senate District in Midtown Manhattan, Northern Brooklyn, and Western Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: I am the chair of two state senate committees, elections and internet and technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: Over the last four years as chair of the state senate technology committee and as a former tech worker, I have led on the issue of AI in the legislature and have passed some of the state's first laws on generative AI,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: including regulating deepfakes in elections, government use of AI, protecting workers from automation, adding warning labels on chatbots, responsible data center development, and more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: I want to be clear, AI is not inevitable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: We do not have to accept a vision for innovation driven by the very same tech oligarchs who have raised alarm that their models could lead to catastrophic events.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: And we certainly can't trust the same people who have rushed to roll out imperfect AI tools to regulate themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: As government bodies, we have the responsibility to set guardrails on this new technology and the power to establish regulations that protect workers, consumers, and members of the public from potential danger.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: Interventions at every level of government are needed to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: to ensure AI is developed in a responsible way that benefits the public and not just the billionaires.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: Responsibly regulating AI absolutely means guardrails on frontier models and superintelligence that pose significant threats.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: However, meaningfully reining in these technologies to protect New Yorkers means regulating the AI-powered tools these companies are rushing to embed into every part of our lives with little oversight and little accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: We shouldn't have to wait for future harms to take action, because the harms of imperfect AI tools are already being felt across the country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: For example, uses for mass surveillance of immigrant communities and workers, chatbots creating intimate partner relationships with children and adults going as far as to encourage self-harm,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: and documented cases of algorithmic bias in decision-making, such as in hiring, healthcare, and housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: I believe we have the power to set the terms of innovation so that this technology is used for the maximum public good.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: That is why our state legislation has prioritized a rights-based approach to AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: We should have the fundamental right to privacy, which is why I've introduced the New York Privacy Act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: We should have a right to protections in the workplace, which is why I've introduced the BOT Act to protect workers from workplace surveillance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: We should have the right to know when AI is making high risk

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: consequential decisions about our lives and subjecting us to algorithmic bias, which is why I introduced the New York AI Act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: This bill requires third-party audits, compliance with international safety standards, disclosures, transparency, and importantly, for a human to be in the loop in consequential decision-making, much of which we've heard about today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: Finally, two of my bills sitting on the governor's desk this year include the right to keep our kids safe online from chatbots and the right to protect all of us from the build-out of massive data centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: Our bill, S9051B, bans unsafe features for kids and passed unanimously in both chambers of the legislature.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: Just like with that bill, New Yorkers are united in the fight against hyperscale data centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: At the end of August, I embarked on a statewide tour of communities that are affected by these data centers, and I went to 13 different communities facing major noise pollution, health impacts, environmental degradation, and threats to their water supplies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: I was proud to work with the governor on her first in the nation moratorium on the largest data centers, and I'm now working to get the Responsible Data Center Development Act signed into law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: While the tech CEOs say they want regulations, they have spent their time in Albany fighting against each of the common sense guardrails I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: For the lip service they pay to supporting legislation, it is only ever for the most watered-down version of a bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: Together, we have the ability to meet the moment, pass real legislation, protect New Yorkers, and build a future that allows us to benefit from innovation while protecting New Yorkers from real harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: Thank you to the council again today for our testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Senator.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You can continue, whoever wants to go next.

chapters.summary: Assemblymember Clyde Vanel says AI is a net good but ignoring mortal risks is absurd. He describes his Assembly Bill 3356, the Artificial Intelligence Act, which licenses high-risk AI systems, requires malfunction reporting, and sets up an independent ethics risk board.
chapters.title: Assemblymember Clyde Vanel presents the High Risk AI Act

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: Good evening, Madam Speaker, and also good evening to the chair, Carmen de la Rosa, and to my council member, Deputy Speaker Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: Nantasha Williams, who is the sponsor of Resolution 175.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: The resolution supporting the bill High Risk Advanced Artificial Intelligence Act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: Artificial intelligence, when used properly, is a net good.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: Education, healthcare, business, these are great uses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: But talking about them while ignoring the risk that AI could actually kill and strike us,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: It, to me, seems absurd.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: Companies are racing towards general artificial intelligence, and some of their systems are already too dangerous to release publicly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: This is by their own admission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: We saw this coming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: So with Assembly Bill,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: 3356, the Artificial Intelligence Act, a few years ago, the idea is simple.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: The more harm that an AI system can do,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: the more accountability that it should carry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: The bill identifies high-risk artificial intelligence systems, AI that diagnoses patients,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: that runs our power grid, or helps police or judges make decisions, and far more, it requires them to be licensed before operating in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: Under the act,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: The companies must report malfunctions and hacks like the recent Hugging Face case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: It must get states signed off before major changes and set up an independent ethics risk board that reports to the state annually.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: Finally, it writes a binding ethical code into the law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: New York took its first step with the RAISE Act, and I commend our colleagues and the state for passing it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: But now none of this that we're doing is meant to stop innovation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: We can't know that AI will be capable of in a few years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: But for tomorrow and for today, we must decide properly the path forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: I'd like to thank the council for putting this hearing together, and we must work on this together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Assemblymember Jordan Wright says his legislation requires independent third-party verification that AI developers follow their safety standards, and asks who the auditors are, whether they're truly independent, and what happens when they find problems.
chapters.title: Assemblymember Jordan Wright on independent third-party verification

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker Manon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Thank you to all the members of the Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair De La Rosa.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: I'm New York State Assemblymember Jordan Wright, representing the 70th Assembly District, which is Harlem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: One of the things I've been focused on in Albany is pretty simple.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Who is checking on AI companies?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: I have legislation that requires certain AI developers to have an independent third party

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: third party verify that they're actually following the safety standards that they say they are following.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Because we can't have a system where a company builds the technology, writes the safety rules, tells us they follow the rules, and then we just take their word for it?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Doesn't make much sense to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: We have to make sure that these third party audits actually mean something.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Who are the auditors?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Are they really independent?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Do they have conflicts of interest?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: And what happens when they find something wrong?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Those are questions that we're trying to answer at the state level, and I'm glad the city council is having this discussion as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: New York should be a place where AI companies want to build and innovate, but the accountability to innovate can exist at the same time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: I want to thank all the members of the council for having us today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: I thank you guys for taking this issue seriously once again, and please enjoy your evenings and be safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: UK Member of Parliament Jess Asato tells the Council that sexualized non-consensual images of her were created using SpaceX AI's Grok, and she is suing in UK courts. She calls it 'AI made wrong, not AI gone wrong' and says AI companies must be held to account regardless of wealth.
chapters.title: UK MP Jess Asato testifies about Grok deepfake abuse

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: Good evening and thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: My name is Jess Asato and I am a member of the United Kingdom Parliament for Lowestoft in Suffolk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: In January of this year, sexualized and degrading non-consensual images were created of me using SpaceX AI's tool, Grok.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: I was one of thousands of victims, including victims in New York, of Grok.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: Grok is an AI tool that was engineered to create sexualized content, even if that content had, and I quote, dark or violent themes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: I am seeking remedies against SpaceX AI in the English courts for the misuse of my private information and for contravening UK data protection laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: I made a long journey of 3,400 miles to be here because AI needs to be safe around our world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: But I note that SpaceX AI couldn't manage a trip of what I understand is just 20 minutes or four subway stops from their offices in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: It's a shame because the evidence in my case and other cases suggests that Grok was not built with sufficient safety in its design.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: It was not built to address consent of those subjected to sexualized content.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: To the contrary, the evidence in my claim suggests Croc added sexualized content without any user prompting to do so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: That is AI made wrong, not AI gone wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: And as a result, those responsible for its creation must be held to account.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: No one is above the law, no matter how rich they are, no matter how powerful they are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: The equal protection of the laws is a founding principle in the 14th Amendment, as it is in the British Magna Carta.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: We were promised that artificial intelligence could hold the cure to cancer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: Yet it is turning into a cancer which left unchecked has the potential to harm us all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: Today, the New York City Council is bringing forward some important checks and balances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: You do so as responsible legislators at a time when AI companies are failing to take responsibility for the design and impact of their products.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: Until they do, and until those designs are corrected so women and girls are protected from the harm that my claim and others'evidence is, we must play our part.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: This technology does not respect...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: geographic boundaries, and without international cooperation, our citizens will be left defenseless against those who put profit before protection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: So I bring a message of bipartisan solidarity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: I fight my legal action in the name of all the women and children whose likeness was misused by Grok and other AI tools built without their protection in mind.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: I hope my cause in some way helps to inform your proceedings today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jess Asato
utterances.text: And I look forward to your questions.

chapters.summary: Assemblymember Alex Bores, RAISE Act author, says OpenAI opposed the bill from introduction to signature and suggests the Council should be extremely angry at the company's testimony. He urges the Council to build muscle against AI company lobbying and note that New York City is larger than 38 states.
chapters.title: Alex Bores says OpenAI lied under oath about RAISE Act support

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Assemblyman Boris.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: Chair De La Rosa, Speaker Menon, members of the City Council, thank you for having us today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: I'm the author of the RAISE Act, and I can definitively say that OpenAI opposed it from the moment it was introduced to the moment it was signed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: I am no lawyer, but to me, my common man understanding of lying under oath is that it's perjury.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: And at the very least, you should be extremely angry at the company for disrespecting this council and saying things they know to be false to you directly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: I'm very happy to cooperate with you or any of your lawyers if you want more information about what they said and when.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: Second,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: There have been a discussion of a lot of different issues today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: We can and should solve all of them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: In my time in the Assembly, I passed the RAISE Act on catastrophic risk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: I also worked with Senator Gonzalez on a bill on chatbots.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: I worked with Senator Gernardis on a bill on content provenance and training data transparency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: And I found that the advocates that I worked with on each sub-issue were different, but the opposition was always the same.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: Don't let the tech companies, don't let the AI companies divide us and say that in advocating for one issue, you're somehow harming advocacy for another issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: What we are doing is building the muscle to hold them accountable and to ensure that it's the American people who decide the future of this most important technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: Third, the time for voluntary commitments is over.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: The voluntary commitments that were signed at the White House last week largely mirror voluntary commitments that were signed in 2023 in the Biden White House.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: Promises have been made.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: It is time for laws to hold people accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: And lastly, thank you, New York City, for stepping into your power.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: There's going to be a lot online from the tech companies about how they can't comply with different cities doing all these different things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: It's the argument they use every time you try to regulate them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: But New York City is larger than 38 states.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: All of the companies have large offices here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: It is absolutely within your power, and I dare say your responsibility, to take these threats seriously and to help decide the future of this technology to benefit all of us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: So thank you for recognizing that, and thank you for doing it.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you all so much.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We've also been joined by Senator Gernardis on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Senator, when you're ready.

chapters.summary: State Senator Andrew Gounardes, RAISE Act Senate sponsor, quotes James Madison's Federalist 51 and argues government exists because humans are imperfect. He says the tech companies cannot be trusted to regulate themselves and that New York must set guardrails given federal inaction.
chapters.title: Senator Andrew Gounardes urges state and city AI guardrails

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Thank you very much, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I'm sorry I can't be there with you in person, but two out of my three children are homesick today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Therefore, I am playing doctor at home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I want to thank Speaker Menon and the members of the New York City Council for the opportunity to testify before you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I'm State Senator Andrew Gernardis from Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And I am the Senate sponsor of the Responsible AI Safety and Education, or RAISE Act, one of only three AI safety laws passed anywhere in this country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And, you know, we've heard a lot about the RAISE Act already.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: We've heard a lot about AI safety throughout this really remarkable hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I've been listening to a good portion of it all day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I really want to reflect on the fact that we're celebrating the nation's 250th anniversary this year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And I want us to think about a quote that comes from one of our founding fathers, James Madison.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Who wrote in Federalist No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: 51, if men were angels, no government would be necessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: In other words, government exists because humans are imperfect, and there are certain problems that the free market or individuals left to their own devices cannot solve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: In these past few weeks, we have seen and heard headline after terrifying headline after terrifying headline about AI agents hacking websites, catastrophic risks of frontier AI models, and the like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And I just keep coming back to the imperative of Madison's words that men are not angels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And what I think this tells us, and what I think you have heard very clearly today at this hearing, is that we cannot trust

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: the tech companies who are racing to the bottom to create and perfect a technology that they themselves say and have proven can cause catastrophic harms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: To regulate themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: That we cannot

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: trust that they will do the right thing because they have proven time and time and time again that they will always, when confronted with the choice of doing the right thing or doing what is in the best interest of their own

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: bottom line, that they will always choose to pursue the bottom line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And so my message to the council today is I thank you all for taking on this initiative, for trying to hold these companies accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I echo the comments of my RAISE co-sponsor, Assemblymember Boras.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: What we heard from OpenAI today was certainly news to me that they endorsed and supported the RAISE Act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Certainly not the RAISE Act that would have prevented them from releasing models that they knew were dangerous and could cause catastrophic harms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Certainly the RAISE Act version that required third-party auditing capabilities or extended liabilities for harms caused by their models.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Clearly, none of that was ever on the table when they so said that they had supported this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: We cannot trust these companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: The federal government is failing in its responsibility to take meaningful action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And so therefore, it's left to states like New York to be leaders in this space and work with partners like the New York City Council under all of your collective leadership to make sure that we are setting in place the right guardrails and protections,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: not only to protect New Yorkers from the catastrophic risks that are associated with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: These this AI technology, but frankly, to protect all of us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: all Americans, and everyone worldwide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Because we know that these harms will not be localized.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: We know that the scale of what's being developed will not just limit itself to one block, one borough, one city, one state.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: It'll affect everyone the world over.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And in the face of inaction, it's up to us to stand up and act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And so I thank you all for your attention to this and your support of this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And look forward to work with you all in the future on strengthening things like the RAISE Act so that we can actually hold these companies accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa thanks the state and international panel, emphasizing state-city partnership as the first line of defense and thanking MP Asato for her vulnerability. Speaker Menin also thanks the officials for their legislation and expertise.
chapters.title: De La Rosa and Menin thank state officials panel

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Senator.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We have a few questions for this panel, but I wanted to take a moment to thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: You know, we do believe that city and state government have to work hand in hand, and we have to be the first line of defense in order to make sure that New Yorkers are protected.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And each and every one of you has been such an important partner in making that accountability a reality on the state level.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And to the Member of Parliament, thank you for sharing your story and your vulnerability and moving from that experience to action to hold these companies accountable.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: My colleagues do have some questions for you all, but before we do that, speaking of questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I just want to thank all of our incredible elected officials for being here today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We know how hard you've all worked on various legislation, and we really appreciate it so much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And your expertise on this, and particularly in terms of the RAISE Act, we really appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's very helpful to have you here and to hear directly from you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you for waiting it out with us.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We so appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We are going to hear from Councilmember Osei, followed by Gutierrez, Deputy Speaker Williams, and then Councilmember Hanif.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Chi Osse asks Bores why RAISE Act penalties were reduced from $10-30 million to $1-3 million. Bores says companies argued they'd pay fines in every state; he disagrees and says the small fines won't change behavior. Gonzalez describes DSA organizing and data center harms.
chapters.title: Osse asks Bores about RAISE Act fine reductions

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: I have a question for Assemblymember Boris.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: We heard today from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta that they supported the RAISE Act but felt like they wanted stronger regulations.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: But we know that during negotiations for New York State's RAISE Act, there was a push to lower penalties from $10 million to $30 million to $1 million to $3 million, which is chump change for these corporations.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Why were the fines in the RAISE Act reduced from $10 to $30 million to only $1 to $3 million?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: Council member, thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: In the early drafts of the RAISE Act, the penalties were up to $10 million for the first violation, and of course that would be based on the severity of the violation, and up to $30 million for a second violation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: The companies argued that that was too high because they were predicting that every state and perhaps municipalities would pass similar versions of the bill

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: and they would end up paying the fine in 50 states plus in additional municipalities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: I disagreed at the time with that argument.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: I think that's been borne out since we've seen only three states.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: to pass it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: But perhaps what's most confusing to me is that now they turn around and say that no other state should pass bills like this or that no city should pass bills like this because they're already paying the fines.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: Their rhetoric, their testimony was explicit that they are expecting to pay fines in many, many jurisdictions for the same action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: And so I think that testimony is quite supportive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: Of the bills that are being put forward today that would hold them accountable and put additional fines on behavior, even if it is covered by the RAISE Act, because again, that was their own testimony as to why those fines should be lowered.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: And Senator Gonzalez, I would love to hear from you about some of the organizing that you've been doing, especially within the New York City Democratic Socialists of America, around AI regulation and the vision that is being put forward within that regard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: As a fellow member of the Democratic Socialists of America, one thing I spoke about in my testimony was prioritizing a rights-based approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: I think it is so important to put New Yorkers first by clarifying and setting the terms for what our digital rights should be over the profit-driven motives of so many of these tech companies and tech oligarchs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: That's why we've worked hard on the New York AI Act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: We've certainly supported legislation on frontier models and reining them in, but New Yorkers who are marginalized are feeling the impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: of imperfect tools every single day, and I'm proud that the Tech Action Working Group has focused on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: In addition, I've worked with a statewide coalition beyond the Democratic Socialists of America, but that include environmental justice organizations like Food and Water Watch and more that are in the fight against hyperscale data centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: Because as we're talking about the real world harms that are being felt and the potential catastrophic risks,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: Every single day, people in upstate New York, in the Capital Region, in the Hudson Valley, are feeling what it means to live near a hyperscale data center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: There are millions of gallons of water being pulled from our state's lakes right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: Communities are dealing with noise pollution and air pollution right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: And it's really important to legislate not only the risks, but legislate those data center-driven harms.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you both.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Councilmember Gutierrez.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Jennifer Gutierrez asks MP Asato what guardrail could have prevented her deepfake harms, and asks Senator Gonzalez what she felt hearing the companies.
