Asato describes UK data protection law and non-consensual intimate imagery criminalization; Gonzalez expresses frustration at companies speaking out of both sides of their mouths.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks Asato on possible guardrails and Gonzalez on company testimony

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Senator from London, I'm sorry, I didn't catch your name.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony and for educating us on the volatility of this tech company.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I know you're in process right now, but could you share a little bit about legislatively what you think, if existed, if in place,

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: a guardrail, what could have in any way prevented what happened.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: been to you?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How can we, whether the state or the city, legislate specifically to objectifying and potentially images that include sexual harm to people?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What have you learned or have you seen that we can potentially legislate?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And then I just had one more question for Senator Gonzalez.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I love hearing you talk about your disdain for data centers.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Can you share for a minute afterwards just what you were feeling hearing some of these tech companies during their testimony.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: I'll try to be brief.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: Within the UK, we already have data protection and privacy laws, which is the basis under which I'm bringing my claim.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And of course, we're going to test that in court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: But clearly, if your image and your likeness forms part of your data,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: the making sure that everybody has that aspect understood by AI companies could mean that they would then have to treat our likeness and our data differently in future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: But also the UK government has recently made the sort of generation of non-consensual intimate imagery a criminal offence and as part of that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: has brought the operation of AI chatbots into our online safety act so that our regulator Ofcom can also make sure that if

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: an AI company is allowing users to create non-consensual intimate imagery, that that is a criminal sort of act happening on their platform.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And so it gives it more of an ability to be taken down.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: But from my own perspective, it's about consent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: In the end, whether it is non-consensual intimate imagery or just non-consensual imagery,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: If we haven't consented to it, then it shouldn't be allowed to do it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I just want to interject and thank you so much for coming.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, to...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: come, you know, as far as you travel to be here personally to testify, it really means a lot to us and we deeply appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: And thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: Again, I think this is a great segue to the fact that there are international safety standards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: So much of the work that I've done has been to call out the fact that there are not only standards like ISO 42001

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: or national standards like the RISC-AI framework that these companies could comply with, but actively lobby against bills that would require them to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: And to the council member's question and what I was feeling, I was feeling so much of the same frustration that my colleagues on this panel expressed earlier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: These companies are speaking out of both sides of their mouths.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: On the one hand, they'll say that they want regulation, but any time a single bill that would meaningfully hold them to account is brought in front of them, they will say, but not like that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: When we talk about catastrophic risks, many of the bills that have been put forward, and even what the state had passed, for example, had set definitions at 100 deaths or billions of dollars of damage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: Even that was considered too low of a threshold for many of these AI companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: And bills like the one that I mentioned that protects our kids, that seeks to say that a single kid being coached to commit suicide, which has actively happened in multiple...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: cases across the country, is one kid too many, is considered unacceptable to these tech companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: So I feel an incredible amount of frustration while I feel an incredible amount of hope seeing you not only have this hearing, but all of us as legislators step up to meet the moment and regulate and rein in these tech companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kristen Gonzalez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Deputy Speaker Williams, followed by Councilmember Hanif and then Maloney.

chapters.summary: Deputy Speaker Nantasha Williams asks how city and state officials can help each other. Vanel emphasizes coordination; Gounardes says state legislators need Council members' voices in Albany; Bores suggests sharing notes with the EU and engaging in the governor's budget process.
chapters.title: Williams asks state officials how city can support their work

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, I also just wanted to thank you all for coming.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So the question I have for the state members is how can we be helpful?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I know that there are a ton of resolutions that are supporting state bills.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It would be helpful just to let us know how we can be helpful and how we can work more closely together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: Well, Deputy Speaker, thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: Thank you for asking that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: What's really important is this step toward this hearing and this step towards this is very important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: You know, it's a big deal that you guys are having this hearing calling the, you know, the industry here and the different panels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: We have to work on it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: Now, this is hard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: This is difficult.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: But we have to work on it head on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: And what's very important is for us to be able to coordinate our efforts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: To see that, you know, we have a good relationship with many of the members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: I have a great relationship with the chair of technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: It's very important for us to be able to work on this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: And there are many layers to addressing this technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: And we touched on a lot of them today, but we have to work on this together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Ditto, and I know how appealing Albany can be, so please come on up and help us as we're rallying for different pieces of legislation and hitting the pavement and getting hard at work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And I'll just chime in there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I think, you know, what we heard here today, what you all heard today was many of these companies basically speak out of both sides of their mouths about what they think the appropriate role of government to be is in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: So next year, when we're up in Albany trying to fight to pass all of these different laws and we're, you know, being bombarded by

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: tens of millions of dollars from these companies with lobbyists and ads and radio ads and text messages and everything, having your voices to go back into your communities and to come up to talk to our colleagues and say, hey, we held this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: They lied to us about X, Y, and Z, A, B, and C.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And like, here's the proof of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: This is where we can call these companies out when they're trying to have it both ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: You all experienced that firsthand and you being able to speak to that and remind the public about that time and time and time again

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: will only further to bolster the momentum that we have on our side to put in place these guardrails and protections, whether it's around bias or safety or any of the other issues that we've been talking about during this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: To follow on on the senator's comments, the companies say different things to different levels of government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: A few weeks ago, I was actually in Brussels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: I met with a few members of the European Parliament to talk about the passage of the EU AI Act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: And we compared what we were lobbied on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: Surprising to me, catastrophic risk didn't really come up in the EU, but they got a lot of lobbying around copyright.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: And my assumption is because they thought the courts are stronger on copyright in Europe, and so that's what they lobbied on there, and said very different things in America, in New York State.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: I imagine they're saying different things in Albany, as they will say here to you in the city council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: And we should all be sharing notes on what's being said and holding them to account and making sure that it's a consistent message.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: The other bit that I would add is the governor has signaled that she wants to strengthen the RAISE Act and put new proposals in her budget proposal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: Please be part of that conversation when the city council submits its budget requests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: Obviously, you should focus on the fiscal needs first and foremost, but the state budget tends to be a broad document.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: And if you have policy ideas that for some reason or another need state approval, think of that as another mechanism, another lever that you have to help ensure that you can do the best job for your constituents.

chapters.summary: Williams asks about state workforce legislation and about US deepfake law and international cooperation. Bores mentions Senator Gonzalez's workforce bill and pending deepfake and chatbot bills; Vanel describes recent deepfake laws and a new artist-impersonation issue; Asato explains gendered deepfake harms and consent-based approaches.
chapters.title: Williams questions officials on workforce bills and deepfake legislation

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Just two more quick questions.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I passed a bill and the chair has a bill on AI's impact on the municipal workforce.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Just wondering if there was any traction on that for the state's workforce.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And then just a question for the member of parliament.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: My bill that we're hearing today is to address unauthorized use of deepfakes.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So in addition to the privacy.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: laws and Britain just wanted to know if you all have specific legislation around deep fakes.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And how you envision the cooperation with the international community, because you mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And what does that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: We know that female elected representatives are 33 times more likely to be targeted by sexual deepfakes than men.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: The whole issue around sexualized deepfakes is deeply gendered, and I think it's very important that we acknowledge that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: Because what it does is it drives women from the public space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: We know that women are less likely to talk about politics online than men are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And that is because they become a target as soon as they raise their heads in this place, which is not social.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: That is why taking action on this is so important and to be commended in terms of looking at this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: But when we're looking at these deep fakes, it needs to be for all of our citizens because it's not just about protecting those of us who have the honour of being elected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: It is about co-workers who may be targeted because

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: they didn't smile at the right time or your last date who wouldn't go on a second date with you or teachers who are being targeted by their male students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: All of these people need protection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: That's why in the UK we have taken steps to make sure that there is the criminalization of the creation of non-consensual sexual deepfakes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: But my view is that we need to go further than just the sexualized deepfakes because any act could be harmful to women.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: The removal of a woman's hijab.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: Through AI could put that woman in harm's way, but there's nothing sexualized about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And so we have to look at this as an issue, as I said, of consent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And that is where data and privacy is so, so important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And that's where I think there could be international agreement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: We can see, as you said, that things are moving forward within the EU space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: Really, though, what we need is for tech companies to be safe by design.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And every single country has those rules.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: We should be looking at product regulation just as we do in the offline sphere.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: At the end of the day, we have cars that have seatbelts and they have airbags.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And that's because we expect them to be safe by design.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: It is not too much to expect that of the tech products that we use today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: On the question about the state workforce, I wish Senator Gonzalez could have heard that because she wrote the Loading Act, which helps to protect the state workforce.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: And I think there's an update to it pending before the governor, which leads me to you asking about deep fakes as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: There's a bill from Senator Granardis and I pending before the governor on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: Senator Gonzalez also mentioned chatbots to protect kids.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: There's a bill pending before the governor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: So I should have also added on ways you can help out is we are really happy to be here and advocate for the legislation you are putting forward and invite you, if you agree with some that's pending before the governor, to be a partner in pushing that as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: Yeah, we have a number of deepfake bills, and we passed actually a number of, a couple of my bills became law with respect to deepfakes, with respect to elections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: One of the new bills that just came out was just very recently, I discovered an artist that I fell in love with on Apple Music, and I downloaded all her music.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: I've been listening to her music for a while.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: I actually went to go look for her a couple of days ago to follow her to go to a concert or something like that, found out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: It's not a person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: So there's no law, there's no regulation at all for these platforms to tell you whether or not you're listening to a real person or not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: So, you know, the bill, so one of the things that we have to do is figure out what that looks like moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: So we're going to need your help on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Clyde Vanel
utterances.text: That's something that we're going to really need your help on.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, ask them specifically a question about it.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And it was very fluffy.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But I literally asked a question about that to the companies.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Menin tells MP Asato that SpaceX AI was the only invited company that refused to appear and has been subpoenaed, and asks for her reaction. Asato says it's a shame given her journey, looks forward to the subpoena outcome, and says elected representatives must hold AI companies accountable.
chapters.title: Menin asks MP Asato about SpaceX AI's subpoena defiance

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: One last question for Member of Parliament Asada.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you, as you may know, when we called this hearing, we sent letters to five companies, to Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, Google, and SpaceX AI.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: SpaceX AI is the only company that would not appear.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We have subpoenaed them.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Given your personal story, I just wanted to get your reaction to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: Well, as I said in my opening statements, it's a huge shame given that they are so close and I have come so far.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: But in the end, you've subpoenaed them and we look forward to seeing what then happens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: In the end, everybody should be accountable to elected representatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And you're very powerful here in the city of New York because of the fact that these companies are based here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And therefore, those of us who are in other countries across the world are looking to you to hold these companies to account.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And we very much look forward to doing so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: I will do my own part in terms of my legal action in the UK.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Council Member Haneef, followed by Maloney.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Shahana Hanif asks MP Asato to speak on gender justice in AI. Asato says the online space was developed without social norms and mostly by men, and that when women and minorities decide not to participate online, they lose their freedom of speech.
chapters.title: Hanif asks MP Asato about gender justice in AI systems

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, and thank you to the Member of Parliament.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Your experience really shows how generative AI can be weaponized against women, queer people, trans people, and particularly those of us in public life.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I'm super, super grateful that you're using your platform as a legislator centering gender justice and tech surveillance.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I think all day it's in this panel that we're really able to tease into that particular issue, which is devastating.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: There are so many survivors of AI-generated sexual abuse who have no recourse.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I know we touched on several components of this issue in terms of legislation and policy.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Could you speak more broadly about gender justice as it comes to AI systems?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I mean, certainly we're going to be regulating these systems, but the responsibility that

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: our communities have in addition to, of course, as legislators passing stronger regulations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: I think that one of the issues here is that the whole of the online space has been developed without the sort of social norms that we would actually expect of each other in our offline world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And therefore, when it comes to gender justice, as you talk about it, that is ignored because actually the Internet and these platforms were created by men.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: In the main, they were not shaped by women, they were not shaped with children in mind.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And therefore we're having to try to reverse decades now of a wild west of development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: But that doesn't mean that it's impossible to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And I think we're seeing that actually our communities are actually fighting back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And one of the things that has been really sort of fantastic in terms of my own case is the number of people coming forward saying, I'm so glad that somebody somewhere is trying to stand up for those of us who think that this is wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And we don't want to live in this space where so many...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: many people are being discriminated against.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: Having said that, of course, there are very, very strong, you know, sort of positions taken out there around freedom of speech.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And what I would say is, is that when

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: women and other minorities decide not to be in a space, they lose their freedom of speech.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: And I think it's something that we simply aren't recognizing enough, because freedom of speech should not be about the loudest voices, the ones who have the most money or the most power.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: Freedom of speech should be about all of us equally being able to be in these spaces on an equal basis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Sackman
utterances.text: So that's what I hope we're all fighting for today.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Councilmember Maloney.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Virginia Maloney asks about the RAISE Act's final penalties and what teeth it now has. Bores says penalties fell to $1-3 million partly due to companies' arguments, and he wishes the original amounts had held; Gounardes notes the new Digit Office's role in proposing stronger future rules.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about the RAISE Act's enforcement teeth

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you all for being here.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: A special welcome to my state colleagues who also represent the constituents of District 4, Assemblymember Alex Perez and State Senator Gonzalez, who was here before.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And I also want to thank you for your work in Albany to pass the RAISE Act.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Because of you, New York was the first in the nation to pass a frontier AI safety bill that went into law.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: But I wanted to ask about the process.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The original bill had penalties of $10 million up to $30 million.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And the final version is looking more like $1 million to $3 million.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: These companies are able to spend millions of dollars training models.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: What teeth does this bill actually have now as law?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And can you speak to why those fines were reduced?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Open to anyone who'd like to comment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: Those fines were reduced because the companies insisted that they would be paying similar fines in every municipality and every state because obviously every state municipality would pass a copycat law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: The fact that here we are and there are three states that have passed such a law suggests that they significantly underestimated their own lobbying power, but also I think gives credence to the effort of what you are doing here at TEDx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: today of holding them accountable and that multiple municipalities and jurisdictions should do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: One to three million dollars is nothing for these companies, absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: It's about what they are going to pay just to register in New York to the digit office that will be regulating them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: Depending on the number of companies that qualify, it'll be one to two million dollars.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: So that is not an amount that provides an incentive strong enough to change behavior.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Bores
utterances.text: Maybe private rights of action, maybe whistleblower protections, maybe requiring outside audits, maybe a lot of the things that this council is considering will, but certainly a million to three million won't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I'll just add to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: I totally agree with what a submember Boris said.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: The one, I think, novel thing about the digit office that we created as part of the RAISE Act is that we empowered the state regulator to not only receive the safety reports and the safety plans of these companies and to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: assess the validity and the legitimacy of those reports, but also we empower them to propose and study the issue of continuing improvement to our AI safety laws

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: so that we develop the expertise over time about how we can make our laws like the RAISE Act stronger.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: So today, that function does not do anything currently, but it is our hope and our expectation that as the RAISE Act is implemented,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: As the changes to this technology become more evident, we develop a deeper state-based, you know, as an administrative state expertise

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: in this field to be able to propose far-reaching and ambitious guardrails for the next iteration and the next iteration after that and not have to rely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: on, as we did early on, hearing from companies about what they could or could not do and not have sufficient, for lack of a better word, firepower behind us to always be able to answer back in a way that would be able to win over our critics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And so the digital office in the future should have this ability to play a much larger role than it currently does.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Gounardes
utterances.text: And I certainly look forward to seeing that come to fruition as we see the law be further implemented.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa thanks the state officials panel and calls the next hybrid panel including Eli Dorkin, Corrine Worthington, Noelle Hidalgo, Neil Getnick, Gabe Weil, Andrew Reich, and Matt Henning of TechNYC.
chapters.title: De La Rosa calls hybrid business and policy panel

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: All right, well, thank you all again for being here and for taking the time and for your patience.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We're gonna call up the next panel.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Eli Dorkin, Corrine Worthington, Noelle Hidalgo, Neil Getnick, Gabe Weil, and Andrew Reich.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And again, if I mess up your names, correct it for the record, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And Matt Henning, TechNYC, please join this panel as well.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Matt, you can begin.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Identify yourselves for the record just so we know who you are, and you can begin when you're ready.

chapters.summary: Matt Henning of TechNYC speaks on behalf of startups that build on frontier models. He warns that city-level AI rules would hold non-frontier deployers liable for things out of their control and that a city-by-city patchwork could force startups to leave New York City.
chapters.title: TechNYC's Matt Henning warns against city-level AI patchwork

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: Good evening, Speaker Menon, Chair De La Rosa, and members of the Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: My name is Matt Henning, and I'm the Director of Government Affairs at TechNYC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: Thank you for the invitation to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: TechNYC's Frontier AI members already testified today, and we fully support their testimony and are proud to call them TechNYC members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: Today, I want to use my time to speak for the rest of our membership, the startups and businesses that build products on top of Frontier models rather than create them themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: New York's tech ecosystem has never been stronger.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: According to a recent CBRE report, New York is now the largest tech talent market in North America, passing the Bay Area for the first time in the report's 13-year history.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: That momentum isn't guaranteed, and the messaging that the city government sends matters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: That's why I was happy to hear Speaker Menon's comments to that effect in her opening remarks and hope the final language of this packet

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: package

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: aligns with that intent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: Our biggest concern is that this package holds non-frontier companies liable for things out of their control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: Most AI startups and many larger non-frontier companies have a frontier model under the hood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: The difference between a deployer and a developer is something I want to highlight when thinking about the various requirements and liabilities this package imposes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: Under the third-party validation bill, a startup can't deploy that model unless the developer had it validated and assessed, which these downstream companies can't commission or even verify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: If the developer is found to not be in compliance, the startup's product becomes illegal overnight at $25,000 per instance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: The AI misuse, chatbot, and advertising bills follow the same pattern, and the civilian complaint bill multiplies the exposure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: Finally, AI safety standards are most effective at the international, federal, or multi-state level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: A city-by-city patchwork with different rules in each city would be a compliance nightmare that many startups and small businesses could not survive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: Not only for New York City HQ'd startups, but for non-New York City HQ'd startups that serve New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: As drafted, we are truly worried this would result in startups not choosing, but being forced to leave New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: We strongly urge the Council to engage experts at both frontier and non-frontier companies when moving forward with this package to ensure drastic negative unintended consequences are avoided.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: ECNYC stands at the ready to help facilitate those conversations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Andrew Rasiej, founder of Civic Hall, describes a 'new digital divide' between people who understand AI and those it happens to. He calls for a citywide free AI literacy campaign and public-good AI infrastructure with sovereign computing power separate from the major AI companies.
chapters.title: Andrew Rasiej calls for NYC AI literacy campaign and public AI infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: Chair De La Rosa and members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: My name is Andrew Richet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: Nearly 30 years ago, I founded Mouse.org to bring the internet to New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: More recently, I founded Civic Hall at Union Square, the city's largest digital skills training center serving underestimated New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: New Yorkers are scared by the reports that some AI models evaded human control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: I understand why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: But most people can't tell you how a chatbot works, what it does with their data, or how a deepfake gets made.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: They know enough to be alarmed, but not enough to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: And that's the new digital divide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: People who understand AI on one side and people it happens to on the other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: I'm asking the council to act on two fronts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: First, pass legislation requiring the city to launch a free AI literacy campaign for every New Yorker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: Teach people how to protect their jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: AI won't take your job.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: A person who knows how to use AI will.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: Teach families that when grandma gets a call from her grandson's voice asking for money, it may not be him.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: And help small businesses because AI has made phishing and fraud cheaper and more convincing, and the corner store isn't ready.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: Finland built a free public course for more than 2 million people, which more than 2 million people have taken, and it's reached 170 countries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: During COVID, the city reached every resident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: We can do it again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: Fear of AI is not a substitute for comprehension.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: Second, the only real way to stop bad AI is to build good AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: Right now, it's being built by a handful of companies answerable to their shareholders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: The organizations responsible for the public good are nonprofits, community groups, and city agencies are years behind.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: Most can't afford the computing power, and their staff haven't been trained to use these tools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: When the big AI companies offer nonprofits free computing power, it comes on their terms, with the organization's data sitting on their servers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: Public good AI needs sovereign computing power separate from the companies whose business depends on gathering data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: I helped start the foundation for Civic Eye, which offers a supercomputer to the public interest at no cost.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: Few of them have the staff who know how to use it, so investing in public AI infrastructure is a mission that this council should take up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Rasiej
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Neil Getnick, managing partner of Getnick Law with over $1.5 billion recovered in whistleblower cases, gives six recommendations on Intro 2605: set a threshold, set a 15-30% reward range, no caps, public-private partnership, anonymity protections, and clarity in drafting.
chapters.title: Whistleblower attorney Neil Getnick offers six recommendations on Intro 2605

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: Good evening, I'm Neil.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: Oh, there you are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: Good evening, I'm Neil Getnick, the managing partner of Manhattan-based Getnick Law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: Our whistleblower cases have recovered over $1.5 billion for federal, state, and local governments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: Including over $100 million for New York State and New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: Intro number 2605 provides for rewards resulting from recoveries

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: arising from whistleblower complaints alleging that a person or entity has violated legal provisions related to artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: Speaking from my area of whistleblower expertise, I will highlight six key elements relevant to these legislative proposals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: First, threshold, setting a threshold qualifying amount for a reward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: Second, floor and ceiling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: Typically, the range of rewards is set between 15 to 30%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: Third, no caps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: Beyond the percentage limits, there should be no cap on the size of the award, maximizing incentivization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: Fourth, public-private partnership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: The government agency and the whistleblower and council should work together to maximize the recovery.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: Fifth, emphasizing anonymity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: The government should do all that it can to preserve the whistleblowers'anonymity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: Sixth, perhaps most importantly for this council, clarity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: In passing artificial intelligence laws, you will be taking on powerful and well-resourced individuals and entities who will push back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: So ask yourselves, are these laws clear?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: And then do what's necessary to accomplish that at the drafting stage rather than leaving it to the courts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: In conclusion, the legislative proposals before you are an opportunity for the city of New York to lead the way in safeguarding citizens from the potential risks of artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: And in doing so,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Neil Getnick
utterances.text: This council will light the way for the nation as a whole.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Henning
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Professor Gabriel Weil of the University of Houston identifies a liability gap: AI agents aren't legal persons, so no one can be liable when they commit torts or crimes. He proposes that whenever an AI agent does what would be a tort or crime for a human, the developer bears liability if no downstream actor was at fault.
chapters.title: Gabriel Weil proposes developer liability for AI agent harms

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker Menon and Chair De La Rosa.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: I'm Gabriel Weil.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: I'm a law professor at the University of Houston and a fellow at the Institute for Law and AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: And I want to talk to you about what I see as the largest gap in the existing liability law

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: that is not addressed by your legislative package, which is that AI agents could engage in conduct that would be a tort or even a crime for a human.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: and yet no one could be liable under current law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: And that is a consequence of two relevant features of our legal system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: One is that AI agents are not legal persons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: They do not have tort duties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: And that means not only that they can't be held liable, but that their principals cannot be held vicariously liable in the way that an employer is held liable for the torts of their employees within the scope of employment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: And second, the regimes that do apply to these harms, negligence and products liability, have important gaps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: They are inadequate to motivate some of the key precautionary measures that would prevent these kinds of incidents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: And so what I propose is a simple fix, a principle that whenever an AI agent engages in conduct that would be a tort or a crime for a human, someone's liable for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: And so if neither the user nor any intermediary that fine-tuned or scaffolded the model

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: either intended or was negligent with respect to the conduct, so no downstream actor was at fault, then the buck should stop with the developer, and they should be liable regardless of the degree of care they exercised.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: I have worked on legislation to this effect that's been introduced in New York State and in Rhode Island, and I'm talking to several congressional offices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: My written testimony, which will be submitted probably tomorrow, includes proposed legislative text for New York, and I'm happy to answer any questions about that or about any other liability issues, including the legislation that's in the package.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gabriel Weil
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sam Wheeler, executive director of the Writers Guild of America East, describes AI as a key subject in every negotiation and notes a 148-day strike won protections stating AI cannot be a writer under their contract. He argues the public wants news and entertainment written by humans, not AI slop.
chapters.title: WGA East's Sam Wheeler on AI and creative work protections

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: My name is Sam Wheeler, and I'm the executive director of the Writers Guild of America East.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: We are a union of more than 7,000 writers and creators working in film, television, broadcast news, nonfiction television, and digital media.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: Most of the film and television you watch and much of the news you consume is likely produced by Guild members, either our members or the members of our sibling union, the Writers Guild of America West.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: At the outset, I would like to thank Speaker Menon, along with Chair De La Rosa, for convening this whole council hearing on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: Our members are fundamentally storytellers, journalists, and reporters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: They are the people that others turn to to help them understand our increasingly complex and frightening world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: Guild members take that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: Responsibility seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: For most, their work is both a craft and a calling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: AI is of significant concern to our members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: It is a key subject in almost every negotiation we have with our employers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: With very limited exceptions, AI is almost always the last point of contention in bargaining.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: Making gains almost always requires a strike vote, and we rarely get everything that we need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: In 2023, it took a 148-day strike to win the first AI protections in Hollywood, protections that plainly state that AI cannot be a writer under our contract.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: When our members engage in collective activity to address AI, they're fighting not just for themselves, but for their audiences, their readers, and our democracy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: Because we believe that the public wants news written by human journalists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: who can contextualize events, who can verify facts and check that sources are credible, who live in the same physical world as their readers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: They want movies and television shows written by a diverse group of other human beings who can take their real lived experience and turn those experiences into stories that tell universal truths.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: We have a fundamental disagreement with the tech industry on this point.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: They seem to think that what people want is AI-generated slop, content that is so generic that no one would ever bother asking who conceived of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: Because even at its best, AI content...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sam Wheeler
utterances.text: Time's expired.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: It's an important testimony.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Please submit it for the record.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We're going to call Gary Marcus, who is back on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Gary, if you're on, please unmute yourself and begin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: You hear me?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Yes, we hear you, Gary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: My name is Gary Marcus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: I'm a scientist, author, and NYU professor emeritus who co-founded an AI startup that was acquired by Uber.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: My sub stack, Marcus on AI, has about 120,000 subscribers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: On X, I have about 250,000 followers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: I'm frequently in the media, often described as a leading AI expert and voice of reason.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: We stand at a pivotal moment in history.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: New York City has a chance to improve our chances, both for itself and the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: Contemporary AI is like a bull in a china shop, powerful and impressive, but difficult to control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: Already the advocate...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: The advent of general purpose agents with broad internet access has led to tens of thousands of hacking incidents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: Other related technologies like deep fakes and chatbots implicated in suicides and even mass murder have caused other problems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: It is clear by now that AI comes with serious risks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: It's also clear that the current administration in DC, deeply tied to the big tech companies, is unwilling to do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: What we need above all else is an FDA-like regulatory regime for AI in which AI developers bring their software to independent review, much as drug manufacturers bring their new drugs to FDA for review.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: AI developers should be obligated to demonstrate that the benefits of their new products outweigh the risks and not have market access otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: I said the same to Louisiana Senator Kennedy in May 2023 at the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: Senate, and it's still true, but the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: Senate did nothing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: New York City is thus in a position to do what the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: Senate failed to do, demand independent regulatory review for AI used in its borders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: The bill on third-party validation proposes to do just that, and it would protect New York citizens from some of the harms of AI and could allow New York to be a global leader, much as California has been a global leader around clean energy standards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: In the strongest possible terms, I urge Council to support this bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: Finally, events of recent days suggest OpenAI may have fired employees who were whistleblowing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: Without strong protections from whistleblowing, like New York City is considered...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gary Marcus
utterances.text: Your time's expired.

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.text: I can take one percent.

chapters.summary: Mayu Tobin-Miyagi, attorney at EPIC, says AI companies should not release uncontrollable products and avoid liability. She points to ongoing harms including surveillance pricing and worker surveillance, and supports Intros 2599 and 2600 on chatbot liability and private rights of action.
chapters.title: EPIC's Mayu Tobin-Miyagi supports chatbot liability and private right of action

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mayu Tobin-Miyagi
utterances.text: Good evening, Speaker Menon and members of the Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mayu Tobin-Miyagi
utterances.text: My name is Mayu Tobin-Miyagi, and I'm an attorney at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, or EPIC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mayu Tobin-Miyagi
utterances.text: EPIC is an independent nonprofit organization established in 1994 to secure the right to privacy in a digital age.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mayu Tobin-Miyagi
utterances.text: Thank you to the council for organizing this hearing and putting the AI companies on the spot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mayu Tobin-Miyagi
utterances.text: There is no reason that AI companies should be able to release products that they cannot control and then avoid liability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mayu Tobin-Miyagi
utterances.text: Despite the hypothetical harms that receive attention, there are ongoing harms that are currently affecting New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mayu Tobin-Miyagi
utterances.text: The council should focus on holding AI companies liable beyond transparency measures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mayu Tobin-Miyagi
utterances.text: AI companies are deploying AI agents that seek as much sensitive data about its users as possible, training its AI models by default with questionable privacy practices and cybersecurity risks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mayu Tobin-Miyagi
utterances.text: Other harms include AI chatbots that produce false or dangerous outputs, businesses using surveillance pricing, or employers surveilling its workers for union campaigns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mayu Tobin-Miyagi
utterances.text: Some of the bills considered today would address some of those real harms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mayu Tobin-Miyagi
utterances.text: Intro 2599 would implement a version of the People First Chatbot Bill, which EPIC developed with Consumer Federation of America and Fair Play.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mayu Tobin-Miyagi
utterances.text: The bill would treat chatbots for what they are, products, and hold accountable the company

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mayu Tobin-Miyagi
utterances.text: that make them when they cause harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mayu Tobin-Miyagi
utterances.text: Intro 2600 would similarly impose common sense liability on AI companies with a private right of action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mayu Tobin-Miyagi
utterances.text: We support these bills and urge the council to ensure that there are sufficient enforcement resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mayu Tobin-Miyagi
utterances.text: We urge the council to prioritize these bills that address these harms that are already affecting New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mayu Tobin-Miyagi
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today and happy to answer any questions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Bryce Rogers of the RAD Collective describes AI as the product of millennia of human information transfer, arguing it feels alienating because companies trained on our collective achievement to out-compete and spy on us. He urges the Council to center constituent voices over executives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: I thank the council for leading the charge on local AI legislation by convening this historic hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: My name is Bryce Rogers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
utterances.text: I'm a resident of the 34th Council District.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bryce Rogers
